title: JAMB Use of English: Complete Guide to Word Classes and Their Grammatical Functions
excerpt: A comprehensive four-chapter lesson on the eight major word classes, their grammatical functions, sentence usage, and examination-focused examples for JAMB UTME candidates.

chapters.title: Introduction to Word Classes, Nouns and Pronouns
chapters.excerpt: Understand the classification of English words, types of nouns, and the correct use of pronouns in sentences.
chapters.content:
Chapter 1: Introduction to Word Classes, Nouns and Pronouns

English grammar is built around words that perform different functions in sentences. Every word belongs to a grammatical category according to its form, meaning, and function. These categories are called word classes or parts of speech.

Understanding word classes is important for JAMB Use of English because candidates are expected to identify grammatical patterns, understand how words function in sentences, and select appropriate expressions in different contexts.

★ Important Examination Principle

A word's grammatical class is not always determined by its spelling alone. Its function in the sentence is important. For example, the word "book" is a noun in "I bought a book" but a verb in "Please book a seat".

1.1 The Major Word Classes

The traditional classification of English words includes eight major word classes:

Word ClassMain FunctionExample
NounNames a person, place, thing or idea.Teacher, Lagos, table, honesty.
PronounReplaces a noun or noun phrase.He, she, they, it, who.
VerbExpresses an action, occurrence or state.Run, write, become, is.
AdjectiveDescribes or modifies a noun or pronoun.Beautiful, tall, intelligent.
AdverbModifies a verb, adjective, another adverb or an entire clause.Quickly, very, carefully.
PrepositionShows relationships between words, especially location, time and direction.In, on, under, between.
ConjunctionConnects words, phrases or clauses.And, but, because, although.
InterjectionExpresses sudden emotion or reaction.Oh!, Alas!, Hurray!

1.2 Nouns

A noun is a word used to name a person, animal, place, object, substance, quality, condition or idea.

Examples include:

  • Person: teacher, doctor, farmer, student.
  • Place: Abuja, Ibadan, school, market.
  • Animal: goat, lion, elephant, dog.
  • Object: computer, chair, telephone, book.
  • Quality or idea: wisdom, honesty, freedom, courage.

Types of Nouns

A. Proper Nouns

These are the specific names of particular people, places, organisations, institutions or events. They usually begin with capital letters.

  • Adeniyi lives in Ibadan.
  • Chinua Achebe wrote Things Fall Apart.
  • The University of Lagos is a higher institution.

B. Common Nouns

These are general names given to people, places, animals or things rather than specific individuals.

  • The girl bought a dress.
  • The teacher entered the classroom.
  • A farmer planted maize.

C. Collective Nouns

These refer to groups of people, animals or things considered as a unit.

  • A team of footballers.
  • A flock of birds.
  • A herd of cattle.
  • A committee of members.
  • A bunch of keys.

A collective noun may take a singular or plural verb depending on whether the group is considered as one unit or as individuals. British English commonly allows this distinction.

  • The committee has reached its decision. (The committee acts as one unit.)
  • The committee are divided in their opinions. (The members are considered individually.)

D. Abstract Nouns

These name qualities, feelings, states or ideas that cannot normally be touched or physically seen.

  • Love, kindness, poverty, happiness, bravery, justice and intelligence.

E. Material Nouns

These name substances or materials from which things are made.

  • Gold, silver, water, iron, wood, cotton and petroleum.

F. Countable and Uncountable Nouns

Countable nouns can be counted individually and have singular and plural forms. Uncountable nouns are not normally counted as separate units without a suitable measure or container.

Countable NounsUncountable Nouns
One chair, two chairs.Furniture.
One student, five students.Information.
Three books.Knowledge.
Two bottles.Water.
Several suggestions.Advice.
★ Common JAMB Grammar Trap

Words such as advice, information, furniture, equipment and luggage are generally uncountable in standard English. Avoid expressions such as "an advice" and "many informations". Use "a piece of advice" and "much information" instead.

1.3 Grammatical Functions of Nouns

A noun can perform different grammatical functions depending on its position and use in a sentence.

A. Subject of a Sentence: The noun performs the action or is the person or thing being discussed.

Example: The student answered the question.

B. Direct Object: The noun receives the action of a transitive verb.

Example: The teacher marked the scripts.

C. Indirect Object: The noun identifies the person or recipient for whom something is done or to whom something is given.

Example: The principal gave the students new textbooks.

D. Subject Complement: A noun may rename or identify the subject after a linking verb.

Example: Bola became a nurse.

E. Object of a Preposition: A noun may follow a preposition to complete its meaning.

Example: The boy sat beside the window.

1.4 Pronouns

A pronoun is a word used in place of a noun or noun phrase to avoid unnecessary repetition.

Example: Instead of saying "Mary said Mary would bring Mary's book", we can say "Mary said she would bring her book".

Types of Pronouns

A. Personal Pronouns

These refer to particular people or things. They may function as subjects or objects.

Subject FormObject FormPossessive Form
IMeMine
HeHimHis
SheHerHers
WeUsOurs
TheyThemTheirs
YouYouYours
ItItIts

B. Possessive Pronouns

These show ownership and can stand independently without a following noun.

  • This book is mine.
  • The house is theirs.
  • That bag is hers.

Compare: "This is my book" and "This book is mine". The word "my" is a possessive determiner because it comes before a noun; "mine" is a possessive pronoun.

C. Reflexive Pronouns

These refer back to the subject of the sentence.

  • I prepared myself for the examination.
  • She blamed herself for the mistake.
  • They introduced themselves.

D. Demonstrative Pronouns

These point to particular people or things.

  • This is my pen.
  • That belongs to my brother.
  • These are my books.
  • Those are our teachers.

E. Relative Pronouns

These introduce relative clauses and connect them to nouns or pronouns.

  • Who: The girl who won the prize is my sister.
  • Whom: The man whom we invited has arrived.
  • Whose: The student whose bag was stolen reported the incident.
  • Which: The book which I bought is interesting.
  • That: The food that she prepared was delicious.

F. Interrogative Pronouns

These are used to ask questions.

  • Who is at the door?
  • Whom did you invite?
  • Whose is this?
  • Which do you prefer?
  • What happened?

G. Indefinite Pronouns

These refer to people or things without identifying them specifically.

  • Everybody attended the meeting.
  • Someone has taken my phone.
  • Few were able to answer the question.
  • None of the candidates was absent.
★ Pronoun Selection Tip

Distinguish between subject pronouns and object pronouns. Say "John and I went to school" because the pronoun is part of the subject. Say "The teacher praised John and me" because it is part of the object.

chapters.title: Verbs and Their Types, Forms and Functions
chapters.excerpt: Study action verbs, linking verbs, auxiliary verbs, transitive and intransitive verbs, and finite and non-finite verb forms.
chapters.content:
Chapter 2: Verbs and Their Types, Forms and Functions

A verb is a word that expresses an action, an occurrence or a state of being. It is one of the most important parts of a sentence because it helps establish what the subject does, experiences or is.

Examples:

  • Action: The boy runs every morning.
  • Occurrence: The accident happened yesterday.
  • State: The students are ready.

2.1 Main Types of Verbs

A. Action Verbs

These describe physical or mental activities.

  • The farmer cultivates the land.
  • She believes the story.
  • The students solved the problem.

B. Linking Verbs

These connect the subject to a word or expression that describes or identifies it. They do not normally express an action performed by the subject.

  • The soup tastes delicious.
  • She became a doctor.
  • The candidates are confident.

Common linking verbs include be, become, seem, appear, feel, look, smell, sound, taste and remain. Some of these verbs can also function as action verbs in other contexts.

C. Auxiliary or Helping Verbs

These help main verbs form tenses, questions, negatives, passive constructions and other grammatical structures.

AuxiliaryFunctionExample
Be (am, is, are, was, were)Continuous forms and passive voice.She is reading.
Have (has, have, had)Perfect forms.They have arrived.
Do (do, does, did)Questions, negatives and emphasis.Did you attend?

D. Modal Auxiliary Verbs

Modals express ability, permission, possibility, obligation, advice, willingness or necessity.

ModalCommon MeaningExample
CanAbility or permission.She can swim.
CouldPast ability or polite request.Could you help me?
MayPermission or possibility.It may rain.
MightPossibility.He might come.
MustStrong obligation or logical necessity.You must obey the rules.
ShouldAdvice or expectation.You should study.
WillFuture reference or willingness.I will return.
WouldPolite requests or hypothetical situations.Would you like some water?
ShallOffers, suggestions or formal future reference.Shall we begin?
★ Modal Verb Rule

A modal auxiliary is normally followed by the base form of the main verb. Say "She can sing", not "She can sings". Say "They must go", not "They must to go".

2.2 Transitive and Intransitive Verbs

Transitive Verbs: These require an object to complete their meaning in the relevant use.

  • The boy kicked the ball.
  • Mary bought a new phone.
  • The teacher explained the lesson.

The words "the ball", "a new phone" and "the lesson" are objects receiving the actions of the verbs.

Intransitive Verbs: These do not take a direct object in their relevant use.

  • The baby slept.
  • The visitors arrived.
  • The old man laughed.

Some verbs can be transitive in one sentence and intransitive in another.

  • Transitive: She opened the door.
  • Intransitive: The door opened.

2.3 Finite and Non-Finite Verbs

Finite Verbs show tense and may agree with their subjects in person and number. They can form the main verb of an independent clause.

  • He works in Abuja.
  • They worked yesterday.
  • She is intelligent.

Non-Finite Verbs do not independently show tense or agree with the subject in the same way finite verbs do. Their major forms include infinitives, gerunds and participles.

A. Infinitives: The base form of a verb, commonly introduced by "to", although bare infinitives also occur.

  • I want to study.
  • She can dance.

B. Gerunds: The -ing form of a verb functioning as a noun.

  • Swimming is good exercise.
  • She enjoys reading.

C. Participles: Verb forms used in verb phrases or as modifiers.

  • Present participle: The crying baby needs attention.
  • Past participle: The broken window was replaced.
  • Verb phrase: The students are writing their examination.

2.4 Principal Forms of Verbs

Many English verbs have five principal forms: the base form, third-person singular present form, past form, past participle and -ing form.

BasePresent (He/She)PastPast Participle-ing Form
GoGoesWentGoneGoing
WriteWritesWroteWrittenWriting
EatEatsAteEatenEating
BreakBreaksBrokeBrokenBreaking
SpeakSpeaksSpokeSpokenSpeaking
StudyStudiesStudiedStudiedStudying
Important Verb Construction

The present perfect uses has/have + past participle. The past perfect uses had + past participle. The present continuous uses am/is/are + -ing form.

2.5 Common Verb Errors

IncorrectCorrectReason
She has went.She has gone.Present perfect requires a past participle.
He did not came.He did not come.Did is followed by the base verb.
They can sings.They can sing.Modal verbs take the base form.
I am knowing him.I know him.Know is normally a stative verb.

chapters.title: Adjectives and Adverbs: Types, Degrees and Functions
chapters.excerpt: Learn how adjectives describe nouns and how adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs.
chapters.content:
Chapter 3: Adjectives and Adverbs

3.1 Adjectives

An adjective is a word that describes, identifies or gives additional information about a noun or pronoun.

Examples:

  • The beautiful girl won the competition.
  • He bought a new car.
  • The examination was difficult.
  • She is intelligent.

Types of Adjectives

A. Descriptive Adjectives

These describe the quality, appearance, size, colour or condition of a noun.

  • A beautiful woman.
  • A tall building.
  • A difficult examination.
  • A red shirt.

B. Quantitative Adjectives

These indicate the amount or quantity of something.

  • There is little water in the bottle.
  • She has enough money.
  • We have much work to do.

C. Numeral Adjectives

These indicate number or order.

  • Three students were selected.
  • She came first in the examination.
  • He bought five books.

D. Demonstrative Determiners

These identify particular nouns by indicating nearness or distance.

  • This book is mine.
  • Those students are intelligent.
  • These houses are expensive.

In modern grammatical analysis, this, that, these and those are generally called demonstrative determiners when they come before nouns, and demonstrative pronouns when they stand alone.

E. Possessive Determiners

These indicate ownership before a noun.

  • My father is a teacher.
  • Her bag is missing.
  • Their house is beautiful.

3.2 Degrees of Comparison

Adjectives can express different degrees of quality or comparison. The three main degrees are positive, comparative and superlative.

PositiveComparativeSuperlative
TallTallerTallest
ShortShorterShortest
BeautifulMore beautifulMost beautiful
IntelligentMore intelligentMost intelligent
GoodBetterBest
BadWorseWorst
FarFarther/FurtherFarthest/Furthest
LittleLessLeast

Positive Degree: Expresses a quality without making a comparison.

Example: Ada is intelligent.

Comparative Degree: Compares two people or things. It commonly uses -er or more and is often followed by "than".

Example: Ada is more intelligent than Bisi.

Superlative Degree: Expresses the highest or lowest degree among three or more people or things.

Example: Ada is the most intelligent student in the class.

★ Avoid Double Comparison

Do not normally combine "more" with an adjective that already takes -er, or "most" with one that already takes -est. Say "more beautiful", not "more beautifuller"; say "the tallest", not "the most tallest".

3.3 Adverbs

An adverb is a word that modifies a verb, an adjective, another adverb or sometimes an entire sentence. It often tells us how, when, where, how often or to what extent something happens.

  • She sings beautifully. (Modifies the verb sings.)
  • The water is extremely cold. (Modifies the adjective cold.)
  • He runs very quickly. (Very modifies quickly.)
  • Fortunately, nobody was injured. (Modifies the whole statement.)

Types of Adverbs

A. Adverbs of Manner: Explain how an action is performed.

  • The girl spoke politely.
  • The driver drove carefully.
  • The baby slept peacefully.

B. Adverbs of Time: Explain when an action happens.

  • We shall leave tomorrow.
  • She arrived yesterday.
  • He is coming soon.

C. Adverbs of Place: Explain where an action happens.

  • Come here.
  • The children are playing outside.
  • She looked everywhere.

D. Adverbs of Frequency: Explain how often something happens.

  • He always attends lectures.
  • She sometimes visits her grandmother.
  • They rarely travel by air.

E. Adverbs of Degree: Indicate the extent or intensity of an action or quality.

  • The food is very delicious.
  • She is almost ready.
  • The students were quite excited.

3.4 Adjectives Versus Adverbs

A common grammatical problem is confusing adjectives with adverbs. Remember that adjectives generally modify nouns or pronouns, while adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs or clauses.

AdjectiveAdverb
She is a careful driver.She drives carefully.
He is a quick runner.He runs quickly.
She gave a beautiful speech.She spoke beautifully.
He is a good singer.He sings well.

3.5 Adverbs That Do Not End in -ly

Not every adverb ends in -ly. Some common adverbs have the same form as adjectives.

  • He runs fast. (Adverb.)
  • He is a fast runner. (Adjective.)
  • She works hard. (Adverb.)
  • She is a hard worker. (Adjective.)

Also distinguish between "hard" and "hardly". Hard can mean with great effort, while hardly usually means almost not.

  • He works hard to support his family.
  • He hardly eats breakfast. (He almost never eats breakfast.)
★ Important Word Distinction

Good is generally an adjective, while well is commonly an adverb. Say "She is a good student" and "She writes well". However, well can also function as an adjective meaning healthy, as in "I am well".

3.6 Position of Adverbs

Adverbs can appear in different positions depending on their type and the meaning intended.

  • Beginning: Yesterday, we visited our teacher.
  • Middle: She usually arrives early.
  • End: The children played outside.

Position can affect meaning, so candidates should pay attention to the relationship between an adverb and the word or expression it modifies.

chapters.title: Prepositions, Conjunctions, Interjections and Sentence Functions
chapters.excerpt: Understand the remaining major word classes, their correct usage, and how to identify their grammatical functions in sentences.
chapters.content:
Chapter 4: Prepositions, Conjunctions, Interjections and Sentence Functions

4.1 Prepositions

A preposition is a word that expresses a relationship between a noun or pronoun and another word in a sentence. Prepositions commonly indicate location, time, direction, movement, cause or relationship.

Examples:

  • The book is on the table.
  • She lives in Lagos.
  • We arrived at noon.
  • The students walked towards the examination hall.

Types of Prepositions

A. Prepositions of Place: Indicate the location of a person or thing.

  • The cat is under the chair.
  • The school is beside the hospital.
  • The ball is between the two boxes.
  • She lives in Abuja.

B. Prepositions of Time: Indicate when an event happens.

  • The meeting begins at 9 a.m.
  • We travelled on Monday.
  • He was born in 2008.
  • She studied during the night.

C. Prepositions of Direction or Movement: Indicate movement from one place to another.

  • They walked into the classroom.
  • The boy ran across the field.
  • She travelled from Ibadan to Lagos.
  • The bird flew over the building.

4.2 Common Preposition Combinations

Some verbs, adjectives and nouns are conventionally followed by particular prepositions. These combinations must be learnt through usage.

ExpressionCorrect Example
Interested inShe is interested in medicine.
Good atHe is good at mathematics.
Afraid ofThe child is afraid of dogs.
Depend onSuccess may depend on preparation.
Listen toPlease listen to the teacher.
Consist ofThe committee consists of ten members.
Prefer toI prefer tea to coffee.
Married toShe is married to a doctor.
Comply withEveryone must comply with the rules.
Congratulate onWe congratulated him on his success.
★ Common Preposition Error

Avoid saying "discuss about the matter" when discuss is used with a direct object. The correct expression is "discuss the matter". Also say "enter the room", not "enter into the room" when simply referring to going inside.

4.3 Conjunctions

A conjunction is a word that joins words, phrases or clauses. It helps establish relationships such as addition, contrast, choice, reason, result and condition.

Types of Conjunctions

A. Coordinating Conjunctions

These join grammatical units of equal importance. The common coordinating conjunctions are remembered through the mnemonic FANBOYS.

ConjunctionFunctionExample
ForIntroduces a reason.He stayed indoors, for it was raining.
AndAddition.She bought rice and beans.
NorJoins negative alternatives.He did not call, nor did he send a message.
ButContrast.She is poor but honest.
OrChoice or alternative.Would you like tea or coffee?
YetContrast or unexpected result.He is young, yet very responsible.
SoResult or consequence.It was late, so we left.

B. Subordinating Conjunctions

These introduce subordinate clauses and show relationships such as time, reason, condition, purpose and contrast.

  • Because: We stayed indoors because it was raining.
  • Although: Although he was tired, he continued working.
  • When: Call me when you arrive.
  • If: If you study hard, you may succeed.
  • Unless: You will not pass unless you prepare.
  • While: She cooked while he washed the plates.
  • Since: Since you are ready, we can begin.

C. Correlative Conjunctions

These occur in pairs and connect related grammatical structures.

PairExample
Either...orEither John or Peter will attend.
Neither...norNeither the teacher nor the students were ready.
Both...andBoth Ada and Bisi passed.
Not only...but alsoShe is not only intelligent but also hardworking.
Whether...orI do not know whether he will come or stay.
Rather...thanShe would rather read than watch television.

4.4 Interjections

An interjection is a word or short expression used to communicate a sudden feeling, emotion or reaction. It often stands independently from the grammatical structure of the sentence.

InterjectionEmotion or MeaningExample
Oh!Surprise or understanding.Oh! I did not know that.
Alas!Sorrow or grief.Alas! The old man is dead.
Hurray!Joy or celebration.Hurray! We won the match.
Ouch!Pain.Ouch! That hurts.
Bravo!Praise or approval.Bravo! You performed excellently.
Ah!Realisation, surprise or emotion.Ah! Now I understand.

4.5 Articles and Determiners

Articles and determiners help specify or identify nouns. In modern English grammar, determiners form a separate word class, although traditional grammar often groups some of them under adjectives.

Articles: English has three main articles: a, an and the.

A: Used before a singular countable noun beginning with a consonant sound.

  • A teacher.
  • A university. (University begins with the consonant sound /j/.)
  • A European country.

An: Used before a singular countable noun beginning with a vowel sound.

  • An apple.
  • An honest man. (The h is silent.)
  • An hour.

The: Used when referring to a particular or identifiable person or thing, or in other established uses.

  • The book on the table is mine.
  • The sun rises in the east.
  • Please close the door.

Other Determiners: These include this, that, these, those, my, your, some, any, each, every, either, neither, much, many and several.

4.6 How to Identify the Grammatical Function of a Word

JAMB may present a word in a sentence and ask candidates to identify its grammatical class or function. The same word can belong to different classes in different contexts.

SentenceWordGrammatical Class
She bought a new book.BookNoun.
Please book a seat.BookVerb.
He is a fast runner.FastAdjective.
He runs fast.FastAdverb.
We arrived after lunch.AfterPreposition.
We arrived after the meeting ended.AfterSubordinating conjunction.
She is very intelligent.VeryAdverb.
Very few students attended.FewDeterminer.

4.7 Solved JAMB-Style Examination Questions

The following are original practice questions written in the style of UTME grammar testing. They are not presented as verbatim past JAMB questions.

Question 1: Identify the grammatical class of the underlined word: "The poor deserve assistance."

  • A. Verb
  • B. Adjective used substantively
  • C. Adverb
  • D. Preposition

Answer: B. Adjective used substantively.

Explanation: Poor normally functions as an adjective, but in this sentence, "the poor" refers to poor people as a group and functions as a noun phrase.

Question 2: Which of the following sentences contains an adverb of manner?

  • A. She arrived yesterday.
  • B. He lives nearby.
  • C. The girl answered politely.
  • D. They often travel.

Answer: C. The girl answered politely.

Explanation: Politely explains how the girl answered. Therefore, it is an adverb of manner.

Question 3: Choose the correct expression.

  • A. She is good in Mathematics.
  • B. She is good at Mathematics.
  • C. She is good on Mathematics.
  • D. She is good for Mathematics.

Answer: B. She is good at Mathematics.

Explanation: The standard expression is "good at" when describing someone's ability in a subject or activity.

Question 4: In the sentence "Swimming is an excellent form of exercise", the word "Swimming" functions as a:

  • A. Finite verb
  • B. Gerund
  • C. Preposition
  • D. Conjunction

Answer: B. Gerund.

Explanation: Swimming is formed from a verb but performs the function of a noun as the subject of the sentence.

Question 5: Which of the following is an uncountable noun?

  • A. Chair
  • B. Student
  • C. Advice
  • D. Pencil

Answer: C. Advice.

Explanation: Advice is an uncountable noun in standard English. We say "some advice" or "a piece of advice".

Question 6: Identify the conjunction in the sentence: "Although it was raining, the students attended the lecture."

  • A. Raining
  • B. Although
  • C. Students
  • D. Attended

Answer: B. Although.

Explanation: Although introduces a subordinate clause and expresses contrast.

4.8 Quick Revision Table

Word ClassKey Question to AskExample
NounWho or what is being named?Teacher.
PronounWhich noun does it replace or refer to?She.
VerbWhat action, event or state is expressed?Writes.
AdjectiveWhat quality or feature is described?Beautiful.
AdverbHow, when, where or to what extent?Carefully.
PrepositionWhat relationship is expressed?Under.
ConjunctionWhat is being connected?Because.
InterjectionWhat emotion or reaction is expressed?Alas!
★ Final Examination Advice

Do not identify a word class by memorising the word alone. Always examine how the word is used in the sentence. A single word may function as a noun, verb, adjective or adverb in different contexts. Understanding its grammatical function is the key to answering word-class questions correctly.

chapters.title: Sentence Structure, Types and Grammatical Functions
chapters.excerpt: A comprehensive study of sentence construction, sentence elements, structural classifications, sentence purposes, and grammatical relationships, with detailed examples and UTME practice.
chapters.content:
Chapter 5: Sentence Structure, Types and Grammatical Functions

A sentence is a group of words arranged according to the rules of grammar to express a complete thought, statement, question, command or exclamation. Sentences are the foundation of written and spoken communication. Understanding how sentences are constructed will help candidates answer JAMB questions involving sentence interpretation, grammatical functions, clause identification and sentence completion.

In English, a sentence normally contains a subject and a predicate. The subject identifies the person, thing or idea being discussed, while the predicate tells us something about the subject. However, commands may have an understood subject, usually 'you'.

Consider the sentence: 'The young girl passed her examination successfully.' The subject is 'The young girl', while the predicate is 'passed her examination successfully'.

5.1 The Basic Elements of a Sentence

English sentences can be analysed using five major grammatical elements: Subject (S), Verb (V), Object (O), Complement (C) and Adverbial (A). These elements help explain how words and expressions function within a sentence.

A. Subject (S)

The subject is the person, animal, object or idea that performs an action, experiences an event or is being described. It is commonly a noun, pronoun or noun phrase.

  • Amina sells clothes at the market.
  • The children are playing outside.
  • Honesty is an important quality.
  • My elder brother works in Abuja.

In these sentences, the bold expressions are the subjects. They identify what each sentence is about.

B. Verb (V)

The verb expresses the action, event or state associated with the subject. Every complete independent clause contains a finite verb.

  • The students read.
  • My mother cooks.
  • The examination was difficult.
  • The baby is sleeping.

C. Object (O)

An object receives the action of a transitive verb or completes the meaning of certain prepositions. Objects are commonly noun phrases or pronouns.

There are two major types of objects:

  • Direct object: The teacher marked the scripts. The scripts receive the action of marking.
  • Indirect object: The teacher gave the students new textbooks. The students are the recipients of the textbooks.

In the second sentence, 'the students' is the indirect object, while 'new textbooks' is the direct object.

D. Complement (C)

A complement is an element that completes the meaning of a verb or describes or identifies another element in a sentence. Complements may be subject complements or object complements.

  • Subject complement: Bola is a nurse. The expression identifies Bola.
  • Subject complement: The food tastes delicious. The adjective describes the food.
  • Object complement: They elected him president. The word president identifies the object him.
  • Object complement: The news made her happy. The adjective happy describes the object her.

E. Adverbial (A)

An adverbial gives additional information about an action or situation. It may express time, place, manner, frequency, reason or condition.

  • She arrived yesterday. (Time)
  • The children played outside. (Place)
  • He answered the question carefully. (Manner)
  • We stayed indoors because it was raining. (Reason)

5.2 The Five Basic Sentence Patterns

Many English sentences can be analysed using five basic patterns. These patterns show the order in which the subject, verb, object, complement and adverbial occur.

Five Basic Sentence Patterns

S = Subject
V = Verb
O = Object
C = Complement
A = Adverbial

Pattern 1: S + V
Pattern 2: S + V + O
Pattern 3: S + V + C
Pattern 4: S + V + O + O
Pattern 5: S + V + O + C

Pattern 1: Subject + Verb (S + V)

This is the simplest sentence pattern. It consists of a subject followed by a verb that does not require an object.

  • The baby cried.
  • The visitors arrived.
  • The old man laughed.
  • The sun shines.

Analysis: In 'The baby cried', 'The baby' is the subject and 'cried' is the verb. The sentence is complete without an object.

Pattern 2: Subject + Verb + Object (S + V + O)

This pattern contains a transitive verb followed by a direct object.

  • John bought a car.
  • The girl washed the plates.
  • The police arrested the suspect.
  • My father repaired the generator.

Analysis: In 'The girl washed the plates', the girl is the subject, washed is the verb and the plates is the direct object.

Pattern 3: Subject + Verb + Complement (S + V + C)

This pattern contains a linking verb followed by a complement that describes or identifies the subject.

  • Mary is intelligent.
  • My uncle became a lawyer.
  • The soup smells delicious.
  • The children are happy.

The complement is not an object receiving an action. It provides information about the subject.

Pattern 4: Subject + Verb + Indirect Object + Direct Object (S + V + O + O)

This pattern contains two objects. The indirect object usually identifies the recipient, while the direct object identifies what is given, sent, taught or offered.

  • The teacher gave the students assignments.
  • My mother bought me a new shirt.
  • The manager sent the workers a message.
  • He offered his friend some assistance.

Analysis: In 'My mother bought me a new shirt', 'my mother' is the subject, 'bought' is the verb, 'me' is the indirect object and 'a new shirt' is the direct object.

Pattern 5: Subject + Verb + Object + Complement (S + V + O + C)

This pattern contains an object followed by a complement that describes or identifies that object.

  • The committee elected Bola chairman.
  • The news made the woman happy.
  • We consider him intelligent.
  • The students painted the classroom blue.

Analysis: In 'The news made the woman happy', 'the woman' is the object and 'happy' is the object complement describing her condition.

PatternExampleSentence Analysis
S + VThe child slept.The child = S; slept = V.
S + V + OShe bought a bag.She = S; bought = V; a bag = O.
S + V + CHe is a doctor.He = S; is = V; a doctor = C.
S + V + O + OShe gave him money.She = S; gave = V; him = indirect O; money = direct O.
S + V + O + CThey made him captain.They = S; made = V; him = O; captain = C.

5.3 Classification of Sentences According to Structure

Sentences can also be classified according to the number and arrangement of their clauses. The four major structural types are simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences.

A. Simple Sentence

A simple sentence contains one independent clause. It expresses a complete thought and has one main clause, although it may contain a compound subject, a compound verb or several modifiers.

  • The teacher entered the classroom.
  • John and Peter played football.
  • The hardworking students read their books and completed their assignments.
  • My mother, who works in Lagos, visits us every December. (This last example is complex because it contains a subordinate clause.)

Notice that a simple sentence may contain more than one verb or subject. What matters is that it contains only one independent clause.

B. Compound Sentence

A compound sentence consists of two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction, a semicolon or another suitable linking structure.

  • John studied hard, and he passed the examination.
  • The rain stopped, but the road remained flooded.
  • Mary cooked dinner, while her husband washed the plates. (This is normally complex because while introduces a subordinate clause.)
  • The teacher explained the topic; the students understood the lesson.

In the first example, 'John studied hard' and 'he passed the examination' can each stand alone as complete sentences.

C. Complex Sentence

A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one subordinate clause. The subordinate clause depends on the main clause for complete meaning or grammatical connection.

  • Although he was tired, he continued working.
  • The woman who lives next door is a nurse.
  • I will call you when I arrive.
  • She passed the examination because she studied consistently.

In 'Although he was tired, he continued working', the expression 'Although he was tired' is subordinate, while 'he continued working' is the independent clause.

D. Compound-Complex Sentence

A compound-complex sentence contains at least two independent clauses and at least one subordinate clause.

  • Although it was raining, we went to school, and our teacher welcomed us.
  • The woman who owns the shop arrived early, but her assistant was already working.
  • When the examination ended, the candidates left the hall, and the invigilators collected the answer sheets.

These sentences combine the characteristics of compound and complex sentences.

Sentence TypeClause StructureExample
SimpleOne independent clause.The baby is sleeping.
CompoundTwo or more independent clauses.He came, but I left.
ComplexOne independent and at least one subordinate clause.When he arrived, we left.
Compound-complexAt least two independent clauses and one subordinate clause.When he arrived, we greeted him, and he smiled.

5.4 Classification According to Communicative Purpose

Sentences can also be classified according to what the speaker or writer intends to communicate.

A. Declarative Sentences

These make statements or give information. They usually end with a full stop.

  • Lagos is a commercial city.
  • The students are preparing for UTME.
  • My father works in a hospital.

B. Interrogative Sentences

These ask questions and normally end with question marks.

  • Where do you live?
  • Have you completed your registration?
  • Why did the teacher leave?

Interrogative sentences may be yes/no questions or wh-questions.

C. Imperative Sentences

These express commands, instructions, requests, warnings or advice. Their subject is commonly understood to be 'you'.

  • Open the door.
  • Please submit your assignment.
  • Do not touch the electrical wire.
  • Always respect your teachers.

D. Exclamatory Sentences

These express strong emotions such as surprise, excitement, anger, happiness or disappointment.

  • What a beautiful house!
  • How wonderful the performance was!
  • What an unfortunate incident!

5.5 Phrases and Clauses: Understanding the Difference

A phrase is a group of related words that performs a grammatical function but does not normally contain a finite verb forming a complete clause. A clause is a group of words containing a subject and a predicate, although some clauses have an implied subject in certain constructions.

Examples of phrases:

  • In the classroom.
  • A beautiful young woman.
  • After the examination.
  • Running very quickly.

Examples of clauses:

  • Because she was ill.
  • The boy entered the room.
  • When the rain stopped.
  • They completed their assignments.

A phrase may be part of a clause, while a clause contains a subject-predicate relationship.

5.6 Common Sentence Construction Errors

A. Sentence Fragment

A sentence fragment is an incomplete expression incorrectly presented as a complete sentence.

  • Incorrect: Because the teacher was absent.
  • Correct: Because the teacher was absent, the students studied independently.

B. Run-on Sentence

A run-on sentence occurs when independent clauses are joined incorrectly without appropriate punctuation or a conjunction.

  • Incorrect: The boy was hungry he bought food.
  • Correct: The boy was hungry, so he bought food.
  • Correct: The boy was hungry; he bought food.

C. Comma Splice

A comma splice occurs when two independent clauses are joined using only a comma.

  • Incorrect: The teacher arrived, the students stood up.
  • Correct: The teacher arrived, and the students stood up.
  • Correct: The teacher arrived; the students stood up.

D. Misplaced Modifier

A misplaced modifier is positioned too far from the word it is intended to describe, creating confusion.

  • Unclear: She served rice to the children on a plate.
  • Clearer: She served the children rice on a plate.

E. Dangling Modifier

A dangling modifier does not clearly refer to the person or thing it is intended to describe.

  • Incorrect: Walking to school, the rain started.
  • Correct: While I was walking to school, the rain started.

5.7 Solved UTME-Style Questions

These are original practice questions designed to test the grammatical knowledge covered in this chapter. They are not reproduced past JAMB questions.

Question 1: Identify the sentence pattern in: 'The principal appointed Mary prefect.'

  • A. S + V
  • B. S + V + O
  • C. S + V + O + C
  • D. S + V + C

Answer: C. S + V + O + C.

Explanation: The principal is the subject, appointed is the verb, Mary is the object, and prefect is the object complement identifying Mary.

Question 2: Which of the following is a compound sentence?

  • A. Because it was raining, we stayed indoors.
  • B. The boy who won the race is my brother.
  • C. The rain stopped, and the children returned outside.
  • D. The hardworking students passed the examination.

Answer: C.

Explanation: The sentence contains two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction 'and'.

Question 3: Which sentence contains a subject complement?

  • A. She bought a new dress.
  • B. The woman became a doctor.
  • C. The boy kicked the ball.
  • D. The students wrote the examination.

Answer: B.

Explanation: 'A doctor' identifies the subject 'the woman' after the linking verb 'became'.

Question 4: Which of the following is a complex sentence?

  • A. The teacher entered and sat down.
  • B. The boy ran, but his friend walked.
  • C. Although she was ill, she attended the lecture.
  • D. The children sang and danced.

Answer: C.

Explanation: 'Although she was ill' is a subordinate clause, while 'she attended the lecture' is an independent clause.

Question 5: In the sentence 'The manager gave the workers their salaries', the expression 'the workers' functions as the:

  • A. Subject
  • B. Direct object
  • C. Indirect object
  • D. Subject complement

Answer: C. Indirect object.

Explanation: The workers are the recipients of the salaries, while 'their salaries' is the direct object.

Question 6: Which of the following is an imperative sentence?

  • A. Why are you crying?
  • B. The children are playing.
  • C. Kindly close the window.
  • D. What a wonderful performance!

Answer: C.

Explanation: It expresses a polite instruction or request directed at the listener.

Question 7: Identify the grammatical error in: 'The examination was difficult, the candidates were nervous.'

  • A. Incorrect tense
  • B. Comma splice
  • C. Subject-verb disagreement
  • D. Incorrect article

Answer: B. Comma splice.

Explanation: Two independent clauses have been joined using only a comma. A suitable conjunction or semicolon is required.

5.8 Chapter Revision Summary

ConceptWhat to Remember
SubjectThe person or thing being discussed.
VerbExpresses action, occurrence or state.
ObjectReceives the action of a transitive verb.
ComplementCompletes or describes another sentence element.
AdverbialProvides information about circumstances.
Simple sentenceContains one independent clause.
Compound sentenceContains two or more independent clauses.
Complex sentenceContains an independent clause and at least one subordinate clause.
Compound-complex sentenceContains at least two independent clauses and one subordinate clause.
★ Final Examination Tip

When asked to identify a sentence pattern, locate the subject and the main verb first. Then determine whether the words following the verb are objects, complements or adverbials. Do not assume that every noun following a verb is an object. A linking verb normally takes a subject complement, not a direct object.

chapters.excerpt: An in-depth lesson on main clauses, subordinate clauses, noun clauses, relative clauses, adverbial clauses, clause functions and common examination errors.
chapters.content:
Chapter 6: Independent and Dependent Clauses

A clause is a grammatical unit that contains a subject and a predicate. It may form a complete sentence on its own or depend on another clause for its full meaning. Clauses are important in English because they enable speakers and writers to communicate complex ideas, explain relationships, provide reasons and describe people or situations.

JAMB candidates should understand the difference between independent and dependent clauses, recognise different subordinate clause types and identify the grammatical functions performed by clauses within sentences.

6.1 What Is an Independent Clause?

An independent clause, also called a main clause, contains a subject and a finite verb and expresses a complete thought. It can stand alone as a complete sentence.

Examples:

  • The students passed the examination.
  • My father works in Abuja.
  • The rain has stopped.
  • We visited our grandmother yesterday.

Each expression communicates a complete idea without depending on another clause.

6.2 What Is a Dependent Clause?

A dependent clause, also known as a subordinate clause, contains a subject and a verb but does not express a complete thought independently in the context in which it is used. It depends on a main clause or another grammatical structure.

Examples:

  • Because the teacher was absent.
  • Although the road was dangerous.
  • When the examination ended.
  • Who lives beside our house.

These expressions leave the reader expecting additional information. They need an appropriate main clause to complete the intended statement.

Consider the complete sentence: 'Because the teacher was absent, the students studied independently.'

  • Dependent clause: Because the teacher was absent.
  • Independent clause: The students studied independently.
Clause Identification Rule

Independent clause: Subject + finite verb + complete independent meaning.
Dependent clause: Subject + finite verb + a structure that depends on another clause in its context.

6.3 The Three Major Types of Subordinate Clauses

Subordinate clauses are commonly classified according to their grammatical functions. The three major types are noun clauses, adjective clauses and adverbial clauses.

6.4 Noun Clauses

A noun clause is a subordinate clause that performs the grammatical function of a noun or noun phrase. It may function as the subject, object, subject complement or complement of a preposition.

Noun clauses are often introduced by words such as that, what, who, whoever, whether, if, why, where, when and how. The introductory word depends on the meaning and structure of the sentence.

A. Noun Clause as Subject

When a noun clause functions as the subject, it occupies the position normally occupied by a noun or noun phrase.

  • What he said surprised everyone.
  • That she passed the examination pleased her parents.
  • Whoever arrives first will receive the prize.

In the first sentence, 'What he said' is the subject because it identifies what surprised everyone.

B. Noun Clause as Direct Object

A noun clause can function as the object of a transitive verb.

  • I believe that he is innocent.
  • She explained why she was absent.
  • The teacher knows who submitted the assignment.
  • We discovered that the door was open.

C. Noun Clause as Subject Complement

A noun clause may follow a linking verb and explain or identify the subject.

  • The problem is that nobody has enough information.
  • My concern is whether he will arrive on time.
  • The truth is that she never received the letter.

D. Noun Clause as Object of a Preposition

A noun clause may complete the meaning of a preposition.

  • We talked about what happened yesterday.
  • She was worried about whether the child was safe.
  • They disagreed on how the money should be spent.

How to Recognise a Noun Clause

One useful method is to examine whether the entire clause can be replaced by a noun phrase or a word such as 'something' without destroying the basic grammatical structure.

  • She knows what happened.
  • She knows the truth.
  • She knows something.

The expression 'what happened' functions as the object of knows, just as 'the truth' does.

6.5 Adjective Clauses (Relative Clauses)

An adjective clause, also called a relative clause, is a subordinate clause that modifies a noun or pronoun. It provides additional information about the person, place, animal or thing being discussed.

Relative clauses are commonly introduced by relative pronouns such as who, whom, whose, which and that. They may also begin with relative adverbs such as where, when and why.

A. Defining Relative Clauses

A defining relative clause provides information necessary to identify the noun it modifies. Without the clause, the intended person or thing may not be clear. It is not normally separated from the rest of the sentence by commas.

  • The woman who teaches Mathematics is my aunt.
  • The book that I bought yesterday is missing.
  • The student whose father is a doctor won the scholarship.
  • The house where I was born has been renovated.

B. Non-Defining Relative Clauses

A non-defining relative clause provides additional information about a noun that is already sufficiently identified. It is normally separated from the main clause by commas.

  • Mr Ade, who teaches English, is a friendly man.
  • Lagos, which is a major commercial centre, attracts many visitors.
  • My mother, whose birthday is tomorrow, is preparing for a celebration.

In standard written English, that is not normally used to introduce non-defining relative clauses. Who, whom, whose and which are more appropriate according to the intended meaning.

6.6 Relative Pronouns and Their Functions

Relative WordTypical FunctionExample
WhoRefers to people as subjects.The boy who won is my brother.
WhomRefers to people as objects.The man whom we invited arrived.
WhoseExpresses possession.The woman whose car was stolen reported it.
WhichRefers to animals or things.The phone which I bought is expensive.
ThatIntroduces defining relative clauses referring to people or things.The food that she prepared was delicious.
WhereIndicates place.This is the school where I studied.
WhenIndicates time.I remember the day when we met.
WhyIndicates reason.That is the reason why he left.

6.7 Adverbial Clauses

An adverbial clause is a subordinate clause that modifies a verb, adjective or an entire clause by providing information about time, place, reason, purpose, condition, concession, manner or comparison.

A. Adverbial Clause of Time

It indicates when an action occurs. Common introductory words include when, while, before, after, until, as soon as and since.

  • Call me when you arrive.
  • We left after the programme ended.
  • Before she entered the hall, she switched off her phone.
  • Wait here until the teacher returns.

B. Adverbial Clause of Place

It indicates where an action occurs. It may be introduced by where or wherever.

  • Stay where you are.
  • We will follow you wherever you go.
  • Put the bag where you found it.

C. Adverbial Clause of Reason or Cause

It explains why something happens. Common introductory expressions include because, since and as.

  • She stayed indoors because she was ill.
  • Since the road was flooded, we used another route.
  • He was punished because he disobeyed the instruction.

D. Adverbial Clause of Purpose

It explains the intention behind an action. It is commonly introduced by so that or in order that.

  • She studied hard so that she could pass the examination.
  • He saved money in order that his children might attend university.

E. Adverbial Clause of Condition

It expresses a condition that must be fulfilled for another event to happen. Common introductory words include if, unless, provided that, as long as and on condition that.

  • If you study consistently, you may perform well.
  • You will not succeed unless you prepare properly.
  • You may borrow the book provided that you return it tomorrow.

F. Adverbial Clause of Concession

It expresses contrast between two situations. Common introductory words include although, though, even though and whereas.

  • Although he was poor, he remained generous.
  • She continued working even though she was tired.
  • Whereas his brother is quiet, he is very talkative.

G. Adverbial Clause of Manner

It explains how an action is performed. It may be introduced by as, as if or as though.

  • She arranged the books as the teacher instructed.
  • He behaved as if he owned the entire building.
  • The child cried as though she had been injured.

H. Adverbial Clause of Comparison or Degree

It compares actions or qualities. Common structures include than, as...as and as much as.

  • She is more intelligent than her brother is.
  • He works as hard as his father does.
  • The examination was more difficult than we expected.
Adverbial Clause TypeCommon ConnectorsQuestion Answered
TimeWhen, before, after, until.When?
PlaceWhere, wherever.Where?
ReasonBecause, since, as.Why?
PurposeSo that, in order that.For what purpose?
ConditionIf, unless, provided that.Under what condition?
ConcessionAlthough, though, even though.Despite what?
MannerAs, as if, as though.How?
ComparisonThan, as...as.To what degree or in what comparison?

6.8 Finite and Non-Finite Clauses

Clauses can also be classified according to whether their verbs are finite or non-finite.

Finite Clauses

A finite clause contains a finite verb that shows tense or grammatical agreement with its subject.

  • She works in a bank.
  • They were playing football.
  • Because he was tired, he went home.

Non-Finite Clauses

A non-finite clause contains a non-finite verb form, such as an infinitive, an -ing participle or a past participle. It does not express tense independently in the same way a finite clause does.

  • To pass the examination, she studied every day. (Infinitive clause.)
  • Walking along the road, he met his teacher. (Participial clause.)
  • Having completed the assignment, the student submitted it. (Perfect participial clause.)
  • Written in simple English, the book is easy to understand. (Past-participial clause.)

6.9 Clauses and Their Grammatical Functions

JAMB may ask candidates to identify the function of an underlined clause rather than simply naming its type. A noun clause can function as a subject or object, while an adjective clause modifies a noun and an adverbial clause modifies a larger grammatical unit.

SentenceClauseFunction
What she said was surprising.What she said.Subject.
I know that he is honest.That he is honest.Direct object.
The boy who won is my cousin.Who won.Modifies the noun boy.
We left because it was late.Because it was late.Adverbial of reason.
Call me when you arrive.When you arrive.Adverbial of time.
She is certain that he will come.That he will come.Complements the adjective certain.

6.10 Common Errors Involving Clauses

A. Incorrect Use of Relative Pronouns

  • Incorrect: The man which came yesterday is my uncle.
  • Correct: The man who came yesterday is my uncle.

Who is normally used for people, while which is used for animals and things.

B. Incorrect Use of Although and But

  • Incorrect: Although he was tired, but he continued working.
  • Correct: Although he was tired, he continued working.
  • Correct: He was tired, but he continued working.

In the intended construction, although and but should not be used together to introduce the same contrast.

C. Incorrect Use of Because and So

  • Incorrect: Because it was raining, so we stayed indoors.
  • Correct: Because it was raining, we stayed indoors.
  • Correct: It was raining, so we stayed indoors.

D. Incomplete Dependent Clause

  • Incomplete: When the examination ended.
  • Complete: When the examination ended, the candidates left the hall.

6.11 Solved UTME-Style Examination Questions

These original practice questions assess the candidate's ability to identify clause types and grammatical functions.

Question 1: In the sentence 'What the principal announced surprised the students', the underlined clause functions as:

  • A. Direct object
  • B. Subject
  • C. Adverbial of time
  • D. Adjective clause

Answer: B. Subject.

Explanation: 'What the principal announced' is the subject of the verb 'surprised'. It is a noun clause functioning as the subject.

Question 2: Identify the type of subordinate clause in: 'The woman who lives next door is a teacher.'

  • A. Noun clause
  • B. Adverbial clause
  • C. Adjective clause
  • D. Independent clause

Answer: C. Adjective clause.

Explanation: 'Who lives next door' describes the noun 'woman'.

Question 3: Which expression introduces a clause of purpose?

  • A. Although
  • B. So that
  • C. Because
  • D. Wherever

Answer: B. So that.

Explanation: So that can introduce an adverbial clause expressing the purpose or intention behind an action.

Question 4: In 'She will succeed if she works hard', the clause 'if she works hard' expresses:

  • A. Reason
  • B. Time
  • C. Condition
  • D. Place

Answer: C. Condition.

Explanation: The subordinate clause establishes the condition under which she may succeed.

Question 5: Which of the following is an independent clause?

  • A. Because he was sick.
  • B. Although she was late.
  • C. The students completed the assignment.
  • D. When the rain stopped.

Answer: C.

Explanation: The expression contains a subject and a finite verb and communicates a complete thought.

Question 6: Identify the clause in: 'I do not know whether he will attend the meeting.'

  • A. Independent noun clause
  • B. Dependent noun clause
  • C. Adjective clause
  • D. Adverbial clause of time

Answer: B. Dependent noun clause.

Explanation: 'Whether he will attend the meeting' is a subordinate noun clause functioning as the direct object of 'know'.

Question 7: In the sentence 'The book that I borrowed belongs to my brother', the clause 'that I borrowed' modifies:

  • A. Brother
  • B. Belongs
  • C. Book
  • D. I

Answer: C. Book.

Explanation: The relative clause identifies which book is being discussed.

Question 8: Which sentence contains an adverbial clause of concession?

  • A. He left because he was tired.
  • B. Although she was poor, she was generous.
  • C. I know what happened.
  • D. The man who arrived is my father.

Answer: B.

Explanation: Although introduces a contrast between poverty and generosity.

6.12 Comprehensive Revision Table

Clause TypeFunctionExample
IndependentExpresses a complete thought.She passed the examination.
NounFunctions like a noun.What he said was true.
AdjectiveModifies a noun or pronoun.The girl who won is happy.
Adverbial of timeIndicates when.When he arrived, we left.
Adverbial of placeIndicates where.Stay where you are.
Adverbial of reasonExplains why.We left because it was late.
Adverbial of purposeExplains intention.She studied so that she could pass.
Adverbial of conditionExpresses a requirement.If you study, you may succeed.
Adverbial of concessionExpresses contrast.Although he was tired, he worked.
Adverbial of mannerExplains how.Do it as I instructed.
★ Final Examination Advice

When a question asks for the function of a clause, do not stop after identifying its introductory word. Determine what the entire clause does in the sentence. A clause introduced by 'that' may be a noun clause functioning as an object or complement, while a clause introduced by 'because' commonly expresses reason. Always analyse the complete sentence.

chapters.content:
Chapter 7: Mood, Tense and Aspect

English verbs communicate more than actions. They also show when events happen, whether actions are completed or continuing, and whether statements express facts, commands, wishes, possibilities or hypothetical situations. These grammatical features are known as tense, aspect and mood.

JAMB Use of English includes mood, tense and aspect among the grammatical areas candidates should understand. A good knowledge of these topics helps candidates select the correct verb form in sentence completion, interpret statements and identify grammatical errors.

7.1 Understanding Tense

Tense is the grammatical system used to locate an action or situation in time. English commonly distinguishes present and past tense through verb forms. Future time is normally expressed through auxiliary verbs and other constructions rather than a separate inflectional future tense.

For elementary and examination purposes, verb constructions are often taught using three broad time references:

  • Present: Refers to current situations, habits, general truths or events connected with the present.
  • Past: Refers to events or situations that occurred before the present.
  • Future: Refers to events expected or planned to happen after the present.

7.2 The Difference Between Tense and Aspect

Tense and aspect are related but different grammatical concepts.

Tense indicates the grammatical time reference of an action or situation. Aspect explains how the action or situation is viewed in relation to its duration, completion or connection with another time.

For example:

  • She writes every day. (Present simple.)
  • She is writing now. (Present continuous.)
  • She has written the letter. (Present perfect.)
  • She has been writing for two hours. (Present perfect continuous.)

All four examples have a present connection, but they express different aspects of the action.

7.3 The Present Simple Tense

The present simple is used to express habits, repeated actions, general truths, permanent situations, states and scheduled events.

Formation:

Present Simple Structure

I/You/We/They + base verb
He/She/It + base verb + s/es
Negative: do/does + not + base verb
Question: Do/Does + subject + base verb?

Uses of the Present Simple

A. Habitual Actions

  • She wakes up at five every morning.
  • My father reads the newspaper daily.
  • The students attend lectures regularly.

B. General Truths and Scientific Facts

  • The sun rises in the east.
  • Water boils at approximately 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure.
  • The earth revolves around the sun.

C. Permanent or Relatively Stable Situations

  • He lives in Ibadan.
  • My mother works in a hospital.
  • She speaks Yoruba and English.

D. Timetables and Scheduled Events

  • The train leaves at 8 a.m. tomorrow.
  • The examination begins next Monday.

Common Time Expressions: Always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never, every day, every week and generally.

★ Common Present Simple Error

Remember that third-person singular subjects normally take an -s or -es form in the affirmative present simple. Say 'She works hard', not 'She work hard'. However, after does or does not, use the base form: 'Does she work?' and 'She does not work'.

7.4 The Present Continuous Tense

The present continuous describes an action happening at the time of speaking, a temporary situation, a changing condition or an arranged future event.

Present Continuous Structure

Subject + am/is/are + verb-ing

Examples:

  • I am reading a novel.
  • The children are playing football.
  • She is preparing for her examination.
  • The weather is becoming colder.
  • We are travelling to Lagos tomorrow.

Uses:

  • Actions occurring now: The teacher is explaining the lesson.
  • Temporary situations: My brother is staying with us this week.
  • Changing situations: Technology is developing rapidly.
  • Arranged future plans: We are meeting the principal tomorrow.

Stative Verbs: Some verbs describe states rather than actions and are not normally used in continuous forms in their ordinary meanings. Examples include know, believe, understand, own, belong, prefer and resemble.

  • Correct: I know the answer.
  • Incorrect in the ordinary meaning: I am knowing the answer.
  • Correct: She owns a car.
  • Incorrect in the ordinary meaning: She is owning a car.

Some verbs can be used in both simple and continuous forms when their meanings change. For example, 'I think you are right' expresses an opinion, while 'I am thinking about the problem' describes a mental activity in progress.

7.5 The Present Perfect Tense

The present perfect connects a past action or situation with the present. It is formed using has or have followed by the past participle of the main verb.

Present Perfect Structure

Subject + has/have + past participle

Examples:

  • She has completed her assignment.
  • They have travelled to Abuja.
  • I have known him for five years.
  • The rain has stopped.

Major Uses:

  • Completed action with a present result: She has broken her phone. The phone is now broken.
  • Life experiences: I have visited Ghana twice.
  • Unfinished time periods: We have attended three lectures this week. The week is not necessarily over.
  • Situations continuing to the present: She has lived here since 2020.

For and Since:

  • For indicates a duration: for two hours, for five years, for a long time.
  • Since indicates a starting point: since Monday, since 2020, since childhood.
★ Present Perfect Examination Trap

In standard English, avoid using the present perfect with a clearly finished past-time expression such as yesterday, last week or in 2020. Say 'I saw him yesterday', not 'I have seen him yesterday'.

7.6 The Present Perfect Continuous Tense

The present perfect continuous describes an activity that began in the past and has continued until the present or has recently stopped with evidence of its activity.

Present Perfect Continuous Structure

Subject + has/have + been + verb-ing

Examples:

  • She has been reading for three hours.
  • They have been working since morning.
  • It has been raining all afternoon.
  • I have been waiting for the bus for thirty minutes.

The tense emphasises the duration or ongoing nature of the activity. Compare 'She has written three letters', which emphasises completed results, with 'She has been writing letters', which emphasises the activity.

7.7 The Past Simple Tense

The past simple describes actions or situations that occurred and were completed at a definite or understood time in the past.

Past Simple Structure

Subject + past form of verb
Negative: did not + base verb
Question: Did + subject + base verb?

Examples:

  • She visited her grandmother yesterday.
  • The students wrote the examination last week.
  • My father bought a new car in 2024.
  • They travelled to Kano during the holiday.

Regular Verbs: Most regular verbs form their past tense by adding -ed or -d.

  • Walk → Walked.
  • Play → Played.
  • Arrive → Arrived.
  • Study → Studied.

Irregular Verbs: These do not follow the normal -ed pattern.

Base FormPast FormPast Participle
GoWentGone
EatAteEaten
WriteWroteWritten
TakeTookTaken
SeeSawSeen
SpeakSpokeSpoken
BreakBrokeBroken
ChooseChoseChosen
BeginBeganBegun
GiveGaveGiven

Important: When did is used to form a negative or question, the main verb returns to its base form.

  • Correct: He did not go to school.
  • Incorrect: He did not went to school.
  • Correct: Did she write the letter?
  • Incorrect: Did she wrote the letter?

7.8 The Past Continuous Tense

The past continuous describes an action that was in progress at a particular time in the past. It is also used for an ongoing action interrupted by another action.

Past Continuous Structure

Subject + was/were + verb-ing

Examples:

  • I was reading when the visitor arrived.
  • The children were playing at 5 p.m. yesterday.
  • She was cooking while her husband was watching television.
  • They were sleeping when the electricity went off.

In the first example, 'was reading' describes the ongoing action, while 'arrived' describes the event that interrupted it.

7.9 The Past Perfect Tense

The past perfect indicates that one action or situation was completed before another past event or reference time. It is formed using had followed by the past participle.

Past Perfect Structure

Subject + had + past participle

Examples:

  • The train had left before we arrived.
  • She had completed her assignment when the teacher entered.
  • By the time I reached the station, the bus had departed.
  • He had already eaten when his mother returned.

The past perfect makes the earlier of two past events clear. It should not be inserted unnecessarily when the sequence of events is already clear from the sentence.

7.10 The Past Perfect Continuous Tense

The past perfect continuous describes an activity that continued for some time before another event or reference point in the past.

Past Perfect Continuous Structure

Subject + had + been + verb-ing

Examples:

  • She had been studying for three hours before the examination began.
  • They had been waiting for the doctor when the nurse arrived.
  • He had been working in the company for ten years before he resigned.
  • It had been raining before the sun appeared.

The tense places emphasis on the duration of an activity before a past event.

7.11 The Future Simple Construction

Future time is commonly expressed using will or shall followed by the base form of a verb. The future simple is traditionally taught as one of the twelve basic tense forms in school grammar.

Future Simple Structure

Subject + will + base verb

Examples:

  • I will attend the meeting tomorrow.
  • She will become a doctor.
  • They will travel next month.
  • We will complete the project soon.

Uses:

  • Predictions: It will rain tomorrow.
  • Promises: I will help you with your assignment.
  • Spontaneous decisions: The phone is ringing; I will answer it.
  • Offers and willingness: We will support the students.

Going to Construction: Be going to + base verb is commonly used for plans and predictions based on present evidence.

  • She is going to study Medicine.
  • Look at those clouds; it is going to rain.
  • We are going to visit our relatives.

7.12 The Future Continuous Tense

The future continuous describes an action that will be in progress at a particular time in the future.

Future Continuous Structure

Subject + will + be + verb-ing

Examples:

  • This time tomorrow, I will be writing my examination.
  • At 8 p.m., she will be preparing dinner.
  • They will be travelling to Abuja next week.
  • We will be waiting for you at the airport.

7.13 The Future Perfect Tense

The future perfect describes an action that will have been completed before a particular time or event in the future.

Future Perfect Structure

Subject + will + have + past participle

Examples:

  • By next week, I will have completed the project.
  • She will have graduated before December.
  • By the time you arrive, we will have finished cooking.
  • They will have paid the money by Friday.

7.14 The Future Perfect Continuous Tense

The future perfect continuous describes an activity that will have continued for a particular duration by a specified future time.

Future Perfect Continuous Structure

Subject + will + have + been + verb-ing

Examples:

  • By December, she will have been teaching for ten years.
  • By 6 p.m., I will have been working for eight hours.
  • Next month, they will have been living in Lagos for five years.

This form emphasises the duration of an activity up to a future reference point.

7.15 Complete Tense and Aspect Reference Table

ConstructionFormulaExample
Present SimpleBase verb / s-esShe writes.
Present ContinuousAm/is/are + ingShe is writing.
Present PerfectHas/have + past participleShe has written.
Present Perfect ContinuousHas/have + been + ingShe has been writing.
Past SimplePast formShe wrote.
Past ContinuousWas/were + ingShe was writing.
Past PerfectHad + past participleShe had written.
Past Perfect ContinuousHad + been + ingShe had been writing.
Future SimpleWill + base verbShe will write.
Future ContinuousWill + be + ingShe will be writing.
Future PerfectWill + have + past participleShe will have written.
Future Perfect ContinuousWill + have + been + ingShe will have been writing.

7.16 Understanding Grammatical Mood

Mood is the grammatical form or construction used to express the speaker's attitude towards an action or situation. It helps communicate facts, commands, requests, possibilities, wishes and hypothetical conditions.

The three major moods traditionally taught in English grammar are indicative, imperative and subjunctive.

A. Indicative Mood

The indicative mood is used for statements and questions that present information as facts, beliefs or possibilities.

  • She lives in Ibadan.
  • The examination begins tomorrow.
  • Did you submit your assignment?
  • He may arrive later.

The indicative mood is the most commonly used mood in ordinary English communication.

B. Imperative Mood

The imperative mood expresses commands, instructions, requests, warnings or advice. The subject is usually understood to be 'you'.

  • Close the window.
  • Please submit your answer sheet.
  • Do not touch the machine.
  • Always obey examination instructions.

C. Subjunctive Mood

The subjunctive mood is used in certain formal expressions, recommendations, demands, wishes and hypothetical situations. It often expresses something that is desired, proposed, imagined or contrary to fact rather than an ordinary statement of reality.

Present Subjunctive: The base form of the verb is used, even where the subject is third-person singular.

  • The teacher recommended that he study harder.
  • It is essential that every candidate be present.
  • The principal insisted that the student submit the assignment.
  • They demanded that the meeting begin immediately.

Notice that the subjunctive does not use the usual third-person singular -s ending. Say 'that he study', not 'that he studies', in this formal mandative construction.

Past Subjunctive and Hypothetical Situations:

  • If I were the president, I would improve education.
  • I wish I were taller.
  • If she were here, she would help us.

In formal hypothetical expressions, were is commonly used with all persons. This is known as the irrealis or past subjunctive use of were.

★ Subjunctive Examination Tip

Expressions such as 'It is important that', 'The doctor recommended that', 'They demanded that' and 'The principal insisted that' may introduce a subjunctive clause. Use the base form of the verb: 'that she be present', not 'that she is present', in the required formal construction.

7.17 Sequence of Tenses

Sequence of tenses refers to the relationship between the tense used in a main clause and the tense used in a subordinate clause. The relationship must make the intended time sequence clear.

A. General Truths Remain in the Present

  • The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.
  • Our science teacher explained that water boils at approximately 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure.

Even though the main verbs are in the past tense, the subordinate clauses use the present because they express general truths.

B. Reporting Past Actions

  • Direct speech: She said, 'I am tired.'
  • Reported speech: She said that she was tired.
  • Direct speech: He said, 'I have completed the work.'
  • Reported speech: He said that he had completed the work.

C. Reporting Future Events from a Past Viewpoint

  • Direct speech: He said, 'I will come tomorrow.'
  • Reported speech: He said that he would come the following day.

Backshifting is common in reported speech, but it is not compulsory in every context. Present tense may be retained when the statement is still true or the speaker wishes to emphasise its continuing validity.

7.18 Conditional Sentences and Tense Relationships

Conditional sentences express situations in which one event depends on another. They commonly contain an if-clause and a main clause.

Zero Conditional: Used for general truths, scientific facts and regular results.

Zero Conditional Structure

If + present simple, present simple.

  • If you heat ice, it melts.
  • If water reaches its boiling point under standard atmospheric pressure, it boils.
  • If people do not eat, they become hungry.

First Conditional: Used for real or possible future situations.

First Conditional Structure

If + present simple, will + base verb.

  • If you study hard, you will pass the examination.
  • If it rains tomorrow, we will stay indoors.
  • If she arrives early, we will begin the meeting.

Second Conditional: Used for imaginary, unlikely or hypothetical present and future situations.

Second Conditional Structure

If + past simple, would + base verb.

  • If I were rich, I would build a hospital.
  • If she studied harder, she would perform better.
  • If he had a car, he would travel more frequently.

Third Conditional: Used for imaginary past situations that did not happen and their possible consequences.

Third Conditional Structure

If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

  • If she had studied harder, she would have passed the examination.
  • If we had left early, we would have caught the bus.
  • If he had listened to the warning, he would not have lost his money.

Mixed Conditional: This combines different time references, usually a past condition and a present result.

  • If I had accepted the offer, I would be working in Abuja now.
  • If she had studied Medicine, she would be a doctor today.
Conditional TypeCondition ClauseMain ClauseMeaning
ZeroPresent simplePresent simpleGeneral truth.
FirstPresent simpleWill + base verbReal future possibility.
SecondPast simpleWould + base verbHypothetical present/future.
ThirdPast perfectWould have + past participleImaginary past situation.
MixedPast perfectWould + base verbPast condition with present result.

7.19 Common Tense Errors and Their Corrections

Incorrect ExpressionCorrect ExpressionExplanation
She has went home.She has gone home.Has requires the past participle.
He did not came.He did not come.Did is followed by the base verb.
I am knowing the answer.I know the answer.Know is normally stative.
If I was you, I would go.If I were you, I would go.Were is preferred in this hypothetical expression.
She is working here since 2020.She has been working here since 2020.Present perfect continuous expresses duration continuing to the present.
By next week, I will finish the work.By next week, I will have finished the work.Future perfect emphasises completion before a future deadline.
He has arrived yesterday.He arrived yesterday.Yesterday requires a finished past-time reference.
She can dances.She can dance.Modal auxiliaries take the base verb.

7.20 Solved UTME-Style Examination Questions

These are original examination-style practice questions prepared to test tense, aspect, mood and conditional constructions. They are not presented as verbatim JAMB past questions.

Question 1: By the time the principal arrived, the students _____ their examination.

  • A. complete
  • B. have completed
  • C. had completed
  • D. will complete

Answer: C. had completed.

Explanation: The students completed the examination before the principal arrived. The past perfect expresses the earlier of two past events.

Question 2: She _____ in this school since 2022.

  • A. works
  • B. has worked
  • C. worked
  • D. is working

Answer: B. has worked.

Explanation: Since identifies the starting point of a situation continuing into the present. The present perfect is appropriate. 'Has been working' could also be appropriate if the continuous aspect is intended, but it is not among the options.

Question 3: If I _____ the principal, I would introduce free textbooks.

  • A. am
  • B. was
  • C. were
  • D. have been

Answer: C. were.

Explanation: The sentence expresses a hypothetical situation. The formal subjunctive form 'were' is preferred.

Question 4: The teacher insisted that every student _____ present.

  • A. is
  • B. was
  • C. be
  • D. being

Answer: C. be.

Explanation: The verb 'insisted' introduces a formal demand construction requiring the base-form subjunctive 'be'.

Question 5: While the children _____ football, their mother prepared dinner.

  • A. play
  • B. were playing
  • C. have played
  • D. will play

Answer: B. were playing.

Explanation: The past continuous expresses an action in progress while another past action occurred.

Question 6: By December next year, she _____ in the company for ten years.

  • A. works
  • B. has worked
  • C. will have been working
  • D. was working

Answer: C. will have been working.

Explanation: The future perfect continuous emphasises the duration of an activity up to a future reference point.

Question 7: If he had prepared properly, he _____ the examination.

  • A. will pass
  • B. would pass
  • C. would have passed
  • D. passes

Answer: C. would have passed.

Explanation: This is a third conditional sentence. The condition is in the past perfect, while the result uses would have and the past participle.

Question 8: Which of the following sentences is in the present perfect continuous tense?

  • A. She has written a letter.
  • B. She is writing a letter.
  • C. She has been writing a letter.
  • D. She wrote a letter.

Answer: C.

Explanation: Has been followed by the -ing form of the main verb is the structure of the present perfect continuous.

Question 9: The doctor recommended that the patient _____ more water.

  • A. drinks
  • B. drink
  • C. drank
