  • D. drinking

Answer: B. drink.

Explanation: The recommendation introduces a subjunctive clause, which uses the base form of the verb.

Question 10: The bus _____ at 7 a.m. tomorrow according to the published timetable.

  • A. left
  • B. leaves
  • C. has left
  • D. was leaving

Answer: B. leaves.

Explanation: The present simple can express fixed schedules and timetables referring to the future.

7.21 Final Revision Guide

TopicEssential Point
TenseShows grammatical time reference.
AspectShows how an action is viewed in relation to duration or completion.
Present simpleHabits, facts and stable situations.
Present continuousActions in progress and temporary situations.
Present perfectPast action connected with the present.
Present perfect continuousActivity continuing from the past or recently stopped.
Past simpleCompleted past action.
Past continuousPast action in progress.
Past perfectAction completed before another past reference point.
Past perfect continuousDuration of an activity before a past event.
Future constructionsExpress predictions, plans, promises and future events.
Indicative moodStatements and questions.
Imperative moodCommands, instructions and requests.
Subjunctive moodFormal demands, recommendations and hypothetical expressions.
Conditional sentencesExpress conditions and their consequences.
★ Final Examination Strategy

When answering tense questions, look for time expressions such as yesterday, since, for, already, by the time, tomorrow and next year. Then examine the relationship between the actions. Do not select a verb form simply because it sounds familiar. Determine whether the question requires a simple, continuous, perfect or perfect continuous construction. Also pay attention to the meaning of the entire sentence.

chapters.title: Number: Singular and Plural Forms of Nouns
chapters.excerpt: Understand singular and plural nouns, spelling rules, irregular forms, collective nouns, uncountable nouns and common JAMB examination traps.
chapters.content:
8.1 Meaning of Number in English

In English grammar, number refers to whether a noun or pronoun represents one person, animal, place, thing or idea, or more than one. The two main forms are singular and plural.

  • Singular: Refers to one person or thing. Examples: boy, woman, book, child, chair.
  • Plural: Refers to more than one person or thing. Examples: boys, women, books, children, chairs.

Number is important in JAMB because it affects subject-verb agreement, pronoun agreement and the correct construction of sentences.

8.2 Formation of Regular Plurals

Most English nouns form their plural by adding -s or -es to the singular form. However, the correct ending depends on the final letters of the noun.

Rule 1: Add -s to most nouns

Examples: book/books, table/tables, car/cars, girl/girls, student/students, house/houses.

Rule 2: Add -es to nouns ending in -s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x and some nouns ending in -z

Examples: bus/buses, class/classes, dish/dishes, church/churches, box/boxes, quiz/quizzes.

The extra syllable in these words makes pronunciation easier.

Rule 3: Nouns ending in consonant + y

Change the -y to -ies when a noun ends in a consonant followed by y.

Examples: baby/babies, city/cities, country/countries, lady/ladies, university/universities.

However, when a vowel comes before y, simply add -s.

Examples: boy/boys, key/keys, day/days, toy/toys, journey/journeys.

Rule 4: Nouns ending in -f or -fe

Some nouns change -f or -fe to -ves.

Examples: leaf/leaves, knife/knives, wife/wives, life/lives, wolf/wolves, shelf/shelves.

Not all nouns follow this rule. Some simply take -s: roof/roofs, chief/chiefs, belief/beliefs, cliff/cliffs.

Rule 5: Nouns ending in -o

Some nouns ending in -o take -es, while others take -s. Examples of -es include tomato/tomatoes, potato/potatoes and hero/heroes. Examples of -s include radio/radios, photo/photos, piano/pianos and video/videos. Some words permit more than one accepted form, so pay attention to standard usage.

8.3 Irregular Plural Nouns

Irregular nouns do not form their plurals by simply adding -s or -es. Their spelling may change completely.

SingularPlural
ManMen
WomanWomen
ChildChildren
ToothTeeth
FootFeet
GooseGeese
MouseMice
LouseLice
OxOxen
PersonPeople

Examples in sentences:

  1. The woman is a teacher. The women are teachers.
  2. The child is playing. The children are playing.
  3. One tooth is missing. Two teeth are missing.

8.4 Nouns with the Same Singular and Plural Forms

Some nouns do not change their form when they refer to more than one. The meaning is understood from the context and the verb used.

Examples: sheep, deer, fish, aircraft, species, series and means.

Correct: One sheep is missing. Five sheep are missing.

Correct: This species is rare. These species are rare.

Be careful with fish. The plural is usually fish when referring to the same kind of fish. Fishes may be used when discussing different species of fish.

8.5 Countable and Uncountable Nouns

Countable nouns can be counted individually. They have singular and plural forms and can be used with numbers.

Examples: one book, three books; one student, ten students; one bottle, two bottles.

Uncountable nouns are not normally counted as separate individual units. They generally do not take a plural -s and are not used directly with a or an.

Examples: information, advice, furniture, equipment, luggage, knowledge, rice, water, traffic, money and bread.

Incorrect: She gave me many advices.

Correct: She gave me much advice. She gave me several pieces of advice.

Incorrect: The school bought new furnitures.

Correct: The school bought new furniture. The school bought several pieces of furniture.

To count uncountable nouns, use expressions such as a piece of, a bottle of, a cup of, a loaf of, a bag of and an item of.

Uncountable nounCorrect counting expression
AdviceTwo pieces of advice
InformationThree pieces of information
FurnitureFour items of furniture
BreadTwo loaves of bread
WaterThree bottles of water
EquipmentSeveral pieces of equipment

8.6 Nouns That Can Be Countable or Uncountable

Some nouns can be countable or uncountable depending on their meaning.

  • Chicken: I ate chicken for lunch. (meat); Three chickens escaped. (animals)
  • Paper: Paper is made from wood. (material); I submitted three papers. (documents or essays)
  • Glass: Glass breaks easily. (material); Two glasses are on the table. (drinking containers)
  • Experience: She has experience in teaching. (knowledge); He had many strange experiences. (events)
  • Work: I have a lot of work. (activity); The museum displays the artist's works. (creations)

8.7 Collective Nouns

A collective noun refers to a group of people, animals or things considered as a unit. Examples include team, family, committee, government, audience, crowd, staff, jury, class and army.

In British English, a collective noun may take a singular or plural verb depending on whether the group is considered as one unit or as individual members.

Examples: The committee has made its decision. (The committee is acting as one body.)

The committee are arguing among themselves. (Attention is on the individual members.)

In many formal examination sentences, a collective noun treated as one unit takes a singular verb. Always examine the intended meaning and sentence construction.

8.8 Compound Nouns and Their Plurals

Compound nouns contain two or more words that work together as one noun. The plural is usually formed by adding the plural ending to the main noun.

  • Mother-in-law → mothers-in-law
  • Father-in-law → fathers-in-law
  • Passer-by → passers-by
  • Editor-in-chief → editors-in-chief
  • Brother-in-law → brothers-in-law
  • Schoolboy → schoolboys
  • Toothbrush → toothbrushes

Some compound nouns are written as one word, so the normal plural rule applies to the final word: bedroom/bedrooms, notebook/notebooks.

8.9 Plural Forms of Foreign Words

Some words borrowed from Latin, Greek and other languages retain traditional plural forms. JAMB may test these forms.

SingularPlural
AnalysisAnalyses
BasisBases
CrisisCrises
ThesisTheses
CriterionCriteria
PhenomenonPhenomena
DatumData
BacteriumBacteria
MediumMedia
CurriculumCurricula

Some borrowed words also have accepted English plural forms. For example, formulas and formulae are both used. The expected form may depend on the context and the convention being followed.

8.10 Common JAMB Errors

  • Writing informations instead of information.
  • Writing childrens instead of children.
  • Using womans instead of women.
  • Writing equipments instead of equipment.
  • Using a plural verb with a singular subject because another noun appears between them.
  • Writing criterias instead of criteria.
  • Assuming that every noun ending in -f changes to -ves.
  • Assuming that every noun ending in -o takes -es.
JAMB Exam Tip: Do not form a plural by guessing. Learn common irregular plurals and identify whether a noun is countable or uncountable. In sentence-completion questions, check whether the noun agrees with its verb and determiner.

8.11 Worked JAMB-Style Questions

Question 1: The principal gave the students useful ______ before their examination.

A. advices
B. advice
C. an advice
D. pieces advices

Answer: B. advice. Advice is an uncountable noun. It does not normally take a plural -s. The expression pieces of advice is also correct.

Question 2: The two ______ were invited to address the meeting.

A. woman
B. womans
C. women
D. womens

Answer: C. women. Women is the irregular plural form of woman.

Question 3: The laboratory purchased new ______ for the experiment.

A. equipments
B. equipment
C. an equipment
D. equipmentses

Answer: B. equipment. Equipment is generally uncountable and does not take a plural -s.

Question 4: Several ______ were observed during the scientific study.

A. phenomenon
B. phenomenons
C. phenomena
D. phenomenas

Answer: C. phenomena. Phenomena is the plural of phenomenon.

Question 5: The ______ of the two houses are respected teachers.

A. mother-in-laws
B. mothers-in-law
C. mothers-in-laws
D. mother-in-law

Answer: B. mothers-in-law. In this compound noun, mother is the main noun, so it takes the plural form.

8.12 Chapter Revision

  • Singular refers to one; plural refers to more than one.
  • Most nouns form plurals by adding -s or -es.
  • Some nouns have irregular plural forms, such as man/men and child/children.
  • Some nouns have the same singular and plural form, such as sheep and deer.
  • Uncountable nouns include advice, information, furniture and equipment.
  • Compound nouns usually take the plural ending on the main noun.
  • Foreign plurals include analysis/analyses and criterion/criteria.

8.13 Self-Assessment Questions

Choose the correct option in each question.

  1. The farmer bought five ______ for his farm. A. oxes B. oxen C. ox D. oxens
  2. She gave me two ______ of information. A. informations B. pieces C. information D. piece
  3. The ______ are grazing in the field. A. sheeps B. sheep C. sheepes D. shep
  4. The school has employed three new ______. A. woman teachers B. women teachers C. womens teachers D. womans teachers
  5. The research produced several important ______. A. analysis B. analysises C. analyses D. analysi

Answers: 1-B, 2-B, 3-B, 4-B, 5-C.

chapters.title: Concord: Subject-Verb Agreement
chapters.excerpt: Master the rules of concord, including singular and plural subjects, intervening phrases, collective nouns, indefinite pronouns and tricky examination sentences.
chapters.content:
9.1 Meaning of Concord

Concord is the grammatical agreement between words in a sentence. In JAMB Use of English, the most frequently tested form is subject-verb agreement. This means that the verb must agree with its subject in number and person.

A singular subject generally takes a singular verb, while a plural subject generally takes a plural verb.

Examples:

  • The boy plays football.
  • The boys play football.
  • My sister is at home.
  • My sisters are at home.

Notice that in the simple present tense, many verbs add -s or -es when the subject is third-person singular. The opposite happens with most plural subjects.

9.2 Rule One: A Singular Subject Takes a Singular Verb

A subject that refers to one person or thing normally takes a singular verb.

Examples:

  • The teacher explains the lesson.
  • My father drives carefully.
  • The child cries loudly.
  • Every student has a textbook.

Incorrect: The teacher explain the lesson.

Correct: The teacher explains the lesson.

9.3 Rule Two: A Plural Subject Takes a Plural Verb

A plural subject normally takes a plural verb.

Examples:

  • The teachers explain the lesson.
  • My parents live in Ibadan.
  • The children play outside.
  • The students have completed the assignment.

Remember that the verb be has different forms: is/am/are in the present and was/were in the past. Has and have also depend on the subject.

9.4 Rule Three: Words Between the Subject and Verb Do Not Change Agreement

One common JAMB trap is to place a phrase between the subject and its verb. Candidates sometimes mistakenly make the verb agree with the nearest noun instead of the actual subject.

Example: The box of books is on the table.

The subject is box, not books. The phrase of books only describes the box.

More examples:

  • The list of names is on the notice board.
  • The quality of the products has improved.
  • The students in the classroom are quiet.
  • The manager, together with his assistants, is attending the meeting.
Exam Tip: When a long phrase appears between the subject and verb, temporarily remove that phrase. Identify the main subject and choose the verb that agrees with it.

9.5 Rule Four: Subjects Joined by AND

Two or more subjects joined by and normally take a plural verb because they represent more than one person or thing.

Examples:

  • John and Peter are friends.
  • The teacher and the principal have arrived.
  • Rice and beans are my favourite meals.

However, when two words joined by and refer to one person, one thing or one combined idea, a singular verb may be used.

Example: The owner and manager of the shop is absent.

This sentence suggests that one person performs both roles. Compare it with: The owner and the manager are absent. Here, two different people are being discussed.

9.6 Rule Five: Subjects Joined by OR or NOR

When two subjects are joined by or or nor, the verb generally agrees with the subject nearest to it.

Examples:

  • Either the teacher or the students are responsible.
  • Either the students or the teacher is responsible.
  • Neither the boy nor his friends are ready.
  • Neither the friends nor the boy is ready.

This rule is known as the proximity principle. In a sentence with two subjects joined by either...or or neither...nor, examine the subject closest to the verb.

9.7 Rule Six: Each, Every, Everyone and Similar Expressions

Words such as each, every, everyone, everybody, someone, somebody, anyone, anybody, no one and nobody are grammatically singular in standard formal English.

Examples:

  • Everyone is expected to attend.
  • Each of the students has a textbook.
  • Every boy and every girl was invited.
  • Somebody has taken my pen.
  • Nobody knows the answer.

Incorrect: Each of the students have a textbook.

Correct: Each of the students has a textbook.

Although students is plural, the subject of the sentence is each.

9.8 Rule Seven: Either and Neither

When either or neither is used alone as the subject, it normally takes a singular verb.

Examples:

  • Either of the two answers is acceptable.
  • Neither of the boys has arrived.
  • Neither is suitable for the position.

Do not allow the plural noun after of to confuse you. In formal examination grammar, either of and neither of generally take singular verbs.

9.9 Rule Eight: Collective Nouns

Collective nouns refer to groups, such as family, committee, team, government, audience, staff and jury.

When the group is considered as one unit, use a singular verb.

Examples:

  • The committee has submitted its report.
  • The team is playing well.
  • The family lives in Lagos.

When attention is on the individual members, plural agreement may occur in British English.

Example: The committee are disagreeing among themselves.

In JAMB questions, examine the meaning of the sentence and the variety of English being used. Where the group acts as one unit, singular agreement is normally expected.

9.10 Rule Nine: Uncountable Nouns

Uncountable nouns are normally treated as singular and take singular verbs.

Examples:

  • The information is useful.
  • The furniture was expensive.
  • Water is essential for life.
  • His advice has helped me.
  • The equipment is new.

Incorrect: The information are useful.

Correct: The information is useful.

9.11 Rule Ten: Amounts, Measurements and Time

When an amount of money, distance, time or measurement is considered as one total quantity, it normally takes a singular verb.

Examples:

  • Ten thousand naira is enough for the purchase.
  • Five kilometres is a long distance to walk.
  • Two hours is sufficient for the examination.
  • Twenty kilograms is too heavy for the child.

However, when the units are considered separately, plural agreement may be appropriate.

9.12 Rule Eleven: Titles of Books, Films and Organisations

The title of a book, film, newspaper or other work is normally treated as singular, even when it contains a plural-looking word.

Examples:

  • Things Fall Apart is a famous African novel.
  • The United States is a country in North America.
  • Great Expectations is an interesting novel.

The grammatical subject is the title as one work or entity.

9.13 Rule Twelve: There Is and There Are

In sentences beginning with there, the verb agrees with the real subject that follows it.

Examples:

  • There is a book on the table.
  • There are two books on the table.
  • There was a problem yesterday.
  • There were several problems yesterday.

Do not choose is simply because the sentence begins with there. Identify the noun that follows the verb.

9.14 Rule Thirteen: Relative Pronouns

When who, which or that introduces a relative clause, the verb in the relative clause generally agrees with the noun or pronoun being referred to.

Examples:

  • She is one of the students who work hard.
  • He is the only student who works hard.
  • The books that are on the shelf belong to me.

In the first sentence, who refers to students, so work is plural. In the second sentence, who refers to the only student, so works is singular.

9.15 Rule Fourteen: A Number of and The Number of

These two expressions are often tested because they require different agreement.

  • A number of + plural noun: takes a plural verb. Example: A number of students are absent.
  • The number of + plural noun: takes a singular verb. Example: The number of students is increasing.

A number of means several. The number of refers to the total count as one figure.

9.16 Common Errors in Concord

  • Each of the players are ready. Correct: Each of the players is ready.
  • The list of items are missing. Correct: The list of items is missing.
  • Neither John nor his friends is present. Correct: Neither John nor his friends are present.
  • A number of people is waiting. Correct: A number of people are waiting.
  • The number of applicants are high. Correct: The number of applicants is high.
  • There is many reasons. Correct: There are many reasons.

9.17 Worked JAMB-Style Questions

Question 1: Each of the candidates ______ expected to arrive early.

A. are
B. were
C. is
D. have

Answer: C. is. Each is singular and takes a singular verb.

Question 2: The quality of the products ______ improved considerably.

A. have
B. has
C. are
D. were

Answer: B. has. The subject is quality, not products. Quality is singular.

Question 3: Neither the principal nor the teachers ______ available.

A. is
B. was
C. are
D. has

Answer: C. are. With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, teachers.

Question 4: A number of students ______ applied for admission.

A. has
B. is
C. have
D. was

Answer: C. have. A number of means several and takes a plural verb.

Question 5: The number of students in the school ______ increasing.

A. are
B. have
C. were
D. is

Answer: D. is. The number refers to one total figure and takes a singular verb.

9.18 Chapter Revision

  • A singular subject normally takes a singular verb.
  • A plural subject normally takes a plural verb.
  • A phrase between the subject and verb does not change the subject.
  • Subjects joined by and usually take plural verbs.
  • With either...or and neither...nor, the verb generally agrees with the nearer subject.
  • Each, everyone, everybody, somebody and nobody are singular.
  • Uncountable nouns generally take singular verbs.
  • A number of takes a plural verb; the number of takes a singular verb.
  • There is and there are depend on the real subject that follows.

9.19 Self-Assessment Questions

  1. Every one of the players ______ a certificate. A. have B. has C. are D. were
  2. The teacher, together with the pupils, ______ attending the programme. A. are B. were C. is D. have
  3. Neither the boys nor their father ______ arrived. A. have B. are C. has D. were
  4. Five hundred naira ______ not enough for the item. A. are B. were C. have D. is
  5. There ______ several reasons for his decision. A. is B. are C. was D. has
  6. The news ______ encouraging. A. are B. have C. is D. were

Answers: 1-B, 2-C, 3-C, 4-D, 5-B, 6-C.

chapters.title: Question Tags
chapters.excerpt: Learn how to form correct question tags using auxiliary verbs, positive and negative statements, special expressions and common exceptions.
chapters.content:
10.1 Meaning of Question Tags

A question tag is a short question added to the end of a statement. It is commonly used to ask for confirmation, check information or encourage someone to agree with the speaker.

Examples:

  • You are a student, aren't you?
  • She has finished the work, hasn't she?
  • They came yesterday, didn't they?

The short question at the end of each statement is the question tag.

10.2 The Basic Rule

The most important rule is that a positive statement normally takes a negative tag, while a negative statement normally takes a positive tag.

StatementQuestion tag
He is a doctor,isn't he?
She can swim,can't she?
They are not ready,are they?
We did not win,did we?
You have arrived,haven't you?

Positive and negative in this rule refer to the grammatical form of the statement, not whether the information is good or bad.

10.3 Rule One: Use the Auxiliary Verb in the Statement

If the statement contains an auxiliary verb, repeat that auxiliary in the tag. Change it to the opposite polarity.

Examples:

  • She is reading, isn't she?
  • They are working, aren't they?
  • He has eaten, hasn't he?
  • We have finished, haven't we?
  • You will come, won't you?
  • They can drive, can't they?
  • He should apologise, shouldn't he?

Do not introduce a different auxiliary when the correct one is already present.

10.4 Rule Two: Use Do, Does or Did When There Is No Auxiliary

In simple present and simple past statements that do not contain an auxiliary verb, use do, does or did in the tag.

Examples:

  • You like football, don't you?
  • She speaks French, doesn't she?
  • They play well, don't they?
  • He went to school, didn't he?
  • Mary cooked dinner, didn't she?

Use does for a third-person singular subject in the simple present, do for I, you, we, they and plural subjects, and did for all subjects in the simple past.

10.5 Rule Three: The Pronoun in the Tag

The subject in the tag is normally a pronoun that refers to the subject of the statement.

  • John is here, isn't he?
  • Mary is here, isn't she?
  • The children are playing, aren't they?
  • Your father has arrived, hasn't he?
  • The car is new, isn't it?

Do not repeat the noun as the tag subject. Use the correct personal pronoun.

10.6 Rule Four: Negative Statements Take Positive Tags

A statement containing a negative auxiliary or negative expression normally takes a positive tag.

Examples:

  • He isn't serious, is he?
  • They haven't arrived, have they?
  • She cannot swim, can she?
  • You don't know him, do you?
  • We never met before, did we?

Words such as never, nobody, no one, nothing, hardly, scarcely and seldom have negative meanings. They normally take positive question tags.

Examples:

  • She never comes late, does she?
  • Nobody called you, did they?
  • Nothing happened, did it?
  • He hardly speaks, does he?

10.7 Rule Five: The Special Case of I Am

The normal question tag for a positive statement beginning with I am is aren't I?

Example: I am late, aren't I?

For a negative statement, use am I?

Example: I am not disturbing you, am I?

This is a special conventional form. Do not use amn't I in standard examination English.

10.8 Rule Six: Imperative Sentences

Imperative sentences give instructions, commands, requests or advice. Their tags commonly use will you? or won't you? depending on the tone and construction.

Examples:

  • Open the door, will you?
  • Please help me, will you?
  • Don't make noise, will you?
  • Have a seat, won't you?

These forms can vary with meaning and tone. For JAMB, pay attention to the command and the expected conventional tag.

10.9 Rule Seven: Let's and Let Us

When let's is used to make a suggestion involving the speaker and listener, the tag is shall we?

Examples:

  • Let's go home, shall we?
  • Let's begin the lesson, shall we?
  • Let's help the poor, shall we?

Do not confuse let's with let us in a request for permission or instruction addressed to another person. The meaning and sentence structure matter.

10.10 Rule Eight: There and This/That

When a statement begins with there, the tag uses there.

Examples:

  • There is a problem, isn't there?
  • There are many students, aren't there?
  • There wasn't enough food, was there?

When the subject is this or that, the tag normally uses it. When the subject is these or those, use they.

  • This is your bag, isn't it?
  • That was difficult, wasn't it?
  • These are your books, aren't they?
  • Those were expensive, weren't they?

10.11 Rule Nine: Everybody, Someone, Nobody and Similar Words

Indefinite pronouns such as everybody, everyone, somebody, someone, nobody and no one are grammatically singular in the statement. However, they commonly take they in the question tag when referring to people.

Examples:

  • Everybody is ready, aren't they?
  • Someone has taken my pen, haven't they?
  • Nobody complained, did they?
  • Everyone enjoyed the party, didn't they?

In some formal contexts, he or she may appear, but singular they is widely accepted in modern English. Follow the sentence and examination convention provided.

10.12 Rule Ten: Must and Other Modal Verbs

When must, should, could, would, may or might is used as an auxiliary, the same modal is normally used in the tag.

Examples:

  • You must obey the rules, mustn't you?
  • She should apologise, shouldn't she?
  • They could have waited, couldn't they?
  • He would help us, wouldn't he?

Must can express different meanings, including obligation and logical deduction. Some sentences may therefore require interpretation rather than mechanical substitution. In ordinary obligation statements, mustn't you? is a common tag.

10.13 Common JAMB Mistakes

  • He is coming, doesn't he? Correct: He is coming, isn't he?
  • She does not sing, doesn't she? Correct: She does not sing, does she?
  • Let's go, will we? Correct: Let's go, shall we?
  • I am correct, amn't I? Correct: I am correct, aren't I?
  • Nobody came, didn't nobody? Correct: Nobody came, did they?
Exam Tip: First identify whether the statement is positive or negative. Next, locate the auxiliary verb. Finally, choose the correct pronoun. This three-step method solves most question-tag problems.

10.14 Worked JAMB-Style Questions

Question 1: The students have submitted their assignments, ______?

A. haven't they
B. have they
C. don't they
D. didn't they

Answer: A. haven't they. The statement is positive and uses have as an auxiliary. The tag is negative.

Question 2: She hardly visits her parents, ______?

A. doesn't she
B. does she
C. isn't she
D. did she

Answer: B. does she. Hardly has a negative meaning, so the tag is positive. The statement is in the simple present.

Question 3: Let's discuss the matter, ______?

A. will we
B. do we
C. shall we
D. won't we

Answer: C. shall we. Let's used for a suggestion normally takes shall we?

Question 4: I am your friend, ______?

A. am I
B. amn't I
C. aren't I
D. isn't it

Answer: C. aren't I. Aren't I is the conventional question tag for a positive I am statement.

Question 5: Nobody informed the manager, ______?

A. didn't they
B. did they
C. were they
D. don't they

Answer: B. did they. Nobody is negative in meaning, so the tag is positive. The simple past requires did.

10.15 Chapter Revision

  • Positive statements normally take negative tags.
  • Negative statements normally take positive tags.
  • Repeat the auxiliary verb when one is present.
  • Use do, does or did when the statement has no auxiliary.
  • Use the correct pronoun in the tag.
  • I am takes aren't I? in a positive statement.
  • Let's normally takes shall we?
  • Negative expressions such as hardly and nobody take positive tags.
  • There in the statement remains there in the tag.

10.16 Self-Assessment Questions

  1. She has completed the task, ______? A. has she B. hasn't she C. doesn't she D. didn't she
  2. They seldom attend the meetings, ______? A. do they B. don't they C. are they D. have they
  3. Open your books, ______? A. shall we B. will you C. don't we D. aren't you
  4. There were many people at the event, ______? A. were there B. wasn't there C. weren't there D. didn't they
  5. Let's leave now, ______? A. shall we B. will you C. do we D. aren't we
  6. He does not understand the question, ______? A. doesn't he B. does he C. is he D. did he

Answers: 1-B, 2-A, 3-B, 4-C, 5-A, 6-B.

chapters.title: Comparison: Positive, Comparative and Superlative Forms
chapters.excerpt: Learn how to compare people, places and things using adjectives and adverbs, including irregular forms, double comparatives and common errors.
chapters.content:
11.1 Meaning of Comparison

Comparison is the grammatical process of showing the degree to which people, animals, places, things or actions possess a particular quality. In English, adjectives and some adverbs have three degrees of comparison: positive, comparative and superlative.

Examples using the adjective tall:

  • Positive: tall
  • Comparative: taller
  • Superlative: tallest

The positive form describes a quality without making a comparison. The comparative form compares two people or things. The superlative form identifies the highest or lowest degree among three or more people or things.

11.2 The Positive Degree

The positive degree is the basic form of an adjective or adverb. It describes a quality without showing that one person or thing has more of it than another.

Examples:

  • The girl is intelligent.
  • This road is wide.
  • He runs quickly.
  • The water is cold.

The positive degree can also be used in equality comparisons with as...as and not as...as.

Examples:

  • Mary is as tall as Jane.
  • This book is as interesting as that one.
  • John is not as strong as Peter.
  • The second test was not as difficult as the first.

11.3 The Comparative Degree

The comparative degree is used mainly to compare two people or things. Short adjectives generally form the comparative by adding -er.

PositiveComparative
TallTaller
ShortShorter
FastFaster
SmallSmaller
YoungYounger
CheapCheaper

Longer adjectives generally use more before the adjective.

  • Beautiful → more beautiful
  • Interesting → more interesting
  • Expensive → more expensive
  • Intelligent → more intelligent
  • Comfortable → more comfortable

The comparative degree is commonly followed by than.

Examples:

  • My brother is taller than I am.
  • This phone is more expensive than that one.
  • Her explanation is clearer than mine.

11.4 The Superlative Degree

The superlative degree expresses the highest or lowest degree of a quality among three or more people or things.

Short adjectives generally form the superlative by adding -est.

PositiveComparativeSuperlative
TallTallerTallest
ShortShorterShortest
FastFasterFastest
SmallSmallerSmallest
YoungYoungerYoungest

Longer adjectives generally use most before the adjective.

  • Beautiful → most beautiful
  • Interesting → most interesting
  • Expensive → most expensive
  • Intelligent → most intelligent

Examples:

  • She is the tallest girl in the class.
  • This is the most interesting book I have read.
  • He is the most intelligent candidate in the group.

The superlative is commonly preceded by the, although there are contexts in which another determiner or possessive is used.

11.5 Spelling Rules for Comparison

Rule 1: Add -er and -est

Most short adjectives take -er and -est.

Examples: cold/colder/coldest; dark/darker/darkest; quick/quicker/quickest.

Rule 2: Adjectives ending in -e

Add -r for the comparative and -st for the superlative.

Examples: large/larger/largest; wise/wiser/wisest; nice/nicer/nicest.

Rule 3: Consonant + y

Change y to i before adding -er or -est.

Examples: happy/happier/happiest; easy/easier/easiest; busy/busier/busiest; heavy/heavier/heaviest.

Rule 4: Short vowel followed by a consonant

For many short adjectives with a single final consonant preceded by a short vowel, double the final consonant before adding -er or -est.

Examples: big/bigger/biggest; hot/hotter/hottest; thin/thinner/thinnest; fat/fatter/fattest.

This rule does not apply to every word. For example, new becomes newer and newest.

11.6 Irregular Forms of Comparison

Some adjectives and adverbs have irregular comparative and superlative forms. These forms must be learnt because they cannot be predicted by simply adding -er or using more.

PositiveComparativeSuperlative
GoodBetterBest
BadWorseWorst
FarFarther/FurtherFarthest/Furthest
LittleLessLeast
MuchMoreMost
ManyMoreMost
WellBetterBest

Good and bad are adjectives. Well is commonly an adverb meaning in a good manner, though it can also be an adjective meaning healthy.

Farther often refers to physical distance, while further can refer to additional distance or degree. In many contexts, further is also used for physical distance.

11.7 Comparison of Adverbs

Adverbs can also be compared. Short adverbs may take -er and -est, while many adverbs ending in -ly use more and most.

Examples:

  • Fast/faster/fastest
  • Hard/harder/hardest
  • Carefully/more carefully/most carefully
  • Slowly/more slowly/most slowly
  • Beautifully/more beautifully/most beautifully

Examples in sentences:

  • Chidi runs faster than Emeka.
  • She completed the work more carefully than her colleague.
  • Of all the players, Musa performed best.

11.8 Using As...As

As...as is used to express equality or similarity in degree. The adjective or adverb remains in its positive form.

Examples:

  • She is as intelligent as her brother.
  • The new road is as wide as the old one.
  • He works as carefully as his supervisor.

Incorrect: She is as taller as her sister.

Correct: She is as tall as her sister.

11.9 Using Less and Least

Less expresses a lower degree when comparing two people or things. Least expresses the lowest degree among a group.

Examples:

  • This exercise is less difficult than the previous one.
  • He is the least experienced member of the team.
  • My new bag is less expensive than yours.

Less and least can also be used with uncountable nouns, while fewer and fewest are normally used with countable plural nouns.

Examples:

  • There is less water in this bottle.
  • There are fewer students in the classroom today.
  • She made fewer mistakes than I did.

11.10 Avoid Double Comparatives and Superlatives

Do not normally use more with an adjective that already has the comparative ending -er. Similarly, do not combine most with an adjective that already has the superlative ending -est.

Incorrect: more taller.

Correct: taller.

Incorrect: most tallest.

Correct: tallest.

Incorrect: more better.

Correct: better.

Incorrect: most happiest.

Correct: happiest.

11.11 Comparison Structures That JAMB May Test

The + comparative, the + comparative: This structure shows that a change in one thing is connected to a change in another.

Examples:

  • The harder you work, the better your result will be.
  • The more you practise, the more confident you become.
  • The older he becomes, the wiser he grows.

Comparative + and + comparative: This structure shows a continuous increase or decrease.

Examples:

  • The weather is getting hotter and hotter.
  • Life is becoming more and more expensive.
  • The situation grew worse and worse.

One of the + superlative + plural noun: The noun following the superlative is plural.

Examples:

  • She is one of the best students in the school.
  • Lagos is one of the largest cities in Nigeria.
  • This is one of the most useful books in the library.

11.12 Common JAMB Errors

  • More better → better.
  • Most tallest → tallest.
  • As stronger as → as strong as.
  • One of the best student → one of the best students.
  • She is more wiser → she is wiser.
  • He runs more faster → he runs faster.
  • Fewer water → less water.
  • Less books → fewer books.
JAMB Exam Tip: Identify whether the sentence compares two things or a group of three or more. Use the comparative for two and the superlative for the highest or lowest degree in a group. Check for double comparison before selecting an answer.

11.13 Worked JAMB-Style Questions

Question 1: Of the three candidates, Amina is the ______.

A. intelligent
B. more intelligent
C. most intelligent
D. intelligently

Answer: C. most intelligent. The sentence compares three candidates, so the superlative form is required.

Question 2: This road is ______ than the one we used yesterday.

A. narrow
B. narrower
C. narrowest
D. most narrowest

Answer: B. narrower. The sentence compares two roads, so the comparative form is needed.

Question 3: The more you read, the ______ your vocabulary becomes.

A. rich
B. richest
C. richer
D. more richest

Answer: C. richer. The correct structure is the more..., the richer...

Question 4: She is one of the ______ players in the team.

A. good
B. better
C. best
D. more better

Answer: C. best. One of the is followed by a superlative and a plural noun.

Question 5: There are ______ errors in this essay than in the previous one.

A. less
B. fewer
C. least
D. little

Answer: B. fewer. Errors are countable plural nouns, so fewer is appropriate.

11.14 Chapter Revision

  • Positive degree is the basic form.
  • Comparative degree usually compares two people or things.
  • Superlative degree identifies the highest or lowest degree in a group.
  • Short adjectives often take -er and -est.
  • Long adjectives often use more and most.
  • Good/better/best and bad/worse/worst are irregular forms.
  • As...as takes the positive form.
  • Do not use double comparatives or double superlatives.
  • Use fewer with countable plural nouns and less with uncountable nouns in standard usage.

11.15 Self-Assessment Questions

  1. Of all the girls, Ngozi is the ______. A. taller B. tallest C. more tall D. most taller
  2. This question is ______ than the previous one. A. difficult B. most difficult C. more difficult D. difficultest
  3. He performed ______ than his brother. A. good B. best C. better D. more better
  4. The ______ you practise, the more confident you become. A. much B. most C. more D. many
  5. There are ______ mistakes in this answer than in the first. A. less B. fewer C. least D. little
  6. She is as ______ as her mother. A. wiser B. wisest C. wise D. more wise

Answers: 1-B, 2-C, 3-C, 4-C, 5-B, 6-C.

chapters.title: Punctuation Marks and Their Uses
chapters.excerpt: Understand full stops, commas, semicolons, colons, apostrophes, quotation marks, question marks and other punctuation marks tested in English examinations.
chapters.content:
12.1 Meaning of Punctuation

Punctuation refers to the marks used in writing to organise sentences, separate ideas, show pauses, indicate questions, express strong feelings and make meaning clear. Correct punctuation helps readers understand the writer's message.

Consider these two sentences:

Let's eat, Grandma.

Let's eat Grandma.

The comma in the first sentence shows that Grandma is being addressed. Without it, the second sentence appears to suggest that Grandma is the food. This example shows why punctuation is important.

12.2 The Full Stop (.)

A full stop, also called a period, is used mainly at the end of a complete declarative sentence or statement.

Examples:

  • The examination begins at nine o'clock.
  • My brother lives in Abuja.
  • Education is important for national development.

It is also used in some abbreviations, although many modern writing styles omit full stops in common abbreviations and titles.

Do not use a full stop where a question mark or exclamation mark is required.

12.3 The Comma (,)

A comma indicates a short pause and helps separate parts of a sentence. It is one of the most frequently used punctuation marks.

Use 1: Separating items in a list

Examples:

  • She bought rice, beans, tomatoes and onions.
  • The subjects are English, Mathematics, Biology and Chemistry.

A comma before and in a list is called the serial or Oxford comma. Its use depends on the style being followed, but it can improve clarity when list items are complex.

Use 2: Separating introductory expressions

Examples:

  • After the examination, the students went home.
  • Fortunately, nobody was injured.
  • In my opinion, the decision was correct.

Use 3: Separating a person being addressed

Examples:

  • Mary, please close the door.
  • Thank you, sir.
  • Can you help me, David?

Use 4: Separating additional information

Examples:

  • Mr Ade, our English teacher, is absent today.
  • Lagos, which is a major commercial centre, attracts many visitors.

Use 5: Separating clauses in certain sentence structures

Examples:

  • I wanted to attend the meeting, but I was ill.
  • Although it was raining, the match continued.
  • She studied hard, so she passed the examination.

A comma is not normally placed between a subject and its verb.

Incorrect: The students in the classroom, are writing.

Correct: The students in the classroom are writing.

12.4 The Question Mark (?)

A question mark is placed at the end of a direct question.

Examples:

  • Where do you live?
  • Have you completed your assignment?
  • Why were you absent yesterday?

It is not normally used after an indirect question.

Direct question: She asked, "Where is the station?"

Indirect question: She asked where the station was.

The second sentence is a statement reporting a question, so it ends with a full stop.

12.5 The Exclamation Mark (!)

An exclamation mark expresses strong emotion, surprise, excitement, anger, pain or a forceful command.

Examples:

  • What a wonderful performance!
  • Stop!
  • How beautiful the house is!
  • Alas! We have lost the match.

Use it carefully in formal writing. Too many exclamation marks can make writing look informal or exaggerated.

12.6 The Semicolon (;)

A semicolon is stronger than a comma but weaker than a full stop. It can connect two closely related independent clauses that are not joined by a coordinating conjunction.

Examples:

  • The examination was difficult; many candidates struggled.
  • She studied throughout the night; she was determined to succeed.
  • The rain stopped; the players returned to the field.

A semicolon can also separate complex items in a list, especially when those items already contain commas.

Example: The invited guests came from Lagos, Nigeria; Accra, Ghana; and Nairobi, Kenya.

Do not use a semicolon to join a dependent clause to an independent clause without the appropriate structure.

12.7 The Colon (:)

A colon introduces an explanation, a list, an example or a statement that expands on what comes before it.

Examples:

  • Bring the following items: a pen, a ruler and a calculator.
  • She had one ambition: to become a doctor.
  • The result was clear: the team had won.

The words before a colon should generally form a complete introductory statement when the colon is introducing a list.

12.8 The Apostrophe (')

An apostrophe is used mainly to show possession or to indicate omitted letters in contractions.

Use 1: Singular possession

Add apostrophe and s to a singular noun to show possession.

  • The girl's bag.
  • The teacher's office.
  • James's book is missing.

Some style guides use only an apostrophe after certain names ending in s, but adding 's is also widely accepted. Follow the convention used in the text.

Use 2: Plural possession

For regular plural nouns ending in s, add only an apostrophe.

  • The students' books.
  • The teachers' meeting.
  • The girls' hostel.

For irregular plural nouns that do not end in s, add apostrophe and s.

  • The children's toys.
  • The men's room.
  • The women's association.

Use 3: Contractions

An apostrophe shows that one or more letters have been omitted.

ContractionFull form
Don'tDo not
Can'tCannot
I'mI am
They'reThey are
We'veWe have
It'sIt is or it has
You'reYou are
Who'sWho is or who has

Its and It's

This distinction is important in examinations.

  • Its: Possessive form of it. Example: The dog wagged its tail.
  • It's: Contraction of it is or it has. Example: It's raining. It's been a long day.

Your and You're

  • Your: Shows possession. Example: Your book is here.
  • You're: Means you are. Example: You're welcome.

12.9 Quotation Marks (" ")

Quotation marks are used to show the exact words spoken or written by someone. They are also called inverted commas.

Examples:

  • The teacher said, "Read the passage carefully."
  • Mary asked, "Have you seen my bag?"
  • He replied, "I will return tomorrow."

Quotation marks may also be used around titles of short works or to indicate a word being discussed, depending on the writing style. Single quotation marks may be used for a quotation within another quotation.

Example: The teacher said, "The word 'honest' begins with a vowel sound."

12.10 The Hyphen (-)

A hyphen joins words or parts of words to form a compound expression or to avoid confusion.

Examples:

  • Well-known author.
  • Twenty-one students.
  • Mother-in-law.
  • Part-time worker.
  • Thirty-five candidates.

Hyphens are also used in some compound adjectives before a noun: a well-written essay, a five-year-old child and a full-time job.

12.11 The Dash (—)

A dash marks a break in thought, an interruption or an explanatory addition. It is generally longer than a hyphen.

Examples:

  • My brother — the youngest in the family — has travelled abroad.
  • She had only one choice — to tell the truth.
  • I wanted to explain — but nobody listened.

12.12 Brackets or Parentheses ( )

Brackets are used to add extra information that is not essential to the main sentence.

Examples:

  • Chinua Achebe (the author of Things Fall Apart) was a Nigerian writer.
  • The meeting will hold tomorrow (if there is no change in the programme).

The main sentence should remain grammatically complete when the extra information is removed.

12.13 Common Punctuation Errors

  • Using an apostrophe to form ordinary plurals: book's instead of books.
  • Confusing its with it's.
  • Putting a comma between a subject and its verb.
  • Using a question mark after an indirect question.
  • Using a comma where a full stop or semicolon is needed to separate independent clauses.
  • Leaving out commas when directly addressing someone.
  • Confusing a hyphen with a dash.
  • Using apostrophes incorrectly in plural possession.
JAMB Exam Tip: In punctuation questions, read the entire sentence before selecting an answer. Ask what relationship exists between the clauses: a list, direct question, quotation, possession, explanation or independent statement. The meaning determines the correct punctuation mark.

12.14 Worked JAMB-Style Questions

Question 1: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?

A. The students, are writing their examination.
B. The students are writing, their examination.
C. The students are writing their examination.
D. The students are, writing their examination.

Answer: C. No comma is needed between the subject, verb and object in this simple sentence.

Question 2: Choose the sentence that correctly shows possession by several girls.

A. The girl's bags are missing.
B. The girls bags are missing.
C. The girls' bags are missing.
D. The girls's bags are missing.

Answer: C. Girls is a regular plural noun ending in s. Add only an apostrophe to show possession.

Question 3: Choose the correctly punctuated direct question.

A. Where are you going.
B. Where are you going!
C. Where are you going?
D. Where, are you going.

Answer: C. A direct question ends with a question mark.

Question 4: The dog wagged ______ tail.

A. it's
B. its
C. it is
D. its'

Answer: B. its. Its is the possessive form of it. It's means it is or it has.

Question 5: Which punctuation mark is most appropriate to introduce the list in the sentence: "The following items are required ___ a pen, a ruler and an eraser"?

A. Comma
B. Apostrophe
C. Colon
D. Question mark

Answer: C. Colon. A colon introduces the list.

12.15 Chapter Revision

  • Full stop ends a statement.
  • Comma separates list items and certain sentence elements.
  • Question mark ends a direct question.
  • Exclamation mark expresses strong feeling.
  • Semicolon joins closely related independent clauses.
  • Colon introduces a list, explanation or example.
  • Apostrophe shows possession or omitted letters.
  • Quotation marks show direct speech or quotations.
  • Hyphens join parts of compound words.
  • Brackets enclose additional information.

12.16 Self-Assessment Questions

  1. Which sentence is correct? A. Its a beautiful day. B. It's a beautiful day. C. Its' a beautiful day. D. It,s a beautiful day.
  2. Choose the correct possessive form: The ______ uniforms were washed. A. boys B. boy's C. boys' D. boys's
  3. Which mark introduces a list? A. Apostrophe B. Colon C. Question mark D. Hyphen
  4. Which punctuation mark ends a direct question? A. Full stop B. Comma C. Question mark D. Semicolon
  5. Choose the correctly punctuated sentence. A. Let's eat Grandma. B. Let's eat, Grandma. C. Lets eat, Grandma. D. Lets, eat Grandma.
  6. Which sentence is correctly punctuated? A. She asked where I lived? B. She asked, where I lived. C. She asked where I lived. D. She asked where, I lived.

Answers: 1-B, 2-C, 3-B, 4-C, 5-B, 6-C.

chapters.title: Spelling, Commonly Confused Words and Common Errors
chapters.excerpt: Improve spelling accuracy, distinguish commonly confused words, identify frequent grammatical errors and avoid mistakes in JAMB Use of English.
chapters.content:
13.1 The Importance of Correct Spelling

Spelling is the correct arrangement of letters in a word. A word may be pronounced correctly but still be written wrongly. Correct spelling is important because it helps readers understand written communication and distinguishes words that may have similar sounds.

In JAMB Use of English, candidates may encounter questions involving commonly confused words, correct word forms, spelling patterns and errors in sentence construction. Careful reading is therefore essential.

13.2 Common English Spelling Patterns

Rule 1: Words ending in -ie and -ei

Many learners remember the expression "i before e except after c", but this is not a rule without exceptions. It is only a general spelling guide.

Examples with ie:

  • Believe
  • Chief
  • Field
  • Piece
  • Friend

Examples with ei after c:

  • Receive
  • Ceiling
  • Deceive
  • Receipt

Important exceptions include weird, seize, foreign and leisure. Learn frequently used words rather than depending completely on the rhyme.

Rule 2: Doubling consonants when adding endings

Some words double their final consonant when adding endings such as -ing, -ed, -er or -est. This commonly happens when a one-syllable word ends in a single consonant preceded by a single short vowel.

Examples:

  • Run → running
  • Stop → stopped
  • Big → bigger
  • Hot → hottest
  • Swim → swimming

Do not double the consonant unnecessarily.

Examples: open/opening, visit/visited, clean/cleaning.

Rule 3: Dropping final e

When a word ends in a silent e, the e is often dropped before adding a suffix that begins with a vowel.

Examples:

  • Make → making
  • Write → writing
  • Hope → hoping
  • Dance → dancing
  • Use → using

However, the final e is normally retained before suffixes beginning with a consonant.

Examples: hope/hopeful, care/careless, use/useful.

Rule 4: Changing y to i

When a word ends in consonant + y, the y often changes to i before adding certain suffixes.

Examples:

  • Happy → happiness
  • Easy → easier
  • Carry → carried
  • Beauty → beautiful

But when adding -ing, the y is normally retained: carrying, studying, playing.

When a vowel comes before y, the y is normally retained: enjoy/enjoyed, play/played.

13.3 Commonly Confused Words

Some English words look or sound alike but have different meanings and grammatical uses. JAMB may test whether a candidate understands the difference in context.

WordMeaning and example
AcceptTo receive or agree to something. She accepted the offer.
ExceptExcluding. Everyone came except John.
AdviceA noun meaning guidance. His advice was helpful.
AdviseA verb meaning to give guidance. I advise you to study.
AffectUsually a verb meaning to influence. Rain may affect the journey.
EffectUsually a noun meaning result. The medicine had an effect.
LooseNot tight. The shirt is loose.
LoseTo misplace or fail to win. Do not lose your key.
PrincipalThe head of a school or something most important. The principal spoke.
PrincipleA rule or belief. Honesty is an important principle.
StationaryNot moving. The vehicle remained stationary.
StationeryWriting materials. I bought some stationery.
ComplementSomething that completes or goes well with another. The shoes complement the dress.
ComplimentAn expression of praise. She received a compliment.
WeatherConditions of the atmosphere. The weather is cold.
WhetherExpresses a choice or possibility. I do not know whether he will come.
PeaceFreedom from conflict. The country needs peace.
PieceA part of something. Give me a piece of bread.
ThereRefers to a place or introduces a statement. Put it there.
TheirShows possession. Their house is large.
They'reMeans they are. They're coming.
YourShows possession. Your bag is here.
You'reMeans you are. You're welcome.
ItsPossessive form of it. The dog wagged its tail.
It'sMeans it is or it has. It's raining.

13.4 More Words Commonly Confused in Examinations

  • Beside: At the side of. The school is beside the hospital.
  • Besides: In addition to. Besides English, she studies French.
  • Among: Used for more than two people or things in many contexts. The prize was shared among the students.
  • Between: Commonly used for two people or things, and also for distinct individual relationships involving more than two. The agreement was made between the three countries.
  • Borrow: To receive something temporarily. May I borrow your pen?
  • Lend: To give something temporarily. Please lend me your pen.
  • Bring: To carry something towards the speaker or a stated destination. Bring your book here.
  • Take: To carry something away from the speaker or to another place. Take this book to the office.
  • Emigrate: To leave one's country to live elsewhere. He emigrated from Nigeria.
  • Immigrate: To enter another country to live there. She immigrated to Canada.
  • Ensure: To make certain. Ensure that the door is locked.
  • Insure: To provide financial protection through insurance. They insured the vehicle.
  • Allusion: An indirect reference. The poem contains an allusion to history.
  • Illusion: A false impression. The magician created an illusion.
  • Personal: Belonging to an individual. This is my personal opinion.
  • Personnel: The employees of an organisation. The personnel were trained.

13.5 Commonly Misspelt Words

The following words are frequently misspelt by learners. Study their correct forms.

Correct spellingCommon wrong spelling
AccommodationAcommodation
AchievementAchievment
ArgumentArguement
BeginningBegining
BusinessBussiness
CommitteeComittee
DefinitelyDefinately
EnvironmentEnviroment
GovernmentGoverment
IndependentIndependant
NecessaryNeccessary
OccasionOcassion
OccurrenceOccurence
PrivilegePriviledge
SeparateSeperate
SuccessfulSuccesful
TomorrowTommorrow
ReceiveRecieve
RecommendReccommend
MaintenanceMaintainance
EmbarrassEmbarass
QuestionnaireQuestionaire
ConscienceConcience
PronunciationPronounciation

13.6 Common Grammatical and Usage Errors

Some errors occur because learners translate directly from their first language or use expressions that sound familiar but are not standard English. JAMB may test the correct form in sentence-completion or error-identification questions.

Error 1: Wrong use of discuss

Incorrect: We discussed about the matter.

Correct: We discussed the matter.

Discuss is a transitive verb and normally takes its object directly without about.

Error 2: Wrong use of explain

Incorrect: Please explain me the problem.

Correct: Please explain the problem to me.

The correct structure is explain something to someone.

Error 3: Wrong use of prefer

Incorrect: I prefer rice than beans.

Correct: I prefer rice to beans.

The standard structure is prefer one thing to another.

Error 4: Wrong use of request

Incorrect: She requested for assistance.

Correct: She requested assistance.

In standard formal English, request can take an object directly. The expression make a request for assistance is also correct.

Error 5: Wrong use of order

Incorrect: The teacher ordered the students to not make noise.

Better formal construction: The teacher ordered the students not to make noise.

Error 6: Wrong use of despite and although

Incorrect: Despite he was tired, he continued working.

Correct: Although he was tired, he continued working.

Correct: Despite being tired, he continued working.

Although introduces a clause, while despite is followed by a noun, pronoun or -ing form.

Error 7: Wrong use of unless

Incorrect: Unless you do not study, you will fail.

Correct: Unless you study, you may fail.

Unless already has a negative meaning similar to if not. Avoid adding another negative unless the meaning specifically requires it.

Error 8: Wrong use of one of

Incorrect: She is one of the best student in the class.

Correct: She is one of the best students in the class.

One of is followed by a plural noun.

Error 9: Wrong use of married

Incorrect: She is married with a doctor.

Correct: She is married to a doctor.

Error 10: Wrong use of enter

Incorrect: He entered into the room.

Correct: He entered the room.

Enter normally takes a direct object without into. Enter into is correct in other expressions, such as enter into an agreement.

Error 11: Wrong use of return back

Incorrect: Please return back tomorrow.

Correct: Please return tomorrow.

Return already means to come or go back. Back is usually unnecessary.

Error 12: Wrong use of more preferable

Incorrect: This option is more preferable.

Correct: This option is preferable.

Preferable already expresses suitability in comparison, so more is generally unnecessary.

13.7 British and American Spelling

English has different spelling conventions, especially between British and American English. JAMB generally follows British English conventions. Candidates should recognise common British forms.

British EnglishAmerican English
ColourColor
LabourLabor
CentreCenter
TheatreTheater
OrganiseOrganize
RecogniseRecognize
TravellingTraveling
CancelledCanceled
DefenceDefense
Licence (noun)License (noun)
Practise (verb)Practice (verb)
ProgrammeProgram

Some British forms use -ise while American English commonly uses -ize. British English also distinguishes licence as a noun from license as a verb, and practice as a noun from practise as a verb.

13.8 Common Word-Form Errors

Words may have related forms that perform different grammatical functions. Learn to identify whether a sentence requires a noun, verb, adjective or adverb.

NounVerbAdjectiveAdverb
BeautyBeautifyBeautifulBeautifully
SuccessSucceedSuccessfulSuccessfully
DecisionDecideDecisiveDecisively
CareCareCarefulCarefully
StrengthStrengthenStrongStrongly
DifferenceDifferDifferentDifferently

Examples:

  • She made a wise decision. (Noun)
  • She must decide quickly. (Verb)
  • That was a decisive action. (Adjective)
  • He acted decisively. (Adverb)

In a sentence-completion question, examine the word immediately before and after the gap to determine the grammatical form required.

13.9 Strategies for Avoiding Spelling and Usage Errors

  1. Read the whole sentence: Do not choose a word based only on how it sounds.
  2. Identify the grammatical function: Decide whether the gap requires a noun, verb, adjective or adverb.
  3. Check the meaning: Words such as accept and except have different meanings even though they look similar.
  4. Look for collocations: English words commonly occur together. For example, make a decision, take a risk, pay attention and do homework.
  5. Learn difficult spellings: Keep a list of words you frequently misspell and revise them regularly.
  6. Use British English consistently: Become familiar with the spelling conventions commonly used in Nigerian formal education.
  7. Proofread: Read your written work again to identify missing letters, repeated letters and incorrect word forms.
JAMB Exam Tip: When two options look similar, do not rush. Read the sentence for meaning and grammar. A word may be correctly spelt but still be wrong because it does not fit the context.

13.10 Worked JAMB-Style Questions

Question 1: The principal advised the students to ______ their studies seriously.

A. take
B. accept
C. except
D. advice

Answer: A. take. The correct expression is take one's studies seriously. The other options do not fit the sentence.

Question 2: The new policy may ______ the activities of the students.

A. effect
B. affect
C. except
D. accept

Answer: B. affect. Affect is used here as a verb meaning to influence. Effect is commonly a noun meaning result.

Question 3: The school purchased writing materials from a ______ shop.

A. stationary
B. stationery
C. stationaries
D. stationeries

Answer: B. stationery. Stationery refers to writing materials. Stationary means not moving.

Question 4: The teacher asked us to ______ the correct answer.

A. chose
B. choosing
C. choose
D. choice

Answer: C. choose. The infinitive marker to is followed by the base form of the verb.

Question 5: Which of the following is correctly spelt?

A. Accomodation
B. Acommodation
C. Accommodation
D. Accommmodation

Answer: C. Accommodation. The correct spelling contains double c and double m.

Question 6: She prefers reading ______ watching television.

A. than
B. from
C. to
D. over than

Answer: C. to. The standard construction is prefer one thing to another.

Question 7: The student was punished ______ arriving late.

A. because
B. despite
C. for
D. although

Answer: C. for. The expression punished for something is grammatically correct.

Question 8: Which sentence is correct?

A. She discussed about the problem.
B. She discussed the problem.
C. She discussed on the problem.
D. She discussed over the problem.

Answer: B. Discuss takes a direct object in this construction and does not require about.

13.11 Chapter Revision

  • Spelling is the correct arrangement of letters in a word.
  • Remember common spelling patterns involving -ie and -ei, doubled consonants and silent e.
  • Accept means receive; except means excluding.
  • Advice is a noun; advise is a verb.
  • Affect is usually a verb; effect is usually a noun.
  • Principal refers to a school head or something most important; principle means a rule or belief.
  • Stationary means not moving; stationery means writing materials.
  • Its is possessive; it's means it is or it has.
  • JAMB commonly tests correct word forms and standard expressions.
  • British English spelling conventions are important in Nigerian formal English examinations.

13.12 Self-Assessment Questions

  1. Choose the correctly spelt word. A. Definately B. Definitely C. Definetely D. Definitly
  2. The teacher gave us useful ______. A. advise B. advices C. advice D. advising
  3. The heavy rain may ______ the match. A. effect B. affect C. except D. accept
  4. The head of the school is the ______. A. principle B. principal C. principel D. principall
  5. She bought pens and books from the ______ shop. A. stationary B. stationery C. stationeries D. stationarity
  6. Which sentence is correct? A. He entered into the room. B. He entered the room. C. He entered in the room. D. He entered at the room.
  7. We prefer football ______ basketball. A. than B. from C. to D. over than
  8. The child has lost ______ school bag. A. it's B. its C. it D. its'
  9. Which word means to receive something temporarily? A. Lend B. Borrow C. Bring D. Take
  10. Which sentence is correct? A. Despite he was ill, he came. B. Although his illness, he came. C. Although he was ill, he came. D. Despite he is ill, he came.

Answers: 1-B, 2-C, 3-B, 4-B, 5-B, 6-B, 7-C, 8-B, 9-B, 10-C.

13.13 Final Examination Preparation Checklist

Before moving to the next topic, make sure you can:

  • Recognise common spelling patterns and exceptions.
  • Distinguish words that look or sound alike.
  • Identify correct British English spelling forms.
  • Choose the correct noun, verb, adjective or adverb form in a sentence.
  • Recognise common errors involving prepositions and verb patterns.
  • Correct expressions such as discuss about, prefer than and enter into the room.
  • Explain why an option is correct rather than relying on guesswork.

Consistent revision is more effective than memorising a long list once. Practise using each word in a sentence and review the words you frequently confuse.

chapters.title: Phrases and Clauses
chapters.excerpt: Understand the difference between phrases and clauses, their types, functions and how JAMB tests their use in sentences.
chapters.content:
Introduction

Words do not always work alone. They combine to form groups that perform different functions in sentences. Two important groups of words in English are phrases and clauses. Understanding them will help you identify sentence structures, correct grammatical errors and answer questions on sentence construction in JAMB Use of English.

1. What Is a Phrase?

A phrase is a group of related words that works as a unit in a sentence but does not contain a complete subject-and-finite-verb combination. A phrase does not normally express a complete thought on its own.

Examples:

  • under the table
  • a beautiful young woman
  • very carefully
  • to win the competition
  • after the meeting

In the sentence 'The young boy ran across the road', the words 'the young boy' form a noun phrase, while 'across the road' forms a prepositional phrase.

2. Types of Phrases

A. Noun Phrase

A noun phrase is a group of words that performs the function of a noun. It may act as the subject, object or complement of a sentence.

Examples:

  • The tall man is my uncle. (Subject)
  • I bought a new school bag. (Object)
  • She became a successful businesswoman. (Complement)

B. Verb Phrase

A verb phrase consists of a main verb and any helping verbs associated with it. It expresses an action, state or condition.

Examples:

  • She is reading.
  • They have completed the assignment.
  • We will be travelling tomorrow.

C. Adjective Phrase

An adjective phrase performs the function of an adjective by describing or giving more information about a noun or pronoun.

Examples:

  • The woman in the blue dress is my mother.
  • The boy full of confidence answered the question.
  • We saw a building very close to the river.

D. Adverbial Phrase

An adverbial phrase performs the function of an adverb. It gives information about how, when, where, why or to what extent an action happens.

Examples:

  • She spoke with great confidence. (Manner)
  • We shall meet in the evening. (Time)
  • The children played under the tree. (Place)
  • He studied hard to pass the examination. (Purpose)

E. Prepositional Phrase

A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and usually ends with a noun or pronoun called its object.

Examples include 'on the table', 'behind the house', 'with my friend' and 'during the holiday'. A prepositional phrase can function as an adjective or an adverb depending on its use.

F. Infinitive Phrase

An infinitive phrase begins with 'to' followed by the base form of a verb. It may function as a noun, adjective or adverb.

  • To succeed requires hard work. (Noun function)
  • She has a book to read. (Adjectival function)
  • He came to apologise. (Adverbial function)

3. What Is a Clause?

A clause is a group of words containing a subject and a verb. Some clauses express a complete thought, while others depend on another clause to complete their meaning.

Example: 'The students cheered when the teacher entered.' The first clause is 'The students cheered'. The second clause is 'when the teacher entered'. Both contain a subject and a verb, but only the first expresses a complete thought independently.

4. Types of Clauses

A. Independent or Main Clause

An independent clause contains a subject and a verb and expresses a complete thought. It can stand alone as a sentence.

Examples:

  • The examination has started.
  • My mother prepared dinner.
  • The students passed the test.

B. Dependent or Subordinate Clause

A dependent clause contains a subject and a verb but does not express a complete thought on its own. It depends on another clause.

Examples:

  • because he was hungry
  • when the rain stopped
  • although she was tired
  • who won the competition

C. Noun Clause

A noun clause performs the function of a noun in a sentence. It can serve as the subject, object or complement.

Examples:

  • What he said surprised everybody. (Subject)
  • I know that she is honest. (Object)
  • The truth is that we are late. (Complement)

D. Adjectival or Relative Clause

An adjectival clause describes a noun or pronoun. It commonly begins with relative pronouns such as who, whom, whose, which and that.

Examples:

  • The woman who teaches us English is kind.
  • This is the book that I bought yesterday.
  • The boy whose father is a doctor won the prize.

E. Adverbial Clause

An adverbial clause performs the function of an adverb. It tells us when, where, why, how, under what condition or despite what circumstances an action occurs.

Examples:

  • We left when the meeting ended. (Time)
  • She stayed at home because she was ill. (Reason)
  • Although he was tired, he continued working. (Concession)
  • You will succeed if you work hard. (Condition)

5. Phrase Versus Clause

PhraseClause
Does not contain a subject-and-finite-verb combination.Contains a subject and a verb.
Does not normally express a complete thought.May express a complete or incomplete thought.
Example: in the classroomExample: when I entered

6. Common JAMB Examination Traps

  • Do not assume that every group of words is a clause. Check whether it contains a subject and a verb.
  • A dependent clause has a subject and a verb but cannot stand alone as a complete sentence.
  • A noun clause performs a noun's function, even though it contains a verb.
  • A relative clause describes a noun; it does not automatically become a noun clause because it begins with 'who' or 'that'.
  • A prepositional phrase can function adjectivally or adverbially depending on the sentence.

7. Worked JAMB-Style Questions

Question 1: Identify the noun clause in the sentence: 'What the principal announced surprised the students.'

  1. the principal
  2. What the principal announced
  3. surprised the students
  4. the students

Answer: B. 'What the principal announced' is a noun clause functioning as the subject of the sentence.

Question 2: In the sentence 'The man who lives next door is a doctor', the clause 'who lives next door' is:

  1. a noun clause
  2. an adverbial clause
  3. an adjectival clause
  4. an independent clause

Answer: C. It describes the noun 'man', so it is an adjectival or relative clause.

Question 3: Which of the following is a phrase?

  1. because he was late
  2. when she arrived
  3. under the old bridge
  4. the children were playing

Answer: C. 'Under the old bridge' is a prepositional phrase and does not contain a subject-and-verb combination.

8. Revision Points

  • A phrase is a group of related words without a subject-and-finite-verb combination.
  • A clause contains a subject and a verb.
  • Main clauses express complete thoughts.
  • Subordinate clauses depend on other clauses.
  • Noun clauses act as nouns; adjectival clauses describe nouns; adverbial clauses modify verbs, adjectives or other adverbs.

9. Self-Assessment

Answer these questions without checking the explanations above.

  1. What is the major difference between a phrase and a clause?
  2. Identify the phrase in: 'The boy with the red cap is my brother.'
  3. What type of clause is used in: 'I believe that he is innocent'?
  4. Identify the adverbial clause in: 'We waited until the rain stopped.'
  5. Explain the function of the clause 'who stole my phone' in: 'The boy who stole my phone has been arrested.'

chapters.title: Sentence Types and Sentence Patterns
chapters.excerpt: Learn how sentences are classified by purpose and structure, and understand the patterns that help you construct correct English sentences.
chapters.content:
Introduction

A sentence is a group of words arranged according to grammatical rules to express a complete thought. Every well-formed sentence normally has a subject and a predicate. The subject tells us who or what the sentence is about, while the predicate says something about the subject.

Example: 'The students passed the examination.' The subject is 'The students', while the predicate is 'passed the examination'.

1. Types of Sentences According to Function

A. Declarative Sentence

A declarative sentence makes a statement or gives information. It usually ends with a full stop.

Examples:

  • Lagos is a busy city.
  • My brother works in Abuja.
  • The students are preparing for JAMB.

B. Interrogative Sentence

An interrogative sentence asks a question. It ends with a question mark.

Examples:

  • Where do you live?
  • Have you completed your assignment?
  • Why did the teacher leave?

C. Imperative Sentence

An imperative sentence gives a command, instruction, request or advice. Its subject is usually the understood pronoun 'you'.

Examples:

  • Open the door.
  • Please sit down.
  • Do not waste your time.
  • Always read your questions carefully.

D. Exclamatory Sentence

An exclamatory sentence expresses strong emotion such as surprise, joy, anger or sadness. It commonly ends with an exclamation mark.

Examples:

  • What a wonderful performance!
  • How beautiful the building is!
  • What a terrible experience!

2. Types of Sentences According to Structure

A. Simple Sentence

A simple sentence contains one independent clause. It may have a compound subject or a compound predicate, but it still contains only one independent clause.

Examples:

  • The baby is sleeping.
  • John and Mary travelled yesterday.
  • The teacher entered and greeted the students.

In the third example, there is one subject and a compound predicate. It remains a simple sentence because it has one independent clause.

B. Compound Sentence

A compound sentence contains two or more independent clauses joined by coordinating conjunctions or appropriate punctuation.

Common coordinating conjunctions can be remembered using FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet and so.

Examples:

  • I wanted to travel, but the road was blocked.
  • She studied hard, so she passed the examination.
  • He did not call, nor did he send a message.

C. Complex Sentence

A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

Examples:

  • We stayed indoors because it was raining.
  • When the teacher arrived, the students became quiet.
  • The woman who owns the shop is my aunt.

D. Compound-Complex Sentence

A compound-complex sentence contains at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.

Example: 'Although it was raining, we went to school, and our teacher welcomed us.' The sentence has two independent clauses: 'we went to school' and 'our teacher welcomed us'. It also has the dependent clause 'Although it was raining'.

3. Common Sentence Patterns

English sentences follow recognisable patterns. Learning these patterns helps you identify grammatical functions and avoid errors.

A. Subject + Verb (S + V)

This pattern contains a subject followed by an intransitive verb.

Examples: The baby cried. The sun rises. The visitors arrived.

B. Subject + Verb + Object (S + V + O)

The verb is followed by an object that receives the action.

Examples: She bought a dress. The boy kicked the ball. My father repaired the car.

C. Subject + Verb + Complement (S + V + C)

The complement describes or identifies the subject. Linking verbs such as be, become, seem and appear commonly occur in this pattern.

Examples: She is a nurse. The food smells delicious. He became angry.

D. Subject + Verb + Adverbial (S + V + A)

The adverbial provides information such as place, time or manner.

Examples: The children are outside. My uncle lives in Ibadan. The meeting starts tomorrow.

E. Subject + Verb + Indirect Object + Direct Object (S + V + IO + DO)

This pattern contains a recipient and the thing given or communicated.

Examples: The teacher gave the students an assignment. My mother bought me a phone. He sent his friend a message.

F. Subject + Verb + Object + Complement (S + V + O + C)

The complement describes or renames the object.

Examples: They elected him president. The news made her happy. We painted the wall blue.

4. Active and Passive Sentence Patterns

In an active sentence, the subject performs the action. In a passive sentence, the subject receives the action.

Active: The police arrested the thief.

Passive: The thief was arrested by the police.

The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence. The passive voice is formed using an appropriate form of 'be' plus the past participle of the main verb.

5. Common JAMB Traps

  • A sentence with a compound subject is not automatically a compound sentence.
  • A simple sentence may contain several verbs if they form one predicate.
  • A compound sentence must have at least two independent clauses.
  • A complex sentence contains at least one dependent clause.
  • Do not confuse a subject complement with an object complement.
  • Not every verb takes an object. Some verbs are intransitive.

6. Worked JAMB-Style Questions

Question 1: 'Although the road was bad, the driver continued the journey.' This is a:

  1. simple sentence
  2. compound sentence
  3. complex sentence
  4. compound-complex sentence

Answer: C. It contains one independent clause and one dependent adverbial clause.
