Worked Example: One angle on a non-parallel side is 65°. Find the interior angle beside it on the same side.

65° + x = 180°.

x = 115°.

24.17 General Properties of Polygons

A polygon is a closed shape made from straight line segments. Polygons are classified by the number of sides they have.

Number of sidesName
3Triangle
4Quadrilateral
5Pentagon
6Hexagon
7Heptagon
8Octagon
9Nonagon
10Decagon
12Dodecagon

24.18 Interior and Exterior Angles of Polygons

The sum of the interior angles of an n-sided polygon is:

(n - 2) × 180°.

For a regular polygon, each interior angle is:

[(n - 2) × 180°]/n.

The sum of one exterior angle at each vertex of a convex polygon is:

360°.

For a regular polygon, each exterior angle is:

360°/n.

Worked Example: Find each exterior angle of a regular octagon.

n = 8.

Each exterior angle = 360°/8.

= 45°.

24.19 Diagonals of Polygons

A diagonal is a line segment joining two non-adjacent vertices of a polygon.

The number of diagonals in an n-sided polygon is:

n(n - 3)/2.

Worked Example: Find the number of diagonals in a decagon.

n = 10.

Number of diagonals = 10(10 - 3)/2.

= 10 × 7/2.

= 35 diagonals.

24.20 Symmetry in Plane Shapes

Line symmetry occurs when a shape can be divided by a line into two matching halves. The line is called a line of symmetry.

Rotational symmetry occurs when a shape looks unchanged after being rotated through an angle less than 360°.

ShapeLines of symmetryOrder of rotational symmetry
Square44
Rectangle that is not a square22
Equilateral triangle33
Regular pentagon55
Regular hexagon66
Non-square rhombus22
Parallelogram that is not a rectangle or rhombus02

24.21 Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Assuming every triangle has equal sides or equal angles.
  • Applying Pythagoras' theorem to a triangle that is not right-angled.
  • Confusing congruent triangles with similar triangles.
  • Forgetting to square the scale factor when comparing areas of similar shapes.
  • Confusing the properties of a rectangle, square, rhombus and parallelogram.
  • Using the wrong number of sides in polygon formulas.
  • Confusing a diagonal with a side of a polygon.

24.22 Chapter Summary

  • A triangle has three sides and its interior angles total 180°.
  • Pythagoras' theorem applies to right-angled triangles.
  • Congruent triangles have the same shape and size.
  • Similar triangles have the same shape but may have different sizes.
  • A quadrilateral has four sides and its interior angles total 360°.
  • Squares, rectangles, parallelograms, rhombuses, trapeziums and kites have different properties.
  • The sum of the interior angles of an n-sided polygon is (n - 2) × 180°.
  • The sum of the exterior angles of a convex polygon is 360°.
  • The number of diagonals in an n-sided polygon is n(n - 3)/2.
Key idea: Learn the defining properties of each shape. Correctly identifying a shape is the first step toward choosing the right geometrical rule or formula.

chapters.title: Circles: Theorems and Applications
chapters.excerpt: Understand the parts of a circle, important circle theorems, angles in circles, chords, tangents, and how to solve circle geometry problems step by step.
chapters.content:
1. Introduction to Circles

A circle is a closed plane shape made up of all points that are at the same distance from a fixed point called the centre.

Circles are common in everyday life. Examples include wheels, clocks, coins, plates, and rings. In mathematics, circles have special properties that help us solve problems involving angles, lengths, and positions.

2. Parts of a Circle

  • Centre: The fixed point at the middle of a circle.
  • Radius: A straight line from the centre to any point on the circumference.
  • Diameter: A straight line passing through the centre and joining two points on the circumference. It is twice the radius.
  • Circumference: The distance around the circle.
  • Chord: A straight line joining two points on the circumference.
  • Arc: A part of the circumference.
  • Sector: The region enclosed by two radii and an arc.
  • Segment: The region enclosed by a chord and its corresponding arc.
  • Tangent: A straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point.
  • Secant: A straight line that cuts a circle at two points.

Important relationship

Diameter = 2 × Radius

Radius = Diameter ÷ 2

For example, if a circle has a radius of 7 cm, its diameter is 2 × 7 = 14 cm.

3. Important Properties of Circles

  • All radii of the same circle are equal.
  • The diameter is the longest chord of a circle.
  • A perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
  • Equal chords of the same circle subtend equal angles at the centre.
  • Equal chords are equally distant from the centre.
  • The perpendicular distance from the centre to a chord is the shortest distance from the centre to that chord.

4. Angles at the Centre and Circumference

One important circle theorem states that the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc is twice the angle subtended at the circumference by the same arc.

In simple terms:

Angle at the centre = 2 × Angle at the circumference

Also:

Angle at the circumference = ½ × Angle at the centre

Worked Example 1

An arc of a circle subtends an angle of 100° at the centre. Find the angle it subtends at the circumference.

Solution:

Angle at circumference = ½ × 100°

= 50°

Worked Example 2

An angle at the circumference is 35°. Find the angle at the centre standing on the same arc.

Solution:

Angle at centre = 2 × 35°

= 70°

5. Angles in the Same Segment

Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal. This means that angles formed at different points on the same side of a chord, standing on the same chord, have equal values.

Worked Example

Two angles at the circumference stand on the same chord. If one angle is 48°, the other angle is also 48°.

6. Angle in a Semicircle

The angle in a semicircle is always 90°.

This theorem applies when a triangle is formed by joining the two ends of a diameter to another point on the circumference.

Worked Example

A triangle is drawn inside a circle with one side as the diameter. If one of the other angles is 32°, find the third angle.

Solution:

Sum of angles in a triangle = 180°.

Third angle = 180° − 90° − 32°

= 58°

7. Opposite Angles of a Cyclic Quadrilateral

A cyclic quadrilateral is a four-sided shape whose four vertices lie on the circumference of a circle.

The important theorem is:

Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°.

Therefore:

Angle A + Angle C = 180°

Angle B + Angle D = 180°

Worked Example

A cyclic quadrilateral has one angle of 110°. Find the angle opposite it.

Solution:

Opposite angle = 180° − 110°

= 70°

8. Exterior Angle of a Cyclic Quadrilateral

The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to the interior opposite angle.

For example, if an exterior angle is 75°, the interior opposite angle is also 75°.

9. Tangents to a Circle

A tangent is a straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point. The point where it touches the circle is called the point of contact.

Important tangent theorems include:

  • A tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact.
  • Tangents drawn from the same external point to a circle are equal in length.
  • The angle between a tangent and a chord is equal to the angle in the alternate segment.

Worked Example 1: Radius and Tangent

A tangent touches a circle at point P. If OP is the radius from the centre O to P, find the angle between OP and the tangent.

Solution:

The radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact.

Required angle = 90°.

Worked Example 2: Equal Tangents

Two tangents are drawn from an external point P to a circle, touching it at A and B. If PA = 8 cm, find PB.

Solution:

Tangents from the same external point are equal.

Therefore, PB = PA = 8 cm.

10. Alternate Segment Theorem

The alternate segment theorem states that the angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact is equal to the angle in the alternate segment.

For example, if the angle between a tangent and a chord is 42°, the angle subtended by that chord at a point on the opposite segment is also 42°.

11. Chords and Their Properties

A chord is a straight line joining two points on the circumference. The diameter is a special chord because it passes through the centre.

Remember these properties:

  • Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre.
  • Equal chords are equally distant from the centre.
  • A perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.
  • The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre.

Worked Example

A perpendicular from the centre of a circle meets a chord of length 16 cm. Find the length of each part of the chord.

Solution:

The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord.

Each part = 16 ÷ 2 = 8 cm.

12. Common Circle Theorem Summary

TheoremRule
Angle at centre and circumferenceCentre angle = 2 × circumference angle
Angles in the same segmentThey are equal
Angle in a semicircle90°
Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateralSum = 180°
Exterior angle of cyclic quadrilateralEquals interior opposite angle
Radius and tangentMeet at 90°
Tangents from an external pointEqual in length
Perpendicular from centre to chordBisects the chord
Alternate segment theoremTangent-chord angle equals angle in alternate segment

13. Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Do not confuse the angle at the centre with the angle at the circumference. The centre angle is twice the circumference angle when they stand on the same arc.
  • Do not assume every quadrilateral is cyclic. Its four vertices must lie on the same circle.
  • Do not forget that the radius meets a tangent at 90° at the point of contact.
  • Do not use the tangent theorem for a secant line.
  • Do not confuse an arc with a chord. An arc is curved, while a chord is straight.

14. Key Points to Remember

  • The diameter is twice the radius.
  • The angle in a semicircle is 90°.
  • Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
  • Angles in the same segment are equal.
  • A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
  • Tangents from the same external point have equal lengths.
  • The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.
Study Tip: When solving circle geometry problems, identify the chord, arc, tangent, or diameter involved first. Then select the theorem that connects the angles or lengths shown in the diagram.

chapters.title: Mensuration: Perimeter and Area
chapters.excerpt: Learn how to calculate perimeter and area of common plane shapes, including triangles, rectangles, squares, parallelograms, trapeziums, circles, and compound figures.
chapters.content:
1. Introduction to Mensuration

Mensuration is the branch of mathematics concerned with measuring the lengths, perimeters, areas, surface areas, and volumes of shapes.

This chapter focuses on perimeter and area of two-dimensional shapes. A two-dimensional shape has length and width but no thickness.

2. Units of Measurement

Perimeter is measured in ordinary length units, while area is measured in square units.

MeasurementCommon Units
Length or perimetermm, cm, m, km
Areamm², cm², m², km²

Important: Always convert measurements into the same unit before calculating. For example, do not combine a length in metres with another length in centimetres without converting one of them.

3. Perimeter

The perimeter of a plane shape is the total distance around its boundary.

To find the perimeter of a polygon, add the lengths of all its sides.

Worked Example

A rectangular field has a length of 15 m and a width of 8 m. Find its perimeter.

Solution:

Perimeter = 2(length + width)

= 2(15 + 8)

= 2 × 23

= 46 m.

4. Area of a Square

A square has four equal sides and four right angles.

Perimeter = 4s

Area = s²

Here, s represents the length of one side.

Worked Example

A square has a side of 9 cm. Find its perimeter and area.

Solution:

Perimeter = 4 × 9 = 36 cm.

Area = 9 × 9 = 81 cm².

5. Area and Perimeter of a Rectangle

A rectangle has opposite sides equal and four right angles.

Perimeter = 2(l + w)

Area = l × w

Where l is length and w is width.

Worked Example

A classroom is 12 m long and 7 m wide. Calculate its area and perimeter.

Solution:

Area = 12 × 7 = 84 m².

Perimeter = 2(12 + 7) = 2 × 19 = 38 m.

6. Area of a Triangle

A triangle is a plane shape with three sides and three interior angles.

Area = ½ × base × perpendicular height

The height must be measured at right angles to the chosen base. It is not necessarily the length of one of the sloping sides.

Perimeter = sum of the three sides

Worked Example

A triangle has a base of 14 cm and a perpendicular height of 6 cm. Find its area.

Solution:

Area = ½ × 14 × 6

= 7 × 6

= 42 cm².

Heron's Formula

When the three sides of a triangle are known but its perpendicular height is not given, Heron's formula can be used.

First calculate the semi-perimeter:

s = (a + b + c) ÷ 2

Then:

Area = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)]

Here, a, b, and c are the three side lengths.

7. Area of a Parallelogram

A parallelogram is a quadrilateral in which opposite sides are parallel and equal.

Area = base × perpendicular height

Perimeter = 2(a + b), where a and b are the lengths of two adjacent sides.

Worked Example

A parallelogram has a base of 11 cm and a perpendicular height of 5 cm. Find its area.

Solution:

Area = 11 × 5 = 55 cm².

8. Area of a Trapezium

A trapezium is a quadrilateral with one pair of opposite sides parallel. The parallel sides are often called the parallel bases.

Area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × perpendicular height

Using a and b for the parallel sides:

Area = ½(a + b)h

Worked Example

A trapezium has parallel sides of 10 cm and 16 cm. Its perpendicular height is 7 cm. Find its area.

Solution:

Area = ½(10 + 16) × 7

= ½ × 26 × 7

= 13 × 7

= 91 cm².

9. Area of a Rhombus

A rhombus has four equal sides. Its diagonals cross each other at right angles.

Area = ½ × d₁ × d₂

Where d₁ and d₂ are the lengths of the diagonals.

Its perimeter is 4s, where s is the side length.

Worked Example

The diagonals of a rhombus are 12 cm and 8 cm. Find its area.

Solution:

Area = ½ × 12 × 8

= 48 cm².

10. Area of a Kite

A kite is a quadrilateral with two pairs of equal adjacent sides.

Area = ½ × d₁ × d₂

Where d₁ and d₂ are the lengths of its diagonals.

11. Circumference and Area of a Circle

A circle is a plane shape whose boundary is called its circumference.

Circumference = 2πr = πd

Area = πr²

Where r is the radius, d is the diameter, and π is approximately 3.142 or 22/7 when appropriate.

Worked Example 1: Circumference

A circle has a radius of 7 cm. Find its circumference using π = 22/7.

Solution:

Circumference = 2πr

= 2 × 22/7 × 7

= 44 cm.

Worked Example 2: Area

Find the area of a circle with radius 7 cm. Use π = 22/7.

Solution:

Area = πr²

= 22/7 × 7 × 7

= 154 cm².

12. Semicircles and Quadrants

A semicircle is half of a circle. Its area is:

Area of semicircle = ½πr²

Its perimeter includes the curved half of the circumference and the diameter:

Perimeter of semicircle = πr + 2r

A quadrant is one-quarter of a circle.

Area of quadrant = ¼πr²

The perimeter of a quadrant is the sum of its two radii and its quarter-circle arc:

Perimeter of quadrant = 2r + ½πr

Worked Example

Find the area of a semicircle of radius 14 cm, using π = 22/7.

Solution:

Area = ½ × π × r²

= ½ × 22/7 × 14 × 14

= 308 cm².

13. Arc Length and Area of a Sector

A sector is a portion of a circle enclosed by two radii and an arc. If its central angle is θ degrees, then:

Arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr

Area of sector = (θ/360) × πr²

These formulas compare the sector's angle with the full angle of 360° in a circle.

Worked Example

Find the area of a sector with radius 6 cm and central angle 90°. Use π = 3.142.

Solution:

Area = (90/360) × 3.142 × 6²

= ¼ × 3.142 × 36

= ¼ × 113.112

= 28.278 cm².

14. Compound Shapes

A compound shape is formed by combining two or more simple shapes or by removing one shape from another.

To find its area:

  1. Identify the simple shapes that make up the figure.
  2. Calculate the area of each required shape.
  3. Add the areas if the shapes are joined.
  4. Subtract the removed area if a part has been cut out.

Worked Example

A shape consists of a rectangle measuring 10 cm by 6 cm with a semicircle attached along one of its 6 cm sides. Find the total area. Use π = 3.142.

Solution:

Area of rectangle = 10 × 6 = 60 cm².

The semicircle has diameter 6 cm, so its radius is 3 cm.

Area of semicircle = ½ × 3.142 × 3²

= ½ × 28.278 = 14.139 cm².

Total area = 60 + 14.139 = 74.139 cm².

15. Conversion of Area Units

Area conversions involve squaring the length conversion factor.

ConversionEquivalent
1 m100 cm
1 m²10,000 cm²
1 cm²100 mm²
1 hectare10,000 m²
1 km²1,000,000 m²

Worked Example

Convert 3 m² to cm².

Solution:

1 m² = 10,000 cm².

3 m² = 3 × 10,000 = 30,000 cm².

16. Formula Summary

ShapePerimeter or CircumferenceArea
Square4ss²
Rectangle2(l + w)lw
Trianglea + b + c½bh
Parallelogram2(a + b)bh
TrapeziumSum of four sides½(a + b)h
Rhombus4s½d₁d₂
KiteSum of four sides½d₁d₂
Circle2πrπr²
Semicircleπr + 2r½πr²
SectorArc length = (θ/360)2πr(θ/360)πr²

17. Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Do not write area in cm or m. Use square units such as cm² or m².
  • Do not confuse perimeter with area. Perimeter measures the boundary; area measures the surface covered.
  • For a triangle or parallelogram, use the perpendicular height, not a sloping side.
  • For a trapezium, add the two parallel sides before multiplying by half the height.
  • For a semicircle's perimeter, remember to include the diameter.
  • When converting square units, square the conversion factor.
  • Use the radius, not the diameter, in the formula πr².

18. Key Points to Remember

  • Perimeter is the total distance around a shape.
  • Area is the space covered by a plane shape.
  • Area is expressed in square units.
  • The area of a circle is πr², while its circumference is 2πr.
  • The area of a sector is a fraction of the full circle's area.
  • Break compound shapes into simpler shapes before calculating.

chapters.title: Mensuration: Surface Area and Volume
chapters.excerpt: Study three-dimensional shapes and learn how to calculate the surface area and volume of cubes, cuboids, cylinders, prisms, pyramids, cones, and spheres.
chapters.content:
1. Introduction to Three-Dimensional Shapes

A three-dimensional shape has length, width, and height. It occupies space and has volume. Examples include boxes, water tanks, cans, balls, cones, and buildings.

Mensuration of solids deals mainly with two measurements:

  • Surface area: The total area covering the outside of a solid.
  • Volume: The amount of space occupied by a solid.

2. Units of Surface Area and Volume

Surface area is measured in square units, while volume is measured in cubic units.

MeasurementCommon Units
Surface areacm², m², mm²
Volumecm³, m³, mm³
CapacitymL, L

Important conversions:

  • 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³.
  • 1 cm³ = 1 mL.
  • 1,000 cm³ = 1 litre.
  • 1 m³ = 1,000 litres.

3. Cube

A cube has six equal square faces, twelve equal edges, and eight vertices.

Let the length of each edge be a.

Volume = a³

Area of one face = a²

Total surface area = 6a²

Lateral surface area = 4a²

Worked Example

A cube has an edge of 5 cm. Find its volume and total surface area.

Solution:

Volume = 5³ = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 cm³.

Total surface area = 6 × 5²

= 6 × 25 = 150 cm².

4. Cuboid

A cuboid is a solid with six rectangular faces. A rectangular box is an example.

Let length = l, width = w, and height = h.

Volume = lwh

Total surface area = 2(lw + lh + wh)

Lateral surface area = 2h(l + w), when the base is the rectangle with sides l and w.

Worked Example

A rectangular water tank is 4 m long, 3 m wide, and 2 m high. Find its volume and total surface area.

Solution:

Volume = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 m³.

Total surface area = 2(lw + lh + wh)

= 2[(4 × 3) + (4 × 2) + (3 × 2)]

= 2(12 + 8 + 6)

= 2 × 26 = 52 m².

5. Right Circular Cylinder

A cylinder has two equal circular ends joined by a curved surface. A tin can and many water tanks have cylindrical shapes.

Let r be the radius of the circular base and h be the height.

Volume = πr²h

Curved surface area = 2πrh

Total surface area = 2πr² + 2πrh

Alternatively:

Total surface area = 2πr(r + h)

Worked Example

A cylinder has radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. Calculate its volume and curved surface area using π = 22/7.

Solution:

Volume = πr²h

= 22/7 × 7 × 7 × 10

= 1,540 cm³.

Curved surface area = 2πrh

= 2 × 22/7 × 7 × 10

= 440 cm².

6. Prism

A prism is a solid with two identical, parallel ends connected by flat rectangular or parallelogram-shaped faces. The shape of its cross-section determines the type of prism.

For a prism:

Volume = Area of cross-section × Length

Lateral surface area = Perimeter of cross-section × Length

For a closed right prism:

Total surface area = Lateral surface area + 2 × Area of cross-section

Worked Example

A triangular prism has a triangular cross-section with base 6 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm. The length of the prism is 10 cm. Find its volume.

Solution:

Area of triangular cross-section = ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 cm².

Volume = 12 × 10 = 120 cm³.

7. Pyramid

A pyramid has a polygonal base and triangular faces that meet at a single point called the apex.

Volume = ⅓ × Area of base × Perpendicular height

For a regular pyramid, the lateral surface area is:

Lateral surface area = ½ × Perimeter of base × Slant height

The total surface area is the lateral surface area plus the area of the base.

Note: The perpendicular height is the vertical distance from the apex to the base. The slant height is measured along a triangular face. They are not generally equal.

Worked Example

A square-based pyramid has a base side of 6 cm and a perpendicular height of 9 cm. Find its volume.

Solution:

Area of base = 6 × 6 = 36 cm².

Volume = ⅓ × 36 × 9

= 12 × 9

= 108 cm³.

8. Cone

A cone has a circular base and a curved surface that narrows to a point called the vertex.

Let r be the radius, h the perpendicular height, and l the slant height.

Volume = ⅓πr²h

Curved surface area = πrl

Total surface area = πrl + πr²

For a right circular cone:

l² = r² + h²

This relationship comes from Pythagoras' theorem.

Worked Example

A right circular cone has radius 3 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm. Find its slant height and volume. Use π = 3.142.

Solution:

Slant height² = 3² + 4²

= 9 + 16 = 25.

Slant height = √25 = 5 cm.

Volume = ⅓ × 3.142 × 3² × 4

= ⅓ × 3.142 × 36

= 3.142 × 12

= 37.704 cm³.

9. Sphere

A sphere is a perfectly round solid whose surface points are all the same distance from its centre. A football and a ball bearing are examples of approximately spherical objects.

Volume = ⁴⁄₃πr³

Surface area = 4πr²

Worked Example

Find the volume and surface area of a sphere with radius 3 cm. Use π = 3.142.

Solution:

Volume = ⁴⁄₃ × 3.142 × 3³

= ⁴⁄₃ × 3.142 × 27

= 4 × 3.142 × 9

= 113.112 cm³.

Surface area = 4 × 3.142 × 3²

= 4 × 3.142 × 9

= 113.112 cm².

10. Hemisphere

A hemisphere is half of a sphere.

Volume = ⅔πr³

Curved surface area = 2πr²

Total surface area = 3πr²

The total surface area includes the curved surface and the circular flat base. The curved surface area does not include the base.

Worked Example

A hemisphere has radius 7 cm. Find its total surface area using π = 22/7.

Solution:

Total surface area = 3πr²

= 3 × 22/7 × 7 × 7

= 462 cm².

11. Frustum of a Cone

A frustum of a cone is formed when the top of a cone is cut off by a plane parallel to its base. It has two circular ends of different radii.

Let R be the larger radius, r the smaller radius, and h the perpendicular height.

Volume = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²)

The curved surface area is:

Curved surface area = π(R + r)l

Here, l is the slant height of the frustum. The total surface area also includes both circular ends:

Total surface area = π(R + r)l + πR² + πr²

12. Capacity of Containers

Capacity is the amount a container can hold, usually expressed in litres or millilitres.

Useful relationships:

  • 1 cm³ = 1 mL.
  • 1,000 cm³ = 1 L.
  • 1 m³ = 1,000 L.

Worked Example

A rectangular container measures 50 cm by 40 cm by 30 cm. Find its capacity in litres when completely filled.

Solution:

Volume = 50 × 40 × 30

= 60,000 cm³.

Since 1,000 cm³ = 1 L:

Capacity = 60,000 ÷ 1,000

= 60 litres.

13. Summary of Important Formulas

SolidVolumeSurface Area
Cubea³6a²
Cuboidlwh2(lw + lh + wh)
Cylinderπr²h2πr(r + h), total
PrismCross-sectional area × lengthPerimeter of cross-section × length + two ends
Pyramid⅓ × base area × heightDepends on base and slant faces
Cone⅓πr²hπrl + πr², total
Sphere⁴⁄₃πr³4πr²
Hemisphere⅔πr³3πr², total
Frustum of cone⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²)π(R + r)l + πR² + πr², total

14. Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Do not confuse surface area with volume.
  • Use square units for surface area and cubic units for volume.
  • For a cone, use perpendicular height in the volume formula and slant height in the curved surface area formula.
  • Do not forget the two circular ends when calculating the total surface area of a closed cylinder.
  • For a hemisphere, distinguish between curved surface area and total surface area.
  • Convert all measurements to the same unit before calculating.
  • Remember that the volume of a pyramid or cone is one-third of the corresponding prism or cylinder with the same base area and height.

15. Key Points to Remember

  • Surface area measures the outside covering of a solid.
  • Volume measures the space occupied by a solid.
  • A prism's volume is its cross-sectional area multiplied by its length.
  • A cone and pyramid have one-third the volume of a cylinder and prism with the same base area and perpendicular height.
  • 1 cm³ is equal to 1 mL.
  • 1,000 cm³ is equal to 1 litre.

chapters.title: Loci and Geometrical Constructions
chapters.excerpt: Learn the meaning of loci, important locus rules, and how to construct perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors, perpendicular lines, triangles, and other geometric figures using a ruler and compass.
chapters.content:
1. Introduction to Loci

The word locus means a path or set of positions followed by a point that moves according to a given rule. The plural form is loci.

For example, imagine a point moving while keeping the same distance from a fixed point. Its path forms a circle.

In geometry, a locus describes all possible positions of a point that satisfies a particular condition.

2. Important Locus Rules

Rule 1: Fixed Distance from a Point

The locus of a point at a fixed distance from a fixed point is a circle with the fixed point as its centre.

For example, all points 5 cm from point O lie on a circle of radius 5 cm centred at O.

Rule 2: Fixed Distance from a Straight Line

The locus of points at a fixed perpendicular distance from a straight line consists of two parallel lines, one on each side of the original line.

Rule 3: Equidistant from Two Fixed Points

The locus of points that are equally distant from two fixed points A and B is the perpendicular bisector of line AB.

Rule 4: Equidistant from Two Intersecting Lines

The locus of points equally distant from two intersecting straight lines consists of the two angle bisectors formed by the lines.

Rule 5: Fixed Distance from a Circle

For points outside a circle that are at a fixed distance from its circumference, the locus is a larger concentric circle. For a distance smaller than the radius, the corresponding inside boundary is also a concentric circle, provided the distance is measured radially from the circumference.

3. What Is Geometrical Construction?

Geometrical construction is the drawing of accurate geometric figures using mathematical instruments, especially a ruler and compass.

The main instruments are:

  • Ruler: Used to draw straight lines and measure or mark lengths when measurement is permitted.
  • Compass: Used to draw arcs and circles and transfer distances.
  • Protractor: Used to measure or draw angles when the construction allows it.
  • Pencil: Used for accurate and clear drawings.

In classical ruler-and-compass construction, a ruler is used as a straightedge without a marked scale, while the compass transfers distances and draws arcs.

4. Construction of a Perpendicular Bisector

A perpendicular bisector is a straight line that cuts a line segment into two equal parts at 90°.

Steps

  1. Draw the line segment AB.
  2. Open the compass to a radius greater than half of AB.
  3. With A as centre, draw arcs above and below AB.
  4. Without changing the compass width, use B as centre to draw arcs that cross the first pair.
  5. Join the two points where the arcs intersect.
  6. The line formed is the perpendicular bisector of AB.

Result: The constructed line crosses AB at its midpoint and at right angles.

5. Construction of an Angle Bisector

An angle bisector divides an angle into two equal angles.

Steps

  1. Draw the angle ABC.
  2. Place the compass point at B and draw an arc that cuts both arms of the angle at P and Q.
  3. With P as centre, draw an arc inside the angle.
  4. Using the same compass width, with Q as centre, draw another arc to intersect the first at R.
  5. Join B to R.
  6. BR is the angle bisector.

Result: Angle ABR = Angle RBC.

6. Construction of a Perpendicular to a Line at a Point on the Line

This construction produces a line that meets a given straight line at 90° at a specified point on it.

Steps

  1. Draw a straight line and mark the required point P on it.
  2. With P as centre, draw an arc cutting the line at A and B on opposite sides of P.
  3. With A and B as centres and the same compass width, draw arcs that meet above the line at C.
  4. Join P to C.
  5. PC is perpendicular to the original line at P.

7. Construction of a Perpendicular from an External Point to a Line

This construction is used when the required point is outside the given straight line.

Steps

  1. Draw the straight line AB and mark the external point P.
  2. With P as centre, draw an arc that cuts AB at C and D.
  3. With C and D as centres and equal compass widths, draw arcs that meet at Q on the side of the line opposite P.
  4. Join P to Q.
  5. The line PQ meets AB at 90°.

8. Construction of a Triangle

A triangle can be constructed when enough information about its sides and angles is provided.

Constructing a Triangle from Three Sides (SSS)

Suppose the required sides are 5 cm, 6 cm, and 7 cm.

  1. Draw a base AB of 7 cm.
  2. With A as centre, draw an arc of radius 5 cm.
  3. With B as centre, draw an arc of radius 6 cm.
  4. Mark one intersection of the arcs as C.
  5. Join AC and BC.
  6. Triangle ABC has the required side lengths.

Important: The sum of any two sides of a triangle must be greater than the third side.

Constructing a Triangle from Two Sides and the Included Angle (SAS)

  1. Draw one of the given sides as the base.
  2. At the correct endpoint, construct the given included angle.
  3. Measure the second given side along the new ray using the compass.
  4. Join the remaining endpoints to complete the triangle.

9. Construction of a Regular Hexagon

A regular hexagon has six equal sides and six equal interior angles. Each interior angle is 120° and each exterior angle is 60°.

Compass Method

  1. Draw a circle with a compass.
  2. Without changing the compass width, place the compass point on any point on the circumference.
  3. Use the same radius to mark six consecutive points around the circumference.
  4. Join adjacent points with straight lines.
  5. The result is a regular hexagon.

The side of an inscribed regular hexagon is equal to the radius of its circumcircle.

10. Locus Problems in Everyday Situations

Locus rules can be applied to practical situations.

Example 1: A School Playground

A student must stay exactly 10 m from a flagpole. The possible positions form a circle of radius 10 m centred at the flagpole.

Example 2: Equal Distance from Two Houses

A water point is to be placed at a position equally distant from two houses represented by points A and B. The possible positions lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB.

Example 3: Equal Distance from Two Roads

A point equally distant from two intersecting roads lies on one of the angle bisectors formed by the roads.

11. Combining Two Locus Conditions

Sometimes a problem gives two conditions at the same time. The required positions are the points where the two loci intersect.

Worked Example

A point P must be 5 cm from a fixed point O and equally distant from two points A and B. Describe how to locate the possible positions of P.

Solution:

  1. Draw a circle with centre O and radius 5 cm. This represents all points 5 cm from O.
  2. Construct the perpendicular bisector of AB. This represents all points equally distant from A and B.
  3. The intersection point or points of the circle and the perpendicular bisector give the possible positions of P.

12. Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Do not confuse a perpendicular bisector with an angle bisector.
  • A perpendicular bisector cuts a line segment into two equal parts at 90°.
  • An angle bisector divides an angle into two equal angles.
  • When constructing equal arcs, keep the compass width unchanged unless the construction requires a different width.
  • For a fixed distance from a point, draw a circle, not a straight line.
  • When two locus conditions are given, the answer must satisfy both conditions.
  • Use clear, light construction arcs so that the final lines can be identified.

13. Summary of Important Loci

ConditionLocus
Fixed distance from a pointCircle
Fixed perpendicular distance from a straight lineTwo parallel lines
Equidistant from two fixed pointsPerpendicular bisector
Equidistant from two intersecting linesAngle bisectors
Two locus conditions togetherIntersection of the two loci

14. Key Points to Remember

  • Locus means the path or set of positions satisfying a condition.
  • A circle is the locus of points at a fixed distance from a fixed point.
  • The perpendicular bisector is the locus of points equidistant from two fixed points.
  • Angle bisectors give the locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines.
  • Geometrical constructions require accuracy and clear use of instruments.

chapters.title: Coordinate Geometry
chapters.excerpt: Learn how to work with Cartesian coordinates, distance between points, midpoint, gradient, straight-line equations, parallel and perpendicular lines, and the geometry of triangles on a coordinate plane.
chapters.content:
1. Introduction to Coordinate Geometry

Coordinate geometry combines algebra and geometry. It uses numbers and equations to describe the positions of points and shapes on a plane.

It is also called analytical geometry.

2. The Cartesian Coordinate Plane

The Cartesian plane consists of two perpendicular number lines:

  • x-axis: The horizontal number line.
  • y-axis: The vertical number line.
  • Origin: The point where the two axes meet, represented by (0, 0).

A point is represented by an ordered pair (x, y). The first number gives its horizontal position, while the second gives its vertical position.

For example, point A(3, 2) is 3 units to the right of the origin and 2 units above it.

3. The Four Quadrants

The two axes divide the coordinate plane into four regions called quadrants.

QuadrantSign of xSign of y
FirstPositive (+)Positive (+)
SecondNegative (−)Positive (+)
ThirdNegative (−)Negative (−)
FourthPositive (+)Negative (−)

Points on the x-axis have y = 0. Points on the y-axis have x = 0. The origin has both coordinates equal to zero.

4. Distance Between Two Points

The distance between two points is found using the distance formula, which comes from Pythagoras' theorem.

For points A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂):

AB = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]

Worked Example

Find the distance between A(2, 3) and B(6, 6).

Solution:

AB = √[(6 − 2)² + (6 − 3)²]

= √[4² + 3²]

= √(16 + 9)

= √25

= 5 units.

5. Midpoint of a Line Segment

The midpoint is the point exactly halfway between two endpoints.

For A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂):

Midpoint = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2)

Worked Example

Find the midpoint of A(2, 4) and B(8, 10).

Solution:

x-coordinate = (2 + 8)/2 = 5.

y-coordinate = (4 + 10)/2 = 7.

Midpoint = (5, 7).

6. Gradient of a Straight Line

The gradient or slope of a straight line measures how steep the line is. It is the change in the y-coordinate divided by the change in the x-coordinate.

For two points A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂):

m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), provided x₂ is not equal to x₁.

A positive gradient means the line rises from left to right. A negative gradient means it falls from left to right. A horizontal line has gradient zero. A vertical line has an undefined gradient.

Worked Example

Find the gradient of the line joining A(1, 2) and B(5, 10).

Solution:

m = (10 − 2)/(5 − 1)

= 8/4

= 2.

7. Equation of a Straight Line

The common form of a straight-line equation is:

y = mx + c

Where:

  • m is the gradient.
  • c is the y-intercept, the point where the line crosses the y-axis.

Worked Example

Identify the gradient and y-intercept of the line y = 3x + 4.

Solution:

Compare with y = mx + c.

Gradient m = 3.

Y-intercept c = 4.

8. Finding the Equation of a Line Using Its Gradient and a Point

When the gradient m and a point (x₁, y₁) are known, use:

y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)

Worked Example

Find the equation of a line with gradient 2 passing through (3, 5).

Solution:

y − 5 = 2(x − 3)

y − 5 = 2x − 6

y = 2x − 1.

Therefore, the equation is y = 2x − 1.

9. Equation of a Line Through Two Points

To find the equation of a line through two given points:

  1. Calculate the gradient using the two points.
  2. Substitute the gradient and either point into y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
  3. Simplify the equation.

Worked Example

Find the equation of the line passing through (1, 3) and (3, 7).

Solution:

Gradient m = (7 − 3)/(3 − 1) = 4/2 = 2.

Using point (1, 3):

y − 3 = 2(x − 1)

y − 3 = 2x − 2

y = 2x + 1.

10. Intercepts of a Straight Line

The x-intercept is where a line crosses the x-axis. At this point, y = 0.

The y-intercept is where a line crosses the y-axis. At this point, x = 0.

Worked Example

Find the x-intercept and y-intercept of 2x + 3y = 12.

Solution:

For the x-intercept, put y = 0:

2x + 3(0) = 12

2x = 12, so x = 6.

X-intercept = (6, 0).

For the y-intercept, put x = 0:

2(0) + 3y = 12

3y = 12, so y = 4.

Y-intercept = (0, 4).

11. Parallel Lines

Parallel lines have the same gradient. They do not meet, even when extended indefinitely.

If two non-vertical lines have gradients m₁ and m₂:

Parallel lines: m₁ = m₂

Worked Example

A line has gradient 4. Find the gradient of a line parallel to it.

Solution:

Parallel lines have equal gradients.

Required gradient = 4.

12. Perpendicular Lines

Two lines are perpendicular if they meet at 90°.

For two non-vertical lines with gradients m₁ and m₂:

m₁ × m₂ = −1

Equivalently, their gradients are negative reciprocals of each other.

Worked Example

A line has gradient 3. Find the gradient of a line perpendicular to it.

Solution:

Let the required gradient be m.

3m = −1.

m = −⅓.

13. Horizontal and Vertical Lines

  • A horizontal line has equation y = k, where k is a constant, and gradient 0.
  • A vertical line has equation x = k, where k is a constant, and its gradient is undefined.

For example, y = 5 is a horizontal line, while x = −2 is a vertical line.

14. Area of a Triangle Using Coordinates

If the vertices of a triangle are A(x₁, y₁), B(x₂, y₂), and C(x₃, y₃), its area is:

Area = ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|

The vertical bars mean that the absolute value of the result is taken, so the area is not negative.

Worked Example

Find the area of a triangle with vertices A(0, 0), B(4, 0), and C(0, 3).

Solution:

Area = ½|0(0 − 3) + 4(3 − 0) + 0(0 − 0)|

= ½|12|

= 6 square units.

15. Coordinate Geometry Formula Summary

ConceptFormula
Distance√[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]
Midpoint((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2)
Gradient(y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)
Straight-line equationy = mx + c
Point-gradient equationy − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
Parallel linesm₁ = m₂
Perpendicular linesm₁m₂ = −1
Triangle area½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|

16. Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Do not reverse the order of coordinates. The first number is x and the second is y.
  • When calculating gradient, subtract the y-coordinates in the same order as the x-coordinates.
  • Do not divide by zero when calculating the gradient of a vertical line.
  • Remember that parallel lines have equal gradients.
  • For perpendicular lines, use the negative reciprocal, not just the reciprocal.
  • When finding an x-intercept, set y = 0. When finding a y-intercept, set x = 0.

17. Key Points to Remember

  • The origin is (0, 0).
  • The distance formula comes from Pythagoras' theorem.
  • The midpoint is the average of the two x-coordinates and the average of the two y-coordinates.
  • The gradient measures the steepness of a line.
  • The equation y = mx + c gives the gradient and y-intercept directly.
  • Parallel lines have equal gradients, while perpendicular non-vertical lines have gradients whose product is −1.

chapters.title: Trigonometric Ratios and Identities
chapters.excerpt: Understand sine, cosine, and tangent, apply SOH-CAH-TOA, solve right-angled triangle problems, use standard angles, and learn important trigonometric identities.
chapters.content:
1. Introduction to Trigonometry

Trigonometry is the branch of mathematics that studies the relationship between the angles and sides of triangles.

It is useful in measuring heights, distances, slopes, and angles. It is also applied in engineering, navigation, surveying, construction, and physics.

This chapter begins with right-angled triangles, which contain one angle of exactly 90°.

2. Parts of a Right-Angled Triangle

In a right-angled triangle, the side names depend on the angle being considered.

  • Hypotenuse: The longest side, opposite the right angle.
  • Opposite: The side directly opposite the angle being considered.
  • Adjacent: The side next to the angle being considered, excluding the hypotenuse.

Important: The hypotenuse never changes, but the opposite and adjacent sides depend on which acute angle is being used.

3. The Three Main Trigonometric Ratios

The three basic trigonometric ratios are sine, cosine, and tangent.

Sine: sin θ = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse.

Cosine: cos θ = Adjacent ÷ Hypotenuse.

Tangent: tan θ = Opposite ÷ Adjacent.

These relationships are commonly remembered as SOH-CAH-TOA:

LettersMeaning
SOHSin = Opposite / Hypotenuse
CAHCos = Adjacent / Hypotenuse
TOATan = Opposite / Adjacent

4. Finding a Side Using Trigonometric Ratios

When an angle and one side of a right-angled triangle are known, trigonometric ratios can be used to find another side.

Worked Example 1: Finding the Opposite Side

A right-angled triangle has an angle of 30° and a hypotenuse of 10 cm. Find the side opposite the 30° angle.

Solution:

sin 30° = Opposite / 10.

Since sin 30° = ½:

½ = Opposite / 10.

Opposite = 10 × ½ = 5 cm.

Worked Example 2: Finding the Adjacent Side

A right-angled triangle has an angle of 60° and a hypotenuse of 12 cm. Find the adjacent side.

Solution:

cos 60° = Adjacent / 12.

Since cos 60° = ½:

Adjacent = 12 × ½ = 6 cm.

Worked Example 3: Using Tangent

A right-angled triangle has an angle of 45° and an adjacent side of 8 cm. Find the opposite side.

Solution:

tan 45° = Opposite / 8.

Since tan 45° = 1:

Opposite = 8 × 1 = 8 cm.

5. Finding an Angle Using Trigonometric Ratios

When two sides of a right-angled triangle are known, an angle can be found using inverse trigonometric functions.

These are written as sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, and tan⁻¹. They are also called arcsine, arccosine, and arctangent.

Worked Example

A right-angled triangle has an opposite side of 3 cm and a hypotenuse of 5 cm. Find the acute angle θ.

Solution:

sin θ = 3/5 = 0.6.

θ = sin⁻¹(0.6).

θ ≈ 36.87°.

Use the degree mode on your calculator when the question gives angles in degrees.

6. Standard Trigonometric Angles

Some angles have exact trigonometric values that are important to remember.

Anglesin θcos θtan θ
0°010
30°½√3/21/√3
45°1/√21/√21
60°√3/2½√3
90°10Undefined

Note: tan 90° is undefined because tan θ = sin θ/cos θ and cos 90° = 0. Division by zero is not defined.

7. Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratios

The three reciprocal ratios are cosecant, secant, and cotangent.

cosec θ = 1/sin θ = Hypotenuse/Opposite

sec θ = 1/cos θ = Hypotenuse/Adjacent

cot θ = 1/tan θ = Adjacent/Opposite

8. Important Trigonometric Identities

An identity is an equation that is true for every value in its stated domain.

The three important Pythagorean identities are:

sin² θ + cos² θ = 1

1 + tan² θ = sec² θ

1 + cot² θ = cosec² θ

These identities are useful for simplifying expressions and finding unknown trigonometric values.

Worked Example 1

If sin θ = 3/5 and θ is acute, find cos θ.

Solution:

sin² θ + cos² θ = 1.

(3/5)² + cos² θ = 1.

9/25 + cos² θ = 1.

cos² θ = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25.

cos θ = ±4/5.

Since θ is acute, cosine is positive.

Therefore, cos θ = 4/5.

Worked Example 2

If tan θ = 3/4, find sec² θ.

Solution:

1 + tan² θ = sec² θ.

sec² θ = 1 + (3/4)².

= 1 + 9/16.

= 16/16 + 9/16.

= 25/16.

9. Complementary Angles

Two angles are complementary when their sum is 90°.

The complementary-angle identities are:

sin(90° − θ) = cos θ

cos(90° − θ) = sin θ

tan(90° − θ) = cot θ

For example, sin 30° = cos 60° = ½.

10. Trigonometric Ratios of Angles Greater Than 90°

Trigonometric ratios can also be used for angles greater than 90°. The sign of each ratio depends on the quadrant where the angle lies.

QuadrantPositive Ratios
First quadrant (0°–90°)All six ratios
Second quadrant (90°–180°)Sine and cosecant
Third quadrant (180°–270°)Tangent and cotangent
Fourth quadrant (270°–360°)Cosine and secant

A useful memory guide is ASTC: All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine, moving through the four quadrants from the first to the fourth.

11. Trigonometric Ratios of Negative Angles

For negative angles, the following identities are useful:

sin(−θ) = −sin θ

cos(−θ) = cos θ

tan(−θ) = −tan θ

Sine and tangent are odd functions, while cosine is an even function.

12. Sine Rule

The sine rule is used in any triangle when a side and its opposite angle are related to another side and its opposite angle.

For triangle ABC, with sides a, b, and c opposite angles A, B, and C:

a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C

It can also be written as:

sin A/a = sin B/b = sin C/c

Worked Example

In a triangle, side a = 8 cm, angle A = 30°, and angle B = 45°. Find side b.

Solution:

a/sin A = b/sin B.

8/sin 30° = b/sin 45°.

b = 8 × sin 45° / sin 30°.

= 8 × (√2/2) ÷ (1/2).

= 8√2 cm, approximately 11.31 cm.

13. Cosine Rule

The cosine rule is useful when two sides and the included angle are known, or when all three sides are known and an angle is required.

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A

Similarly:

b² = a² + c² − 2ac cos B

c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C

Worked Example

Two sides of a triangle are 5 cm and 7 cm, and the included angle is 60°. Find the third side.

Solution:

Let the third side be a.

a² = 5² + 7² − 2 × 5 × 7 × cos 60°.

= 25 + 49 − 70 × ½.

= 74 − 35.

= 39.

a = √39 cm, approximately 6.245 cm.

14. Area of a Triangle Using Trigonometry

When two sides and the included angle are known, use:

Area = ½ab sin C

Here, a and b are the two known sides, while C is the angle between them.

Worked Example

Find the area of a triangle whose two sides are 8 cm and 10 cm, with an included angle of 30°.

Solution:

Area = ½ × 8 × 10 × sin 30°.

= 40 × ½.

= 20 cm².

15. Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Do not identify the hypotenuse as the side next to the angle. It is always opposite the right angle.
  • Choose the correct opposite and adjacent sides for the angle being considered.
  • Do not confuse sin⁻¹ with 1/sin. The inverse sine function is different from the reciprocal cosecant.
  • Check whether your calculator is in degree or radian mode.
  • Remember that tan 90° is undefined.
  • When using the sine rule, match each side with its opposite angle.
  • In the cosine rule, the angle used must be the angle between the two sides being multiplied.
  • For sin² θ, square the value of sine; it does not mean sin(2θ).

16. Formula Summary

TopicFormula
Sinesin θ = Opposite/Hypotenuse
Cosinecos θ = Adjacent/Hypotenuse
Tangenttan θ = Opposite/Adjacent
Pythagorean identitysin² θ + cos² θ = 1
Second identity1 + tan² θ = sec² θ
Third identity1 + cot² θ = cosec² θ
Sine rulea/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
Cosine rulea² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A
Triangle area½ab sin C

17. Key Points to Remember

  • SOH-CAH-TOA helps you remember the three basic ratios.
  • The hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle.
  • Learn the standard values of 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90°.
  • Use inverse trigonometric functions to find an angle from a ratio.
  • The sine rule and cosine rule work for general triangles, not only right-angled triangles.
  • Use the sine rule when you have a known side-angle opposite pair. Use the cosine rule when you know two sides and their included angle or all three sides.

chapters.title: Bearings, Elevation, Depression and Trigonometric Applications
chapters.excerpt: Understand three-figure bearings, compass directions, angles of elevation and depression, and how to apply trigonometry to calculate heights, distances, and positions in real-life situations.
chapters.content:
1. Introduction

Trigonometry is useful for solving practical problems involving heights, distances, directions, and angles. In this chapter, we apply trigonometric ratios to navigation, surveying, and everyday situations.

The main topics are bearings, angles of elevation, and angles of depression.

2. Understanding Bearings

A bearing is the direction of one point from another, measured clockwise from the north direction.

Bearings are normally written using three figures, from 000° to 360°.

For example:

  • 000° means due North.
  • 090° means due East.
  • 180° means due South.
  • 270° means due West.

Other examples include 045°, 120°, 225°, and 315°.

Important Rules for Bearings

  • Always measure a bearing clockwise from North.
  • Write bearings using three digits.
  • North is the starting direction, not the direction of the line connecting the two points.
  • A bearing is measured at the starting point.
  • The bearing of B from A is generally different from the bearing of A from B.

3. Compass Directions and Bearings

The four main compass directions are North, East, South, and West. The intermediate directions are North-East, South-East, South-West, and North-West.

DirectionBearing
North000° or 360°
North-East045°
East090°
South-East135°
South180°
South-West225°
West270°
North-West315°

4. Finding the Reverse Bearing

The reverse bearing is the direction from the second point back to the first point.

To find a reverse bearing:

  • If the original bearing is less than 180°, add 180°.
  • If the original bearing is 180° or more, subtract 180°.

Worked Example 1

A town B is on a bearing of 065° from town A. Find the bearing of A from B.

Solution:

Since 065° is less than 180°:

Reverse bearing = 065° + 180°

= 245°.

Worked Example 2

A ship travels on a bearing of 230° from point P to point Q. Find the bearing of P from Q.

Solution:

Since 230° is greater than 180°:

Reverse bearing = 230° − 180°

= 050°.

5. Angles of Elevation

An angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal line through an observer and the line of sight to an object above the observer.

For example, when a person looks upward at the top of a tall building, the angle formed between the horizontal direction and the upward line of sight is the angle of elevation.

Worked Example

A person stands 20 m from a building. The angle of elevation to the top of the building is 45°. Find the height of the building, assuming the person's eye level is at ground level.

Solution:

Using tangent:

tan 45° = Height / 20.

1 = Height / 20.

Height = 20 × 1.

Height = 20 m.

6. Angles of Depression

An angle of depression is the angle between the horizontal line through an observer and the downward line of sight to an object below the observer.

For example, a person standing on a tower and looking down at a car forms an angle of depression between the horizontal direction and the downward line of sight.

Important theorem: The angle of depression from an observer to an object is equal to the angle of elevation from the object to the observer, provided the horizontal lines are parallel.

Worked Example

A person standing on a 30 m high building observes a car on level ground at an angle of depression of 30°. Find the horizontal distance of the car from the foot of the building.

Solution:

The angle of elevation from the car is also 30°.

Using tangent:

tan 30° = 30 / Distance.

1/√3 = 30 / Distance.

Distance = 30√3.

Distance ≈ 51.96 m.

7. Finding Heights Using Trigonometry

When an object is above the ground, a right-angled triangle can often be formed using its height, the horizontal distance, and the line of sight.

Choose the correct trigonometric ratio based on the information given:

  • Use sine when the opposite side and hypotenuse are involved.
  • Use cosine when the adjacent side and hypotenuse are involved.
  • Use tangent when the opposite side and adjacent side are involved.

Worked Example

A ladder 10 m long rests against a vertical wall. It makes an angle of 60° with the ground. Find the height reached by the ladder.

Solution:

The ladder is the hypotenuse, while the height is opposite the 60° angle.

sin 60° = Height / 10.

√3/2 = Height / 10.

Height = 10 × √3/2.

Height = 5√3 m ≈ 8.66 m.

8. Finding Horizontal Distance

When the height and angle are known, tangent is often used to calculate horizontal distance.

Worked Example

A flagpole is 12 m high. The angle of elevation from a point on the ground to its top is 30°. Find the horizontal distance from the point to the foot of the flagpole.

Solution:

tan 30° = 12 / Distance.

1/√3 = 12 / Distance.

Distance = 12√3.

Distance ≈ 20.78 m.

9. Bearings and Right-Angled Triangles

Bearings can be combined with trigonometry to find the distance between two places or the east-west and north-south components of a journey.

When a distance d is measured on a bearing θ clockwise from North:

Northward component = d cos θ

Eastward component = d sin θ

These signed components can be positive or negative depending on the direction of travel.

Worked Example

A boat travels 20 km on a bearing of 060°. Find its eastward and northward components.

Solution:

Eastward component = 20 sin 60°.

= 20 × √3/2 = 10√3 km ≈ 17.32 km.

Northward component = 20 cos 60°.

= 20 × ½ = 10 km.

10. Solving Problems Involving Two Observations

Some problems involve two observation points, two angles of elevation, or two different positions of an observer. In such situations, draw a clear diagram and identify the common height or distance.

Worked Example

Two points on level ground are 20 m apart on the same straight line with the foot of a tower. The nearer point is 10 m from the tower. Find the angle of elevation to the top if the tower is 10 m high.

Solution:

Using the nearer point:

tan θ = 10/10 = 1.

θ = tan⁻¹(1) = 45°.

11. Important Trigonometric Ratios

RatioFormula
Sinesin θ = Opposite/Hypotenuse
Cosinecos θ = Adjacent/Hypotenuse
Tangenttan θ = Opposite/Adjacent

12. Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Do not measure bearings anticlockwise from North.
  • Always write bearings using three digits, such as 045° instead of 45°.
  • Do not confuse a bearing with an ordinary angle measured from the East or horizontal direction.
  • Remember that the angle of depression equals the corresponding angle of elevation.
  • Identify the correct opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse sides before choosing a ratio.
  • Do not confuse the sloping line of sight with the horizontal distance.
  • Check whether the height given is measured from ground level or from an observer's eye level.

13. Key Points to Remember

  • Bearings are measured clockwise from North.
  • Bearings are written using three figures.
  • The reverse bearing differs from the original bearing by 180°.
  • Angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal.
  • Angle of depression is measured downward from the horizontal.
  • Trigonometry helps calculate unknown heights and distances.
  • Always draw a diagram before solving a practical trigonometry problem.

chapters.title: Differentiation and Derivatives
chapters.excerpt: Understand the meaning of differentiation, learn basic differentiation rules, differentiate polynomial and other common functions, and calculate gradients of curves.
chapters.content:
1. Introduction to Differentiation

Differentiation is a branch of calculus used to find the rate at which one quantity changes with respect to another.

It is especially useful for finding the gradient or slope of a curve at a particular point.

For example, differentiation can be used to calculate the speed of a moving object when its distance travelled is expressed as a function of time.

2. Meaning of a Derivative

The derivative of a function measures its instantaneous rate of change.

If y is a function of x, its derivative can be written in several ways:

  • dy/dx
  • f'(x)
  • y'
  • Differentiating y with respect to x

All these notations represent the derivative of the function with respect to x.

3. Differentiation from First Principles

The derivative can be defined using a limit.

f'(x) = lim[h→0] {f(x + h) − f(x)}/h

This is known as differentiation from first principles.

The expression f(x + h) represents the value of the function when x is increased by a small amount h. The limit considers what happens as h approaches zero.

Worked Example

Differentiate f(x) = x² from first principles.

Solution:

f(x) = x².

f(x + h) = (x + h)².

= x² + 2xh + h².

Using the first-principles formula:

f'(x) = lim[h→0] [(x² + 2xh + h²) − x²]/h.

= lim[h→0] (2xh + h²)/h.

= lim[h→0] (2x + h).

= 2x.

4. The Power Rule

The power rule is one of the most important differentiation rules.

If:

y = axⁿ

Then:

dy/dx = anxⁿ⁻¹

In simple terms, multiply the term by its power and reduce the power by one.

Worked Example 1

Differentiate y = x⁵.

Solution:

dy/dx = 5x⁴.

Worked Example 2

Differentiate y = 4x³.

Solution:

dy/dx = 4 × 3x².

dy/dx = 12x².

Worked Example 3

Differentiate y = 7x⁴ − 3x² + 5x − 8.

Solution:

Differentiate each term separately:

dy/dx = 28x³ − 6x + 5.

The derivative of a constant is zero, so the derivative of −8 disappears.

5. Differentiating Constants and Simple Expressions

The derivative of a constant is zero.

If y = c, then dy/dx = 0.

Examples:

  • If y = 9, dy/dx = 0.
  • If y = −12, dy/dx = 0.
  • If y = 5x + 7, dy/dx = 5.

The derivative of x is 1 because x can be written as x¹.

6. Differentiating Fractions and Negative Powers

Fractions and expressions involving roots can often be rewritten using indices before applying the power rule.

For example:

1/x² = x⁻².

√x = x¹⁄².

Therefore:

d(x⁻²)/dx = −2x⁻³

d(√x)/dx = ½x⁻¹⁄² = 1/(2√x)

Worked Example

Differentiate y = 3/x³.

Solution:

Rewrite as y = 3x⁻³.

dy/dx = 3 × (−3)x⁻⁴.

= −9x⁻⁴.

dy/dx = −9/x⁴.

7. Sum and Difference Rules

The derivative of a sum or difference is the sum or difference of the individual derivatives.

d(u + v)/dx = du/dx + dv/dx

d(u − v)/dx = du/dx − dv/dx

For example, if y = 3x² + 4x, then:

dy/dx = 6x + 4.

8. Constant Multiple Rule

If a function is multiplied by a constant, the constant remains outside when differentiating.

d[cu]/dx = c(du/dx)

For example, if y = 8x⁴, then:

dy/dx = 8 × 4x³ = 32x³.

9. Product Rule

The product rule is used when one function is multiplied by another function.

If y = uv, then:

dy/dx = u(dv/dx) + v(du/dx)

Worked Example

Differentiate y = (x² + 1)(x³ + 2).

Solution:

Let u = x² + 1 and v = x³ + 2.

du/dx = 2x and dv/dx = 3x².

Using the product rule:

dy/dx = (x² + 1)(3x²) + (x³ + 2)(2x).

= 3x⁴ + 3x² + 2x⁴ + 4x.

dy/dx = 5x⁴ + 3x² + 4x.

10. Quotient Rule

The quotient rule is used when one function is divided by another function.

If y = u/v, then:

dy/dx = [v(du/dx) − u(dv/dx)]/v²

The denominator must not be zero.

Worked Example

Differentiate y = (x² + 1)/x.

Solution:

Let u = x² + 1 and v = x.

du/dx = 2x and dv/dx = 1.

dy/dx = [x(2x) − (x² + 1)(1)]/x².

= (2x² − x² − 1)/x².

dy/dx = (x² − 1)/x².

11. Chain Rule

The chain rule is used when one function is inside another function. It is also called differentiation of composite functions.

If y = f(g(x)), then:

dy/dx = f'(g(x)) × g'(x)

Worked Example

Differentiate y = (3x + 2)⁴.

Solution:

Let u = 3x + 2.

Then y = u⁴.

dy/du = 4u³ and du/dx = 3.

Using the chain rule:

dy/dx = 4u³ × 3.

= 12(3x + 2)³.

dy/dx = 12(3x + 2)³.

12. Differentiation of Trigonometric Functions

When angles are measured in radians, the basic derivatives are:

d(sin x)/dx = cos x

d(cos x)/dx = −sin x

d(tan x)/dx = sec² x

Other useful derivatives include:

d(cosec x)/dx = −cosec x cot x

d(sec x)/dx = sec x tan x

d(cot x)/dx = −cosec² x

Worked Example

Differentiate y = 4 sin x + 3 cos x.

Solution:

dy/dx = 4 cos x − 3 sin x.

13. Differentiation of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions

For exponential and natural logarithmic functions:

d(eˣ)/dx = eˣ

d(ln x)/dx = 1/x, for x greater than zero.

For a constant base a, where a is positive and not equal to 1:

d(aˣ)/dx = aˣ ln a

d(logₐ x)/dx = 1/(x ln a), for x greater than zero.

14. Gradient of a Curve

The derivative gives the gradient of a curve at a particular point.

If y = f(x), then the gradient at x = a is found by evaluating f'(a).

Worked Example

Find the gradient of the curve y = x² + 3x at x = 2.

Solution:

Differentiate:

dy/dx = 2x + 3.

At x = 2:

Gradient = 2(2) + 3.

= 7.

15. Equation of a Tangent to a Curve

A tangent is a straight line that touches a curve at a particular point and has the same gradient as the curve at that point.

To find its equation:

  1. Differentiate the curve to obtain the gradient function.
  2. Substitute the given x-coordinate to find the gradient.
  3. Find the corresponding y-coordinate using the original equation.
  4. Use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Worked Example

Find the equation of the tangent to y = x² at x = 2.

Solution:

dy/dx = 2x.

At x = 2, m = 4.

Using y = x², the point is (2, 4).

y − 4 = 4(x − 2).

y − 4 = 4x − 8.

y = 4x − 4.

16. Important Differentiation Rules Summary

FunctionDerivative
c0
xⁿnxⁿ⁻¹
cuc du/dx
u + vu' + v'
uvuv' + vu'
u/v(vu' − uv')/v²
f(g(x))f'(g(x))g'(x)
sin xcos x
cos x−sin x
tan xsec² x
eˣeˣ
ln x1/x

17. Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • When using the power rule, reduce the power by one after multiplying by the original power.
  • The derivative of a constant is zero.
  • Do not forget the negative sign when differentiating cos x.
  • Use the product rule when two functions are multiplied, and the quotient rule when one is divided by another.
  • For composite functions, remember to multiply by the derivative of the inner function.
  • Use radians for the standard trigonometric differentiation formulas.
  • When finding the gradient at a point, substitute the x-coordinate into the derivative, not the original function.

18. Key Points to Remember

  • Differentiation measures instantaneous rates of change.
  • The derivative gives the gradient of a curve at a point.
  • The power rule is one of the most frequently used rules.
  • Product, quotient, and chain rules handle more complicated functions.
  • The derivative of a constant is zero.
  • A tangent's gradient at a point is the derivative evaluated at that point.

chapters.title: Applications of Differentiation
chapters.excerpt: Discover how differentiation is used to find stationary points, maximum and minimum values, increasing and decreasing intervals, rates of change, and optimization in practical problems.
chapters.content:
1. Introduction

Differentiation is not only used to find gradients. It also helps us understand how quantities change and how to identify the highest or lowest values of a function.

Important applications include:

  • Finding maximum and minimum values.
  • Identifying stationary points.
  • Determining where a function increases or decreases.
  • Solving optimization problems.
  • Finding velocity and acceleration from displacement.
  • Finding rates of change in practical situations.

2. Stationary Points

A stationary point is a point on a curve where the gradient is zero.

At a stationary point:

dy/dx = 0

Stationary points may be maximum points, minimum points, or stationary points of inflection.

Worked Example

Find the stationary point of y = x² − 6x + 5.

Solution:

Differentiate:

dy/dx = 2x − 6.

At a stationary point, dy/dx = 0.

2x − 6 = 0.

2x = 6.

x = 3.

Substitute x = 3 into the original function:

y = 3² − 6(3) + 5.

= 9 − 18 + 5.

= −4.

The stationary point is (3, −4).

3. Maximum and Minimum Points

A maximum point is a point where a function reaches a local high value. A minimum point is a point where it reaches a local low value.

For a smooth curve, stationary points are usually identified by setting the first derivative equal to zero. The second derivative can then help classify the point.

4. The Second Derivative Test

The second derivative is obtained by differentiating the first derivative again.

First derivative: dy/dx

Second derivative: d²y/dx²

At a stationary point:

  • If d²y/dx² is positive, the point is a local minimum.
  • If d²y/dx² is negative, the point is a local maximum.
  • If d²y/dx² is zero, the test is inconclusive. Another method is required.

Worked Example 1: Minimum Point

Find and classify the stationary point of y = x² − 4x + 7.

Solution:

First derivative:

dy/dx = 2x − 4.

Set equal to zero:

2x − 4 = 0.

x = 2.

Substitute into the original function:

y = 2² − 4(2) + 7 = 4 − 8 + 7 = 3.

Stationary point = (2, 3).

Second derivative:

d²y/dx² = 2.

Since 2 is positive, the point is a minimum.

Worked Example 2: Maximum Point

Find and classify the stationary point of y = −x² + 6x − 5.

Solution:

First derivative:

dy/dx = −2x + 6.

Set equal to zero:

−2x + 6 = 0.

x = 3.

Substitute into the original function:

y = −3² + 6(3) − 5.

= −9 + 18 − 5.

= 4.

Stationary point = (3, 4).

Second derivative:

d²y/dx² = −2.

Since −2 is negative, the point is a maximum.

5. Increasing and Decreasing Functions

A function is increasing when its value rises as x increases. It is decreasing when its value falls as x increases.

The first derivative helps identify these intervals:

  • If dy/dx is positive, the function is increasing.
  • If dy/dx is negative, the function is decreasing.
  • If dy/dx is zero, the gradient is horizontal at that point.

Worked Example

Determine where y = x² − 4x + 1 is increasing and decreasing.

Solution:

dy/dx = 2x − 4.

For an increasing function:

2x − 4 > 0.

x > 2.

For a decreasing function:

2x − 4 < 0.

x < 2.

Therefore, the function decreases when x < 2 and increases when x > 2. It has a minimum at x = 2.

6. Optimization Problems

Optimization means finding the best possible value of a quantity, such as the greatest area, smallest cost, maximum profit, or minimum distance.

Differentiation can be used to find the maximum or minimum value when the quantity is expressed as a function.

Worked Example: Maximum Area

A rectangle has a fixed perimeter of 40 cm. Find the dimensions that give the maximum area.

Solution:

Let the length be x cm and the width be y cm.

Perimeter = 2x + 2y = 40.

x + y = 20.

Therefore, y = 20 − x.

Area A = xy.

A = x(20 − x).

A = 20x − x².

Differentiate:

dA/dx = 20 − 2x.

For a stationary value:

20 − 2x = 0.

x = 10.

Then y = 20 − 10 = 10.

Second derivative:

d²A/dx² = −2.

Since it is negative, the area is maximum.

Maximum area = 10 × 10 = 100 cm².

7. Rates of Change

Differentiation can be used to determine how quickly one quantity changes with respect to another.

For example, if distance s is a function of time t, then:

Velocity v = ds/dt

Velocity measures the rate of change of displacement with respect to time.

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity:

Acceleration a = dv/dt = d²s/dt²

Worked Example

The displacement of a moving object is given by s = t³ − 6t² + 9t, where s is in metres and t is in seconds. Find its velocity and acceleration at t = 2 seconds.

Solution:

Velocity:

v = ds/dt = 3t² − 12t + 9.

At t = 2:

v = 3(2²) − 12(2) + 9.

= 12 − 24 + 9.

= −3 m/s.

Acceleration:

a = dv/dt = 6t − 12.

At t = 2:

a = 6(2) − 12 = 0 m/s².

8. Marginal Cost and Marginal Revenue

In economics, differentiation can be used to calculate marginal quantities.

Marginal cost is the rate of change of total cost with respect to the number of units produced.

Marginal revenue is the rate of change of total revenue with respect to the number of units sold.

If C(x) is total cost and R(x) is total revenue:

Marginal cost = dC/dx

Marginal revenue = dR/dx

Worked Example

The total cost of producing x items is C(x) = 2x² + 5x + 100. Find the marginal cost function and its value when x = 10.

Solution:

Marginal cost = dC/dx.

= 4x + 5.

At x = 10:

Marginal cost = 4(10) + 5.

= 45.

9. Differentiation and Graphs

The derivative helps us understand the shape of a curve.

  • A positive derivative indicates an upward slope.
  • A negative derivative indicates a downward slope.
  • A zero derivative indicates a horizontal tangent.
  • A change from positive to negative gradient indicates a local maximum.
  • A change from negative to positive gradient indicates a local minimum.

10. Points of Inflection

A point of inflection is a point where a curve changes its concavity, from bending upwards to bending downwards or the reverse.

The second derivative may be zero at a point of inflection, but a zero second derivative alone does not prove that the point is an inflection point. The concavity must actually change across the point.

Worked Example

Consider y = x³. Find the point where the second derivative is zero and identify its nature.

Solution:

First derivative:

dy/dx = 3x².

Second derivative:

d²y/dx² = 6x.

Set the second derivative equal to zero:

6x = 0, so x = 0.

At x = 0, y = 0.

The second derivative changes from negative when x < 0 to positive when x > 0. Therefore, (0, 0) is a point of inflection. It is a stationary point of inflection because the first derivative is also zero there.

11. Steps for Solving Optimization Problems

  1. Identify the quantity that must be maximized or minimized.
  2. Express it as a function of one variable using the given conditions.
  3. Differentiate the function.
  4. Set the first derivative equal to zero to find stationary points.
  5. Use the second derivative test or another suitable method to classify the stationary point.
  6. Substitute the value into the original function to find the required maximum or minimum.
  7. Check that the result makes sense in the context of the problem.

12. Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Do not assume every stationary point is a maximum or minimum.
  • Always calculate the second derivative correctly before applying the second derivative test.
  • Remember that a zero second derivative gives an inconclusive test unless further analysis is done.
  • In optimization problems, form the correct function before differentiating.
  • Do not confuse velocity with acceleration. Velocity is the first derivative of displacement; acceleration is the second derivative.
  • Use the original function to calculate the actual maximum or minimum value.

13. Key Points to Remember

  • Stationary points occur where the first derivative is zero.
  • A positive second derivative at a stationary point indicates a local minimum.
  • A negative second derivative at a stationary point indicates a local maximum.
  • The first derivative determines where a function increases or decreases.
  • Velocity is the derivative of displacement with respect to time.
  • Acceleration is the derivative of velocity with respect to time.
  • Differentiation is useful for maximizing profit, area, and other quantities or minimizing cost and distance.

chapters.title: Integration and Applications
chapters.excerpt: Learn integration as the reverse of differentiation, apply basic integration rules, evaluate definite and indefinite integrals, and calculate areas under curves.
chapters.content:
1. Introduction to Integration

Integration is a branch of calculus used to find antiderivatives and accumulated quantities. It is closely related to differentiation.

While differentiation measures rates of change, integration can be used to recover a function from its derivative or calculate quantities such as areas under curves.

Integration is often described as the reverse process of differentiation.

2. Meaning of an Integral

The symbol for integration is ∫, called the integral sign.

If dy/dx = f(x), then:

y = ∫f(x) dx

The expression dx indicates that integration is being carried out with respect to x.

3. Indefinite Integration

An indefinite integral does not have specified upper and lower limits. Its answer includes a constant called the constant of integration, represented by C.

For example:

∫2x dx = x² + C

This is because differentiating x² + C gives 2x.

Always remember to include + C when evaluating an indefinite integral.

4. The Power Rule of Integration

The basic power rule is:

∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C

provided n is not equal to −1.

In simple terms:

  1. Add 1 to the power.
  2. Divide the term by the new power.
  3. Add the constant of integration C.

Worked Example 1

Evaluate ∫x³ dx.

Solution:

Add 1 to the power: 3 + 1 = 4.

Divide by the new power:

∫x³ dx = x⁴/4 + C.

Worked Example 2

Evaluate ∫5x² dx.

Solution:

= 5 × x³/3 + C.

= 5x³/3 + C.

5. Integration of Constants

The integral of a constant k with respect to x is:

∫k dx = kx + C

Worked Example

Evaluate ∫7 dx.

Solution:

∫7 dx = 7x + C.

6. Integration of Sums and Differences

The integral of a sum or difference is the sum or difference of the individual integrals.

∫(u + v) dx = ∫u dx + ∫v dx

∫(u − v) dx = ∫u dx − ∫v dx

Worked Example

Evaluate ∫(4x³ + 6x − 5) dx.

Solution:

= 4∫x³ dx + 6∫x dx − 5∫1 dx.

= 4(x⁴/4) + 6(x²/2) − 5x + C.

= x⁴ + 3x² − 5x + C.

7. Integration of Negative and Fractional Powers

Expressions involving fractions and roots can be rewritten using indices before integration.

For example:

1/x² = x⁻².

√x = x¹⁄².

The power rule can then be applied, provided the power is not −1.

Worked Example 1

Evaluate ∫x⁻² dx.

Solution:

Increase the power by 1:

−2 + 1 = −1.

Divide by −1:

∫x⁻² dx = x⁻¹/−1 + C.

= −1/x + C.

Worked Example 2

Evaluate ∫√x dx.

Solution:

Rewrite √x as x¹⁄².

∫x¹⁄² dx = x³⁄²/(3/2) + C.

= ⅔x³⁄² + C.

8. Integration of 1/x

The power rule does not apply when the power is −1 because it would require division by zero.

Instead:

∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + C

Here, ln means natural logarithm and x must not be zero.

9. Integration of Exponential Functions

Some useful exponential integrals are:

∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C

For a constant a that is positive and not equal to 1:

∫aˣ dx = aˣ/ln a + C

10. Integration of Trigonometric Functions

Some important trigonometric integrals are:

∫sin x dx = −cos x + C

∫cos x dx = sin x + C

∫sec² x dx = tan x + C

∫cosec² x dx = −cot x + C

∫sec x tan x dx = sec x + C

∫cosec x cot x dx = −cosec x + C

These standard formulas assume angles are measured in radians.

11. Integration by Substitution

Integration by substitution is useful when an expression contains a function and its derivative, or a constant multiple of its derivative.

The method involves replacing part of the expression with a new variable.

Worked Example

Evaluate ∫2x(x² + 1)³ dx.

Solution:

Let u = x² + 1.

Then du/dx = 2x, so du = 2x dx.

The integral becomes:

∫u³ du.

= u⁴/4 + C.

Substitute u = x² + 1:

Answer = (x² + 1)⁴/4 + C.

12. Definite Integration

A definite integral has an upper limit and a lower limit.

It is written as:

∫ from a to b f(x) dx

To evaluate it:

  1. Find the indefinite integral.
  2. Substitute the upper limit b.
  3. Substitute the lower limit a.
  4. Subtract the lower result from the upper result.

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F'(x) = f(x).

The constant of integration is not included in the final evaluation of a definite integral because it cancels out.

Worked Example

Evaluate ∫ from 1 to 3 of 2x dx.

Solution:

First integrate:

∫2x dx = x².

Apply the limits:

[x²] from 1 to 3.

= 3² − 1².

= 9 − 1.

= 8.

13. Area Under a Curve

Definite integration can be used to calculate the signed area between a curve and the x-axis over a specified interval.

If a curve y = f(x) lies above the x-axis between x = a and x = b, then:

Area = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx

If part of the curve lies below the x-axis, the definite integral gives signed area. To find the total geometric area, split the interval at the x-intercepts and add the positive magnitudes of the separate areas.

Worked Example 1

Find the area under the curve y = 2x between x = 0 and x = 3.

Solution:

Area = ∫ from 0 to 3 of 2x dx.

= [x²] from 0 to 3.

= 3² − 0².

= 9 square units.

Worked Example 2: Curve Below the Axis

Find the total geometric area between y = x − 2 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 4.

Solution:

The curve crosses the x-axis when x − 2 = 0, so x = 2.

From x = 0 to x = 2, the curve is below the x-axis. Its signed integral is:

∫₀²(x − 2) dx = [x²/2 − 2x]₀².

= (2 − 4) − 0 = −2.

The geometric area in this section is 2 square units.

From x = 2 to x = 4:

∫₂⁴(x − 2) dx = [x²/2 − 2x]₂⁴.

= (8 − 8) − (2 − 4).

= 2 square units.

Total geometric area = 2 + 2 = 4 square units.

14. Finding a Function from Its Derivative

Integration can be used to find an original function when its derivative is known.

Worked Example

If dy/dx = 6x² + 4x and y = 5 when x = 1, find y.

Solution:

Integrate:

y = ∫(6x² + 4x) dx.

y = 2x³ + 2x² + C.

Use y = 5 when x = 1:

5 = 2(1)³ + 2(1)² + C.

5 = 2 + 2 + C.

C = 1.

Therefore:

y = 2x³ + 2x² + 1.

15. Integration Formula Summary

FunctionIntegral
xⁿ, n ≠ −1xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C
kkx + C
1/xln|x| + C
eˣeˣ + C
sin x−cos x + C
cos xsin x + C
sec² xtan x + C
cosec² x−cot x + C
sec x tan xsec x + C
cosec x cot x−cosec x + C

16. Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Do not forget the constant of integration C in indefinite integrals.
  • When applying the power rule, increase the power by one and divide by the new power.
  • Do not apply the ordinary power rule to 1/x. Its integral is ln|x| + C.
  • For a definite integral, subtract the lower-limit result from the upper-limit result.
  • Do not include C in the final numerical value of a definite integral.
  • Remember that a definite integral gives signed area, not always total geometric area.
  • Check the limits carefully before substituting them.

17. Key Points to Remember

  • Integration is closely related to differentiation.
  • Indefinite integrals include the constant C.
  • Definite integrals have upper and lower limits.
  • The power rule is the main basic integration rule.
  • Integration can recover a function from its derivative.
  • Definite integration can calculate signed area under a curve.

chapters.title: Statistics and Data Presentation
